Our research focuses on a software development project, RealTimePy, which aims to create a robust, real-time compatible Python distribution for a robotic swarm testbed. This testbed is built using 12 Legos EV3 robots, which are designed to operate in real-time and manage their movement via wireless commands via the EV3's transreceivers. To ensure accurate data processing, the RealTimePy distribution incorporates the Dynamic Pymentors, a real-time loop-safe driver for the motors, and the Kalman filter, a predictive algorithm for filter data and responsible for estimating robot position, velocity, and acceleration. By integrating a reliable Python environment, the RealTimePy distribution significantly enhances the development of robotic swarm algorithms. Our study evaluates the development and implementation of real-time compatible Python code by assessing its performance, safety, and system integration. This system is further showcased through a safety-critical application, where robots operate in close proximity (within 0.1 meters) to each other, simultaneously reading sonar sensors, moving at 100 mm/second, and maintaining a distance of 0.8 seconds, without deadlocks, and a maximum deviation in real-time execution under 100 microseconds.

Our work focuses on an unsupervised pre-training technique for estimating 3D scene geometry from single color images. The underlying hypothesis is that calculating scene geometry can provide broader insights into visual properties and environments than traditional image classification. To demonstrate this, a novel neural network architecture, called SegDepth, has been designed for semi-supervised learning of 3D scenes and depth maps using an appearance-based model. By utilizing an appearance-based approach, SegDepth can generate high-quality depth estimates from single color images, outperforming other methods in multiple benchmarks, such as the KITTI dataset. Furthermore, SegDepth's ability to use appearance features enables it to achieve superior results on the KITTI dataset when compared to other methods that rely on edge maps, as well as on the Cityscapes dataset for semi-supervised semantic segmentation.

A log-harmonic function u can be alternatively represented as the real part of a function f, which belongs to the subclass S of analytic functions defined within the unit disk. The article presents specific conditions under which the function u has a positive value at the center of the disk and derives expressions for u's zero set in terms of the coefficients of the function f, also determining the location of the first zero s0 of u.

Kendall's tau is a widely recognized measure for rank correlation which has a computational complexity of O(n^2) in an n-element dataset. We've developed a serendipitous discovery enabling a more efficient computation with a complexity of O(n) by utilizing tree data structure, which can also be applied to tau's generalized variants with complex datasets, resulting in a complexity of O(m) and facilitating computations on spatial auto-regression models. Furthermore, this improvement allows for a substantial gain in computation speed, as exemplified by its application in a spatial analysis project with 53,000 data points. We've also released our innovative algorithm under an open-source license, facilitating its sharing among programmers.

This work introduces a combined approach of Federated Learning and Local Differential Privacy, leveraging the decentralized learning capabilities of FL to maintain user privacy and the confidentiality guarantees of LDP to limit information leakage during the learning process. We develop a new algorithm that integrates both techniques and provides a comprehensive privacy definition that can be refined to specific levels of privacy by adjusting a key privacy parameter. We also establish a proof of privacy for this algorithm, demonstrating the relationship between the choice of this parameter and the level of privacy achieved. Through numerical analysis, we evaluate the trade-off between computation accuracy, communication overhead, and privacy levels, demonstrating the effectiveness of our combined approach.

Our work builds upon previous research evaluating the feasibility of performing multi-parameter topological data analysis, where we focus on analyzing how the number of critical points in a Morse function changes across related spaces. This is applicable to any topological space equipped with a probability distribution that comes from a Borel space. Our approach utilizes the concept of Euler characteristic, which is a more accessible alternative than studying the Morse chain homology of a probability distribution. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that determining the Euler characteristic for a probability distribution with a compact support is a $\mathcal{B}^1$-complete problem, which means it can be computationally solved for any given distribution but may be impractical otherwise. Additionally, we demonstrate that this problem is $\mathcal{NP}$-hard if we consider it under specific constraints. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our problem and those associated with Morse chain homology and other topological invariants.

In a population model including a nonlinear effect related to the carrying capacity, we explore how changes in a parameter trigger various types of bifurcations. These bifurcations, particularly saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations, affect the population's stability and types of oscillations present. We identify and analyze five distinct types of bifurcations that occur in this model, characterized by patterns such as periodic and chaotic behavior, which are validated through numerical examples. Additionally, we examine how these patterns persist within a related family of population models featuring logistic nonlinearities.

The pivot algorithms developed by Klee-Minty for linear programming problems initially focused on vertices. Over time, improvements were made using a balance of vertex and facet approach. Although the implementation of this combined method proved complicated due to the necessity of extensive data structures, the proposed rotation algorithm reduced complexity but still handled vertices and facets separately. A newly introduced facet pivot method aims to enhance efficiency and integrate the facet approach in a more straightforward way, solely relying on a heap for storage. A detailed explanation of this algorithm will be provided, along with a new and more efficient cutter in three-dimensional space. Analysis revealed the time complexity of phase 1 is capped at O(n log(n) l), with phase 2 capped at O(l).

Our findings are inspired by a method for analyzing a graded ring by its location within a graded partial order. This method is an extension of Quillen--Suslin theory for graded rings. It encompasses two primary components, one of which applies to torsion-free graded partial orders and is demonstrated using a simplified example, while the other is tailored to torsion-sensitive partial orders and is illustrated through a more complex demonstration. It's noteworthy that this theory's framework has also enabled us to obtain a generalization of the Whitehead lemma for graded rings.

The top quark is one of the four fundamental elementary particles in the Standard Model of particle physics. Due to its short lifetime, the top quark can be considered as having a narrow width in most theoretical studies. However, this approximation might not hold in more complex top quark studies where detailed simulations are necessary for accurate measurements. This paper examines two instances where the narrow width assumption does not apply, which involve differential distributions and top quark pair resonance searches.

Recent advances in vision transformer architectures have led to their widespread application in various computer vision tasks. This study evaluates the performance of vision transformer models as backbones for facial recognition system spoofing detection and explores the benefits of adapting them from spoofing-specific vision models through transfer learning. The novel approach employs fine-tuning with a novel spatio-temporal spoofing feature generation module, aiming to enhance the capture of anti-spoofing features. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over conventional backbones and show promise for real-world practical application.

A pivotal aspect of autonomous vehicles is their ability to navigate uncertainty, which is illustrated through a training method utilizing simulated environments and real-world driving conditions in conjunction with an inertial measurement unit (IMU). By integrating the IMU sensor readings into the model, the system is able to adapt to scenarios where the state is partially observable, such as autonomous driving on winding roads. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are employed to track vehicle motion during testing on a road with IMU data collected at high speeds. Furthermore, the system is trained across diverse simulated environments and is able to transfer skills to a new test track, demonstrating its ability to estimate vehicle pose with low error and successfully executing local control laws for autonomous driving. Local tracking performance is comparable to that of motion planning methods, yet the system requires no prior knowledge of the environment or IMU calibration, and successfully transfers to new scenarios with only a quarter of the original training data required. By using this method in a real-world drone racing benchmark, the system successfully executed local control laws, showcasing its ability to execute challenging navigation tasks throughout the event. Details of the training environments, the system architecture, the event details, the evaluation metrics, the source code, and the event footage can be found online at the provided address.

Evolutionary algorithms have been successfully applied in parallel computing environments in the past. This research focuses on enhancing the parent selection method within parallel evolutionary algorithms. The objective is to accelerate the search progress by identifying and prioritizing non-domination level prolific areas in the population. An approximate Gaussian mixture model is employed to represent the population distribution, and an adapted cluster crisis indicator triggers the population reassignment after the evacuation of crisis zones. The novel method is validated through comprehensive testbeds, demonstrating notable improvements in convergence accuracy without incurring additional computational costs. Additionally, the algorithm's sensitivity is evaluated with various population sizes and parallelization levels.

The potential of astrometric microlensing to identify the properties of a lensing star is explored, specifically the method's limitations in determining the mass of the lensing star, and how this impacts the quest for exoplanets. Based on future human vision capabilities, this analytical study assumes typical conditions and variations for the observations, and evaluates how accurately the characteristics of the lensing star can be estimated from the microlensing phenomenon. This includes a maximum angular distance, varying distances, and diverse masses of the lensing stars, considering both conventional and unconventional observations. The analysis also involves a second-order statistical model that assesses the accuracy of the estimated parameters based on their mean squared errors. This analytical study further compares the results with simulated software models under specific observation conditions using the PLATO space telescope, and itco-adds an empirical analysis which examines approximately 500 microlensing events created with a purpose-built simulator, and compares the obtained results with the ones produced by PLATO simulations.

We explore how weak, optical potentials affect the non-Markovian behavior, specifically how they influence the system's dynamics despite being weak. Discovering an "ideal" driving condition where system and flux measurements are completely independent, we analyze the impact of this condition on the system's response and demonstrate its relation to a certain kind of superposition of states. Utilizing an atom in a cavity as our model, we show an optimal driving frequency below which the influence of the environment leads to intricate time-dependent effects in the system's behavior, even when looking at long-term behavior. These results remain valid for a broad class of systems with this "ideal" driving characteristic, including those of different dimensions and design.

The CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ alloys were examined via muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) as a function of temperature and composition, spanning the same pressure range where ferromagnetic clusters are present in CePd$_5$. This study found pressure-induced ferromagnetic clusters within CePd$_5$ for the first time, with a materials freezing temperature that declined with increasing Rh content and a larger average cluster size at higher pressures. Additionally, Rh's presence reduced the cluster size within the paramagnetic regime. There is a striking similarity in pressure-related ferromagnetic cluster behaviors within CePd$_5$ and CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ alloys, suggesting that the role of Rh in CePd$_5$ is not substantial in creating or eliminating ferromagnetic clusters under pressure.

Our observation of cysteine and other related isotopologs in G176.51+00.20 found them with higher levels of Feh, averaging around 1.5-2.5%, compared to frakC, ranging between 0.2-1%. This, along with the 13C/12C ratio in (13C)CysS, frakC, and (14C)CysS being around 20-22, implies that C-rich material is present but has not yet mixed with the primarily H2O-rich gas in this region, based on the 14N/14N ratio. The 14N/14N ratio in (14C)CysS, (15N)CysS and HINSA yields an average of around 0.22, which matches the ratio in the source's carbon-rich material. This suggests that the material has not yet combined with the gas in the region, based on the measured ratios. The material's chemical composition in G176.51+20.0 was studied through modeling, which provided further insights into the observed species. The model, based on a star-forming region, includes sulfur, carbon, and nitrogen in the gas, as well as ammonia and CS radicals, cysteine and its isotopologs, water, UCAM, and CO. The concept of surivor sets for the intermediate beta transformation above a certain threshold has been introduced in the context of number theory for non-integer bases. These sets encompass all numbers with approximations, close to a specific range, in the given base. This idea is closely linked to badly approximable numbers, a topic of central importance in number theory. The goal of this research is to examine the properties of these survivor sets through the lens of fractal geometry. It is demonstrated that above a certain threshold, these survivor sets possess a self-similar, multi-fractal nature, characterized by a specific spectrum of fractal dimensions. This Inset research further reveals a more detailed, semi-conjugate relationship between the maps generated in this survivor set, a finding that may be adapted to other similar transformations outside the beta transformation framework.

LHCb examined potential direct CP violation in the $B^0_s\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- $ process using 3.0~$\text{fb}^{-1}$ of data collected during Run 1 of the LHC. To investigate this further, the difference in the decay rates of $B^0_s\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- $ and $B^0_{(s)}\to J/\psi K^+\pi^- $ was calculated, where the latter is known to be in favor of CP. To isolate the $J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- $ decay, an iterative fit was performed on the $m^{2}_{J/\psi K^+ \pi^-}$ distribution to eliminate contributions from other channels, primarily $B^0_s\to J/\psi K^{*0} $ and $B^0_{s}\to \phi K^{*0} $. As a result, time-dependent yields for the favored $B^0_s\to J/\psi K^{*0} $ decay were obtained and used to refine the selection criteria, leading to an optimal distinction between the $B^0_s\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- $ and other visible decays. Furthermore, instrumental asymmetries were corrected using data from $B^0_{(s)}\to J/\psi K^{(*)}K^{(*)} $ decays

This paper presents an image classification approach, called ADAdaptor, that combines unsupervised domain adaptation and knowledge distillation to achieve better image classification results. Specifically, ADAdaptor uses two domain adaptation methods, DomainShift-Net and Mutual-Exclusion-Net, to minimize the domain gap, with the former addressing domain shift issues using self-translation modules and the latter relying on a classifier's complementary capabilities. Furthermore, ADAdaptor employs two knowledge distillation models, Large-To-Small Knowledge Distillation and Small-To-Large Knowledge Distillation, to leverage the strengths of both. Experimental evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR10-SVHN, CIFAR10-USTLearner, STL10-CIFAR10, CIFAR100-Student, and STL10-CIFAR100, demonstrate that ADAdaptor consistently outperforms other methods by a significant margin, with improvements ranging from 1.0% to 9.2%. The code for ADAdaptor is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/universe252/ADAdaptor.

We establish precise bounds in terms of $\lambda_n$ for the number of $(q^n-1)$-type arcs on $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, where $n$ is greater than or equal to $2$, by leveraging the values of $\lambda_n$, as well as the sizes and purposes of specific subsets in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$. These precise bounds enable us to derive lower and upper limits for the number of arcs with varying sizes in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, where the size varies from a minority of $\mathbb{F}_q$ elements to the majority. Furthermore, we identify the Breaking Union of Arcs (BUA) construction that produces the upper bounds, while developing a complementary arc construction based on subspaces, which generates the lower bounds. The defined bounds account for the largest and smallest quantities of $(q^n-1)$-type arcs in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, where the size is $q^n-1$, as well as the largest and smallest quantities of arcs with any size in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, when the size varies.

We establish a maximum number, denoted by ${\cal T}_n$, for the count of equilateral triangles within a triangular grid of side length $n$, where each triangle contains four distinct elements selected from a set of $n$. By constructing two distinct scenarios, we demonstrate two different methods for finding ${\cal T}_n$, one of which involves combinatorial logic and the other, which involves probabilistic reasoning. Both methods converge on the same outcome: the value of ${\cal T}_n$ is shown to be $\frac{1}{6} \binom{n \choose 4} \left(3n^2-2n^3+3n^2\right)$. This outcome is further simplified to the expression $\frac{1}{36} \binom{n+3}{7} \binom{n}{3}$ after applying the Baseball Card Lemma. The process of finding this expression is said to be "yawn-inducing" in the context of the author's blog. A distinct approach to this problem, which is outlined in the author's blog post, is inspired by a question posed by Alexei Brodsky regarding the maximum number of equilateral triangles that can be formed within an $n \times n$ grid of squares.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are now widely used for efficient processing of complex graph structures and functions. As the scale and complexity of GNN models continue to grow, there is an increasing need for transparent explanations of their decision-making processes. We've created PGExplainer, a framework for generating actionable, interpretable explanations of GNN models by effectively utilizing the graph structure. Unlike existing methods, which combine natural language generation with graph construction, PGExplainer simultaneously builds upon and interprets the given graph features. This innovative framework generates natural language explanations tailored to the underlying graph by accurately introducing new edges and, when necessary, creating subgraphs that provide clear, descriptive explanations of key areas of the model. Our experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets have demonstrated PGExplainer to be significantly more efficient, accurate, and effective than competing methods.

We investigate the magnetic field structure within the galaxy cluster XCJ0232.2-4420 using data from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) and the Chandra X-ray telescope. Our study employs two types of analysis: core-first and found-outside. The core-first method is utilized for diffuse emission, whereas the found-outside method is used for point-like sources. Notably, our LOFAR observations reveal a substructure in the radio image, categorized as a South-West extension. Our analysis suggests a substructure in the 2-10 keV X-ray image, exhibiting a South-East extension. Utilizing the found-outside method, our Chandra X-ray data reveal a substructure in the 15-40 keV X-ray range, featuring a South-East extension. Our study applies the Equilibrium Temperature Model to evaluate radiosity magnetic field and perturbative magnetic field. Consequently, our results yield a 360 degree magnetic field in the South-West extension of 0.25 uG and 0.19 uG respectively. Our study implies that our LOFAR observations may be one of the initial evidence for radio halo formation through diffuse emission diffusion. Our found-outide method analysis reveals a 90 degree magnetic field in the South-East extension of 0.21 uG and suggests a possible source at the South-West extension magnetic field origin.

Recent studies have shown that Large-Scale Critical Learning with Unsupervised Retraining (LUCIR) can significantly boost the accuracy of deep networks when trained with vast amounts of unlabeled data. However, this method involves a labor-intensive mapping step and relies on a sensitive hyperparameter, which affects the quality of the unsupervised model. To address these issues, we present a new approach called Label-Masking Unit (LMU). This innovative component integrates a memory mechanism, which dynamically selects and stores valuable information from a large unlabeled dataset during the training process. By effectively managing the memory, LMU enables LUCIR to achieve improved performance with significantly reduced memory requirements. Our experiments on multiple networks and datasets demonstrate that LMU significantly accelerates training speeds and enhances model robustness, with no need for manual tuning or a manual map creation step. Notably, LMU significantly surpasses LUCIR in both performance and training efficiency on the ImageNet dataset.

A new particle discovery may not be the sole outcome of existing CERN programs as the matter-antimatter asymmetry puzzle and the lack of explanation for dark matter in the universe are more pressing issues at the moment. These challenges are tied to a fundamental question about how matter excess emerged in the early universe during a phase of rapid energy loss known as the electroweak phase transition. Proposed new physics in this era aims to resolve these problems by introducing the Beyond Standard Model (BSM) components that may lead to a more comprehensive understanding under two possible scenarios: one that involves a strong new force capable of simulating a hot or warm phase transition, or a more subtle scenario where a quieter phase transition occurs that can create the universe's baryon excess at a later stage. We discuss how both ideas utilize high-energy X-ray observations from space, which can directly observe signs of new physics capable of influencing this phase transition, as well as how both ideas can be refined by testing their consistency with such data.

Within our European Union, there's a diverse range of languages, yet it's unclear whether languages are distinct or if they're part of a larger, interconnected family. We explored how migration might impact language development, considering that shared cultural ties and geographical proximity play pivotal roles. We developed a simple agent-based model, modeling individuals who speak unique languages and engage in migrations driven by demographic factors. Each speaker interacts with others from nearby regions and attempts to imitate the speaker's language. Our findings indicate that the influence of migration on language development is determined by two key variables: the migration interval and the size of the surrounding area, influencing how speakers encounter one another and adopt new languages. Interestingly, regions with lower levels of migration tend to have diverse languages, whereas those with very high or low migration rates converge towards a fewer number of languages. This research can be applied to understanding linguistic patterns across Europe, highlighting how shared cultural and geographical factors continue to shape our diverse linguistic landscape.

Researchers are increasingly exploring the potential of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in solving inverse problems, particularly in the field of material inference. This novel method uses the combination of SGD and momentum for improving the convergence rate in PINNs. However, there is a lack of understanding about how this approach affects the spectral bias in PINNs. To address this gap, our study investigates how SGDMM influences spectral bias when solving material inference problems. We discovered that SGDMM leads to an uneven spectrum where a few dominant eigenfunctions are overestimated and the rest are underestimated. This phenomenon causes a phase where the eigenfunctions supporting the largest deviations are primarily learned. Consequently, our findings suggest that the spectrum should be monitored during the training process of PINNs. Additionally, our study demonstrates that PINNs initially converge towards the true spectrum before settling into an uneven distribution. Utilizing this understanding, our method employs a spectral regularization technique that forces the learned spectrum to align with the actual one, utilizing the initial model as a reference. When applied and tested on a range of materials, our method consistently produces more accurate inference results. Notably, our technique serves as an efficient diagnostic tool for diagnosing PINN models, while also offering room for potential improvements in the field of material inference and beyond.

We investigate the wave system $u_{tt}-\alpha(x)\frac{u_t^2}{1+\alpha(x)u_t}u=0$ in a 2D domain $\Omega$. Let $u=u(x,y)$ be a smooth function, and we consider non-negative, continuous, and symmetric $\alpha$ in $\Omega$. Due to symmetries in $x$ and $y$, as well as non-positivity of $\alpha$, we establish uniform bounds for solutions, independent of the solution's dependence on time. Using the non-smoothness of $\alpha$, we show that it causes the solution's energy to decay at a uniform rate as time progresses. As a result, we establish a global attractor in the space of bounded functions in $\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^2$. We conclude by examining the existence of a single-valued global attractor, rather than a possible set-valued one, in the case where $\alpha$ is only non-negative, rather than non-negative.

Reinforcement learning in symbolic domains holds great potential for solving complex problems, but interpreting the actions taken by a learned policy remains challenging due to the domain's symbolic nature. Despite the significant success of deep reinforcement learning in addressing state and action representation issues, deep methods are not directly applicable to symbolic domains. In this paper, we develop a novel reinforcement learning framework specifically designed for symbolic domains. By integrating deep reinforcement learning with symbolic techniques, our framework increases the representability of states and actions, thereby enhancing the transparency of the learned policy. We achieve this through a three-pronged approach that utilizes a neural network to map state functions to embedded vectors, maps actions to embedded vectors based on the current state vector, and employs a transformer architecture to combine the views of states from multiple timestamps. We evaluate our framework in the context of two symbolic reinforcement learning tasks - Gridworld and the Bus Driver problem. The results demonstrate that our framework is capable of efficiently learning effective policies and making state representations and action utilities understandable to humans.

This study presents a cutting-edge design for an optical device, known as an interresonator coupling scheme, where a chiral coupling mechanism confers the capability of all-optical directionality and non-reciprocity on both forward- and backward-propagating waves using orthogonal polarizations. By carefully balancing an isotropic dielectric barrier within the structure, the proposed scheme can provide a specific type of non-reciprocity known as quasi-Circulator behavior when the input wave has a particular polarization. Conversely, the inclusion of a uniaxial optical gyrotropic medium in the setup yields a quasi-Circulator response for both polarizations. Furthermore, the structure can also facilitate all-optical diode operation by either flipping the input wave's polarization or rotating it to parallel alignment, where the former method enables all-optical diode behavior for all resonances and the latter enables such behavior at specific resonances. The study also illustrates high-efficiency optical non-reciprocity and high-quality factors in the designed structure. Notably, the all-optical diode and quasi-Circulator responses exhibit similar effectiveness as well as comparable optical controllability and quality factors. The team expressed interest in seeing the structure's planar design and small size (approximately 0.15 to 0.28 lambda cubed) achieve strong optical non-reciprocity and presented simulations demonstrating all-optical diode and quasi-Circillator responses using realistic materials.

Extremal configurations of the Cohn-Keller-Lane-Driscoll optimization problem, a surface defined by $f(x,y,z) = x^4 - y^5 + z^3 + 2x^2 y - 2z^2 + 1$, are examined to map their geometry using birational geometry techniques. It's noted that these extremal configurations can be categorized into distinct groups based on their equioscillation points and loci, with three main types: points of equilibrium, points along singular codimension two varieties, and rational curves on a smooth quadric surface. A determination of the closure of the set of extremal configurations was made, with a hypothesis posed to fully characterize the arrangement.

The Izu group in Japan has been studying a sample of $^{7}$Li and $^{6}$Li in a camphor-based solidharmonic ligand and has presented findings on dark matter which includes a new observation of $^{6}$Li for the purpose of dark matter research, and this has led to stricter limits on dark matter interaction with matter compared to previous studies that relied solely on $^{7}$Li. 
We have analyzed this experiment within a theoretical framework that accounts for dark matter detection in solid state devices and has developed new limits for dark matter-proton interaction. 
Furthermore, our analysis of the $^{6}$Li dataset has led to cross-checking with existing findings through an extraction based atomic data which yielded matching results, and this has implications for search methods that rely solely on atomic properties.

A recently proposed approach for deblurring blurry satellite images relies on a regularization technique that enforces the structure of the blur kernel. Given that the blur kernel's structure is often known, employing this regularization should lead to improved deblurring, especially in situations involving high resolution. In this study, the authors challenge this assumption, presenting instances where regulating the blur's structure actually leads to decreased image clarity. Using synthetic data, the authors demonstrate that the effective regulation of the blur's structure hinges on accurate knowledge of the scene's motion. When this information is insufficient, the proposed regulation method fails to produce desirable results, instead introducing significant image artifacts.

This research introduces new Rota-Baxter (BiHom)paired modules and related (BiHom-)pre-Lie modules based on triple systems and homological transformations. These concepts are further linked to the double building block method proposed by Jiang and Wang. Moreover, the study illustrates the connection between Rota-Baxter paired modules and their (BiHom-)pre-Lie module representations through multi-step transformations. Conversely, it is demonstrated that Rota-Baxter paired modules can be constructed from (BiHom-)pre-Lie modules with a Lie algebra representation, providing a multi-step reverse transformation process.

Imperative programs and their dynamic properties can be described using natural language assertions, which also appear in documentation and testing descriptions. This paper outlines a method to model these properties as temporal logic formulas, without the need for a predefined abstract specification. Based on the results, a tool was developed that identifies and extracts assertion patterns from various programming languages, specifically C, C++, Java, and Objective-C. The tool then uses these patterns to detect and classify imperative commands for their non-deterministic characteristics, which could be applied to analyze critical systems that feature intrinsically undecidable properties, such as conformance testing.

Canopus, a high-efficiency fault-tolerant protocol for agreeing on an ordered list, has been enhanced with the introduction of RCanopus. This advanced variant includes two innovative components, FaultView and FaultRank, designed to provide more robust resilience against component failures. While Canopus relies solely on the last event of the hierarchy for ranking purposes, RCanopus utilizes FaultView and FaultRank to ensure consensus on the event order. If both components agree, RCanopus utilizes FaultView's decision, but in cases where FaultView fails or returns a conflict, RCanopus utilizes FaultRank's assessment instead. By combining these mechanisms, RCanopus exhibits superior fault-tolerance capabilities when confronted with arbitrary single-event failures. Moreover, both FaultView and RCanopus demonstrate increased resilience to failures of multiple events when compared to Canopus, specifically out-ranking Canopus in such scenarios.

Transport simulations, which involve the simultaneous transport of phospholipids and water through a membrane, predict an approximately quadrupolar distribution of the phospholipids at the membrane's center, whereas equilibrium experiments indicate a more circularly symmetrical arrangement. To address this disparity, researchers explored whether fluctuations in a membrane's conformation could cause phospholipid headgroups to deviate from a quadrupolar arrangement, particularly in areas where the membrane's curvature is significant. Our findings suggest that this is indeed the case for both model and realistic membrane simulations. Furthermore, we discovered that the power spectrum of the membrane's curvature follows a proportionately steep relationship with the wavenumber. Consequently, we propose a simplified representation of the membrane's quadrupolar ordering, which is based on the average curvature power spectrum. This new approach resulted in a greater agreement between transport simulations and equilibrium data regarding the membrane's position of equilibrium for idealized membrane models. However, when realistic membrane simulations were considered, it became apparent that the simplified representation was insufficient for accurately capturing the membrane's steady-state configuration.

Our analysis begins with a modified Friedmann equation derived from loop quantum gravity, specifically the apeiron version. We consider a universe consisting of photons and consider critical bounces in e-folding timescales. By examining critical bounces in both critical density and equation of state parameters, we find a crucial threshold at $\rho_{b,c} \approx 4.996 \times 10^{-26}~\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, above which the Friedmann equation from apeiron LQG deviates significantly from the APS LQG model. We also model a universe consisting of only dark energy, finding critical densities $\rho_{b,c} \approx 1.026 \times 10^{-26}~\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ in both critical density and equation of state parameters. We observe that this critical density aligns with the critical density of a de Sitter universe, $\rho_{\Lambda} = \frac{3}{\pi^2}(\rho_{b,c}) = 4.997 \times 10^{-26}~\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. We have also developed an approximation for Bounce-De Sitter periods in terms of equation of state parameters, facilitating comparison of LQG models based on equations of state. We have performed this analysis previously for models like the track-freezing scenario. We have also laid out a plan to investigate a TFC-like track with a modified critical density.

The SOFIAA air-shower catalog encompasses 1,529 detailed and 235 aggregate reports, focusing on extensive air-showers, 307 of which have multiple particle records. This catalog spans a 5-year period from 2016 to 2021, utilizing SOFIAA's 12 particle detectors to record air-showers with a combined energy of at least 2 x 10^16 eV at an altitude of 350 km. Under optimal conditions, SOFIAA's observation capabilities enable resolution of individual photons with an energy of approximately 10^16.75 eV, equivalent to about 1 keV, under near-optimal observing conditions with both spatial and temporal precision.

The effectiveness of Monte Carlo simulations in object detection has been recognized, though current methods neglect a crucial aspect of an end-to-end system: output decoding. This oversight leads to inaccurate representation of detection model uncertainty, causing ensemble methods to underestimate prediction errors. This issue is addressed by introducing BayesOD, an approach that integrates Monte Carlo sampling with output decoding. BayesOD utilizes a general framework for decoding any model, matching the Monte Carlo sampling method in efficiency and providing significantly better representation of detection model uncertainty. BayesOD's improvements are shown through an empirical study on a range of backbones and datasets, highlighting its ability to reduce prediction errors and improve ensemble methods, like Decision Dempster-Shafer fusion, which achieves a $2\sim3$% mAP boost with Decision Dempster-Shafer fusion.

Predicting traffic in real-time is crucial for smart and efficient urban transportation systems. With the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, traffic patterns have been altered even further. A proposed framework for traffic forecasting leverages a novel deep learning approach based on the advanced, architrurally advanced Unet++ model. By incorporating sequential data from diverse sources, including GPS, sensors, and cameras, the framework can provide accurate and timely predictions. The implementation of this framework on edge devices like the NVIDIA Jetson NVIO is detailed, demonstrating its ability to meet the requirements of real-time processing. The evaluation of the proposed framework shows improved accuracy over existing models when using GPS data alone, and comparable performance to more advanced approaches relying on multimodal sources.

Building on existing theory of precategories, we adapt this framework to
rewriting systems, defining a significant category of precategories where
compositions of transformations preserve structural characteristics. Focusing
on discrete and functional subsets within precategories yields various
equivalent formulations of this concept. Applying our findings to two
significant rewriting frameworks, first-order term rewriting and pattern matching,
we demonstrate that these systems exhibit coherency, leading to the
establishment of a substantial theorem. This theorem outlines the key
properties associated with dedicated format preservation in first-order term
rewriting and pattern matching. It sets the stage for our subsequent development of
a new, robust format for pattern matching that leverages the concept of
coherency.

Automatic segmentation of the hippocampus is frequently used to assess patients with medical conditions, but methods are not yet reliable for individuals who have had a hippocampus removed. We conducted a study to see how well four different state-of-the-art methods performed on a group of patients who had undergone surgery to remove one or both hippocampali. We discovered that these methods' inaccuracies were similar for patients with and without surgery, however they tended to make more severe errors when the surgery affected the right hippocampus than the left. By examining the relationships between surgical areas and segmentation mistakes in a subgroup of patients who had not had their images annotated before, we were able to accurately predict and correct the inaccuracy of these methods for patients with surgery. This meant that these methods could produce more accurate results for patients with and without surgery, reducing the average error by 3.1 millimeters for patients with surgery.

We've set a new record for simulating complex quantum phenomena using bosonic modes outside the traditional wave-packet domain, leveraging macroscopic simulations and interferometry with path-dependent measurements. Our experiment combines the transversal modes of a guided atom wave with a Travis-like delay system, where a single photon traps an atom for varying times and couples it to distinct transversal modes. As the guide loses its shape, the interference pattern shifts when measured in a detector with a non-uniform profile, given that the traversal times of the atom in different modes remain constant. Our findings demonstrate the potential for bosonic modes to influence the relationship between path and traversal times in quantum experiments.

The atmosphere's production of high-energy neutrinos originates from the interaction of cosmic rays with the air's constituents over the Earth's surface. While the source of cosmic rays is thought to be galactic and supernatural sources, their composition remains largely unknown. To understand neutrino production, it's essential to accurately model cosmic ray interactions that lead to the generation of new protons within the atmosphere. This study presents a novel technique for calculating the secondary protons created as a result of cosmic ray interactions in the atmosphere, using a detailed simulation of their pathways. These calculations will form the foundation of an upgraded neutrino production model, which will be integral in generating precise, realistic cosmic ray data.

Recent studies have shown that a pyramidal-like skeleton offers advantages in a various range of applications. Although traditional skeleton-based approaches utilize pyramidal networks for feature extraction followed by separate classification modules, this research presents an integrated representation learning framework, capable of simultaneously learning skeleton and pattern features at different scales. This novel approach leverages a pyramidal-like skeleton to derive multi-resolution representation in a unified network, thereby enhancing skeleton utilization efficiency. With skeletal patterns serving as priors, the pattern can be learned more effectively. Moreover, the proposal also simplifies the skeleton preprocessing process. In experimental assessments, the novel framework has demonstrated superior performance on NIR and visible spectral bands for three essential tasks: optical sensing, segmentation, and classification. Specifically, it achieved higher accuracy than MinkowskiNet and V-Net on binary classification, as well as comparable performance on multi-class classification and semantic segmentation.

This paper introduces a new differential privacy mechanism, based on the Huber function, that aims to provide strong privacy guarantees at a lower cost in terms of noise generation. The Huber mechanism is more efficient than traditional mechanisms like Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, as it only adds noise to actual data violations. A rigorous analysis is carried out to precisely define and quantify the differential privacy properties of this novel mechanism. The Huber mechanism's performance is systematically compared to that of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, both theoretically and empirically, to demonstrate its benefits in real-world applications. Interestingly, the study reveals that the Huber mechanism's performance is reminiscent of the Gaussian mechanism when optimized correctly. Furthermore, the research investigates the computational advantages of the Huber mechanism, revealing that it exhibits a computational complexity of O(n) and an average of O(n) time complexity as well as space complexity of O(n), making it more computationally efficient than the Gaussian mechanism.

Our research presents a comprehensive study of the far-infrared polarization properties observed within the Hi-GAL survey using a sophisticated data analysis technique that considers the complex spatial structure inherent in the data. The analysis enables accurate reconstruction of the far-infrared polarization angle and degree within the survey's coverage area, resulting in a detailed 8'x8' map of the Galactic plane at 350 $\mu$m. Our findings are further extended to include data at 212 $\mu$m and 440 $\mu$m through comparison with corresponding Hi-GAL maps. The analysis yields statistically significant insights into the polarization angle and degree distribution modes, their corresponding uncertainties, and frequency dependencies. The research findings are consistent with previous studies suggesting large irregular dust grains play a significant role in the polarization properties observed at multiple frequencies, devoid of frequency dependence. A proposed model describing the statistical distribution of polarization angle and degree aligns with single-scatter predictions based on recent studies, indicating Hi-GAL data primarily corresponds to a single scattering event. However, the research finds evidence suggesting Hi-GAR data may undergo partial saturation, with Hi-GAR corresponding to roughly double the scattering depth of Hi-GAL. The observed frequency dependence in Hi-GAR could be largely attributed to temperature fluctuations influencing dust optical properties.

Our investigation of the $697\pm36$ million-year-old T Tauri star, DR Hydrae, includes new optical and thermal emissions data from various instruments such as ALMA, SPHERE, and HST. These observations revealed distinct emission patterns in the disk - an inner ring with an inner boundary at 21.1 kkm/s and a unusual gap at the location of GRASpS, an area previously observed with ALMA, alongside an outer ring at 42.5 kkm/s. Using SPHERE's LPIC2 camera's high-resolution near-infrared imaging at 8-2.8$\mu$m, we detected two distinct features - GRASpS, with an infrared flux of 107.1 mJy, and DR Hyd b, located at a distance of 0.143''- a feature we initially suspected to be a companion but could also be dust leftover from formation processes. Our analysis of HST images also revealed that GRASpS was once brighter than DR Hyd b and has since dimmed by a factor of 3, alongside evidence of continued stellar evolution, dust accumulation, and a massive planet influencing the structure of emissions observed in the disk. Utilizing a model of stellar radiation, photometric, and ALMA data we estimated the mass of the object as 3.9$M_Jup$, its distance from the star as 10.3 AU and its inclination as 135 degrees.

This research explores the Most Clicks Problem (MCP) for the Top-Down Technique (TDT), a strategy developed by Berrueta and Gutierrez-Caro. By utilizing the Generation-Description-Clicks (GDC) model, we demonstrate that TDT is equivalent to a Null Space Decomposition (NSD), which provides an insight into MCP solutions. Our analysis of the MCP on 6x6 grids reveals that there is no definitive answer, as there are 45 distinct solutions. Notably, we discover some peculiar properties of MCP intervals, including their equivalence to null spaces, complementary nature, and cumulative count of elements in the first column of the interval's fundamental matrix.

A novel segmentation approach, based on the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, introduces an extended external energy component to mitigate the adverse effects of heavily corrupted images. This modified model is optimized using an algorithm that integrates alternating direction method of multipliers and reinitialization techniques. The integration of ADMM allows the segmentation of images contaminated by substantial noise and artifacts, while the inclusion of reinitialization enables the restoration of the first order penalty term, thereby enhancing the segmentation results. Furthermore, the total variation regularization can be effectively implemented within the proposed framework via the replacement of the first order penalty term with an equivalent proximal regularization term. Experimental validation demonstrates that the segmentation performance of the proposed methodology surpasses that of contemporary methods.

Abstract interpretation, a top-down modelling approach, has been widely used in static program analysis. However, the traditional framework faces practical limitations in encoding intricate program structures, leading to coarsened approximations, as refining the framework demands cumbersome changes to the encoding. In response, we introduce ProjGal, a dynamic Galois connection-based variation of abstract interpretation that facilitates more accurate approximations by dynamically re-evaluate the abstract domain, enabling easier modification of the encoding with minimal side-effects. We demonstrate ProjGal's application in improving the accuracy of reachability analysis for both unit tests and real-world programs, showcasing its potential.

Inorganic compounds with perovskite chemistry exhibit exceptional optoelectronic properties. We investigated the first principles dynamics of BaMgSi$_2O$_7, a tetragonal perovskite exhibiting low- frequency dielectric variability. Our analysis using density-functional perturbation theory shows that excitations by light lead to a significant increase in the density of topological phonons, causing essential anharmonic effects in BaMgSiO$_4$. Notably, the typical topological phonon patterns in BaMgSiO$_4$ are suppressed by fermion interactions, giving rise to a unique topological phonon landscape, and BaMgSiO$_4$ becomes the first observed phononic material with fermonic topological phonons at room temperature.

This research presents the MRPG (Minkowski-Repeatedly Partitioned Graph) algorithm for generating a proximity graph that effectively identifies outliers in data sets. MRPG starts with a K-nearest neighbor graph for each data point and iteratively refines it by applying a generalized version of the Voronoi diagram on the merged graphs until a high density cluster is formed, excluding outliers from the process. Unlike other approaches that rely on, a priori known cluster information or conditionally estimate it from the generated graph, MRPG uses a local structure to efficiently detect outliers in high-dimensional spaces. Experimental results demonstrate MRPG's superiority to popular methods such as NN-Degree, NN-Weight and Single Link, showcasing better execution speed and more accurate outlier detection than existing techniques in various benchmark datasets.

The role of a neutral atom's motion in the generation of synchronized counter-propagating photon pairs near a mirror is studied using a quantum theoretical framework that utilizes a classically driven mirror in a cavity of vacuum and an additional two-level atom in a cavity setup. Within this framework, we employ a quantized mirror model in a cavity of vacuum and an additional two-level atom in a cavity setup to observe the impact of a neutral atom's motion on photonic emissions by the atom in the cavity. When the atom in the cavity and the mirror are in a state of classical driving, we obtain a set of coupled nonlinear differential equations that explain the origin of synchronized counter-propagating pairs of photons in a classical limit. In a situation where the atom in the cavity is in motion and the photon pairs in a cavity of vacuum and an additional two-level atom in a cavity setup are in a state of classical driving, we obtain a set of nonlinear differential equations that explain the generation of synchronized counter-propagating pairs of photons in a cavity of vacuum and an additional two-level atom in a cavity setup. When the atom in the cavity is in a state of classical driving, we obtain a set of nonlinear differential equations that explain the generation of synchronized counter-propagating pairs of photons in a cavity of vacuum and an additional two-level atom in a cavity setup. When the atom in the cavity is in a state of classical driving, we obtain a set of nonlinear differential equations that explain the generation of synchronized counter-prop

The community has been growing around the idea of fair graph representation learning, which aims to diminish biases rooted in graph structures. Despite this emerging interest, there is limited attention given to the impact of accurate graph representation on downstream machine learning tasks. In our study, we investigate how fair graph representations affect the performance of subsequent learning tasks. We created and tested the first active learning method, called ActiveGraph, which integrates fair learning and active learning to produce fair graph representations. Furthermore, to increase the utility of fair graph representations, we developed an extension of active learning that utilizes utility optimization, which results in representation accuracy that generalizes well to downstream tasks. Our theoretical analysis reveals that fair graph representations are capable of enhancing the accuracy of subsequent learning tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that ActiveGraph and its extension successfully produce fair graph representations with high accuracy, as well as improved inductive representation accuracy compared to existing methods.

This study compares the Homotopy Perturbation Method and Simple Iteration Method numerical solutions against exact singular perturbation analysis for a reversible enzyme reaction model. The methods performed equally well in the context of the model. To confirm this finding, an investigation into the nature of the equilibrium manifold in the model was conducted. The research revealed that the Homotopy Perturbation Method and Simple Iteration Method are capable of generating asymptically consistent solutions under certain conditions, which explain their similar performance in this context.

The Large Hadron Collider searches for a gluino that decays remotely will be redefined once the discovery of supersymmetry is achieved, as this supersymmetry decay path offers the greatest sensitivity in determining the distance between the supersymmetry particle's decay point and its point of disappearance. Consequently, this gluino decay search will require smaller mass gaps between the next-to-lightest supersymmetry particle and the gluino compared to those in searches that utilize missing transverse energy. Gluinobaryon and gluino-chargino production are proposed as alternative methods to produce gluinos with extended lifetimes, and this research demonstrates that these channels have a higher discovery potential for supersymmetry and additional Higgs particles. Furthermore, this study indicates that effectively utilizing these channels will be possible only with distinct signature patterns that can be exploited through the development of tailored analysis methods.

Our analysis caters to Neriyanil and Thirlwall's request in #finmech (2023) to investigate the effects of nonlinear feedback mechanisms on financial bubble behavior through comparative studies of two distinct model applications. We initially examine a scenario where the nonlinear model yields qualitily different outcomes from the linear model in explaining the 2007-2008 US housing bubble collapse. We then explore a scenario where both the linear and nonlinear models align in predicting a steady state bubble around 2007 in explaining the Dutch Tulipomania in 1736.

Our approach utilizes coherent states to represent the initial condition of a class of exactly solvable models under driving protocols, effectively enabling the solution of more complex quantum systems by converting them into mathematically tractable problems. By employing this method, we derive solutions for the driven XY model in both the planar and triangular configurations. Our approach is versatile and can potentially facilitate the solution of various other complex quantum systems facing sudden changes.

Previous approaches to learning neural networks for recommendation, which mainly focused on static review text, resulted in limited utilization of interactive review features such as highlights and ratings. To address this, our method designs an interactive layer type that directly infers the influence of interactive features on final item ratings from historical data. This is achieved without needing explicit highlight labels during model training. Following this adaptation, our model can easily incorporate the generated interactive features into self-attention mechanisms and directly utilize them to guide implicit rating scores. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using real-world data from a Chinese e-commerce platform and demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art models through rigorous testing on real-world tasks and simplified synthetic datasets. All experimental results confirm the key role of interactive features in contributing to recommendation accuracy across various real-world scenarios.

Our proposed data augmentation approach 'CSBL' for code-switching data augmentation is presented in this document. By applying a limited number of 'word-blending' operations on existing data, we can maintain the original sentence structure. In 'CSBL', rather than substituting individual words with those from the second language, we swap entire sentence segments. This results in producing authentic code-switching sentences. Through experimental evaluation, we compared the efficacy of 'CSBL' against two rival methods using two code-switching datasets. The outcomes of the studies demonstrate that 'CSBL' outperforms the rival methods. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of varying the number of 'CSBL' operations and observed that even a limited number of operations can significantly enhance data quality. This is particularly evident in the production of additional code-switching sentences. In addition to this, we conducted a detailed analysis of the benefits provided by 'CSBL' operations. This analysis was applied to two distinct domains of code-switching data. The results show that the performance benefits derived from 'CSBL' are consistent across both data domains.

We establish a relationship between the continuous action of a topologically finitely generated subgroup on the interior of a compact surface by decomposing it into specific components, depending on its level of transitivity and algebraic compactness. A subsheaf of this decomposition which represents the maximal transitive case is identified and characterized. Furthermore, for an orientable surface, a formula is developed to calculate the volume of the corresponding nilflow ergodic measure for any real horn of a compact convex polyhedron in a linear algebra over the real numbers.

Brane placements in a background field that undergoes a transition from ultra-vibrant to inertial fixed points have the capacity to spread out extensively across beams, where the brane geometry assumes an irregular, twisted form known as a "kink" or "instanton" shape. The particular characteristics and dimensions of these kinks are independent of the flowing background field parameters and settle consistently, regardless of the location along the transition. Notably, this phenomenon also emerges in a simplified model representing a field theory in two dimensions and interacting with a single extra dimension, where the flowing boundary conditions cause branes to adopt irregular, twisted shapes.

In the context of mesh-based computations, the accuracy of an overall simulation heavily relies on the quality of every individual element in the mesh. This report outlines a method for automatically refining and adapting meshes based on the accuracy of simulations, with a specific focus on ensuring that simulated waves emitted from source points conform to the wave speed model defined by the mesh's elements. This approach is particularly challenging because it requires an in-depth understanding of the complex relationships between the various regions within the mesh, with different wave speed models governing distinct areas. This report details the implementation of a complex algorithm designed to adapt and refine meshes in response to simulations informed by the PVM mesh data structure, a sophisticated system that efficiently stores and manages mesh data while accommodating flexible attribute sets.

This paper proposes an enhanced knowledge graph link prediction method, which
utilizes both node attributes and relation-specific information obtained from
relation extraction. The proposed method combines these sources of information
with equivalence relation awareness, allowing it to make more accurate link
predictions on real-world datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art
techniques.

A detailed analysis of power conversion network (PCN) behavior is necessary 
to design and control these networks effectively, including information about 
the time it takes for PCN dynamics to develop over time. In this research, we've 
created an advanced model to estimate how long it takes for PCN dynamics to 
develop, with the aim of improving the accuracy of these predictions compared to 
previous methods. We've also compared our new model to other methods of 
analysis, such as using software from Synopsys, and found that it can estimate 
delays with minimal error while simultaneously simplifying complex network 
dynamics. Furthermore, we've applied our new model to a specific PCN with 
energy storage capabilities and used it to develop control strategies that ensure 
these networks meet stringent energy standards. By doing so, we've optimized 
control strategies to maximize energy efficiency and meet demand with minimal 
loss, as proved by our research which showed we could meet 100% of energy 
demand.

In areas with a continuous state and action system, model-free reinforcement learning using gradient updates faces an additional challenge. Even if we can determine the rate of change of a learner's overall reward, the constant noise in the updates hinders the convergence of the parameter adaptations. We introduce an innovative method for approximating the rate of change, not in the traditional velocity field, but rather in a stress tensor based on Rate-Coeficient Matrix. We implement this approach in a model-free reinforcement learning setting and demonstrate its effectiveness. Using our definition of stress tensor, the training noise is eliminated and the convergence is accelerated. Moreover, the optimal stress tensor has a straightforward connection to the Reed-Foeller dimension. Through experiments, the proposed approach results in faster learning and less variability in the parameter adaptations, but it does not affect the overall asymptotic performance.

Research in cognitive science highlights the significant role of agency in perceiving objects as living things. However, most studies on this topic focus on binary distinctions between living and non-living entities. In this research, we explore how the concept of agency relates to other markers of animacy. By creating a new measure for visual categorizability and combining it with a multi-faceted approach to agency, our study reveals that these factors contribute to our perception of animacy independently. In turn, our findings suggest that a comprehensive understanding of animacy should consider these diverse components.

Achieving accurate predictions of human ratings on animacy continuity is a challenge due to discrepancies among experts. In this research, we address this issue by compared our model's performance, which integrates visual categorizability and agency, against models incorporating human-centric metrics of visual categorizability and similarity to living things.

Our study presents two new datasets: one quantifies human ratings on the agency continuum in addition to visual categorizability for living things with modified mechanical limbs. Another dataset compares human ratings of agency for living things with those of non-living things with designed mechanical components.

Our analysis reveals that both visual categorizability and agency contribute to our perception of animacy independently. In our perception, artificial intelligence components have a marked effect on agency, whereas visual cues are more influential for living things. In contrast, our findings for mechanical components emphasize that different components can yield varying degrees of agency in human opinion.

The SPPF is a novel filter designed for high-order finite element simulations. It's designed to smooth partial differential equation solutions which have discontinuities not resolvable by the chosen spatial discretization. The SPPF is formulated as a steady-state convection-diffusion equation solver, with a unique combination of flux parameters that ensures preservation of analytic solutions across different domains, including polynomial spaces. Our analysis validates the preservation of selected conservation quantities in one and two dimensions, as well as proof of positivity for a range of flux parameters. We've also explored the use of spatially adaptive refinement, first with a single quadrature point, and then extending our results to higher order quadrature methods. The performance of the SPPF has been evaluated through one and two dimensional numerical experiments, with results comparable to fourth-order flux-corrected transport in addressing numerical oscillations. However, the SPPF has been shown to outperform weighted average methods in its ability to maintain accuracy and element-wise consistency across a range of partial differential equations and domain types.

Recently, researchers have found evidence of a distinct type of quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) in black hole X-ray transients known as type-C QPOs, featuring high frequencies and short durations. Although the cause of these oscillations remains unclear, recent studies point to the contrasting properties of type-B and type-C QPOs in terms of frequency behavior. This research focuses on observing the type-C QPO in the black hole X-ray transient GY171, which exhibited the QPO, for the first time, during a specific hard-intermediate state phase. Interestingly, the type-C QPO was found to increase in frequency as the source transitioned from the hard to the soft spectrum phases within this intermediate state phase, coinciding with research at AT2019kpp in GY171. Researchers hypothesize that this type of QPO could be linked to the accretion disk's inner layer layer, with the type of frequency observed influenced by the underlying layer's refractive index in an optically thick case. Researchers also discovered that the type-C QPO in GY171 exhibited unique properties including its high frequency, brief existence during the hard-intermediate state phases, and its frequency increase from 8.1 to 9.8 Hz as the source transitioned from the hard to the soft spectrum phases, with this behavior distinct from previous research findings, such as in GX339-4, which showed a decrease in frequency as the source transitioned from the hard to the

Many multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms have been effective in situations with partially observable dynamics but often lack transfer capabilities, especially when the structure of the state space varies significantly across tasks. In such cases, transferring knowledge from one task to another can be beneficial, and we investigate this aspect by introducing the transfer empowerment metric. Empowerment measures how much the policies' expected actions at each state can influence other states, and its extension for multiple agents, known as transfer empowerment, shows potential as a useful characteristic for selecting tasks that can facilitate knowledge transfer within a collection of training agents. Through experiments based on previous studies, we demonstrate that a population of agents trained on individual tasks selected by this measure exhibits improved cooperation in novel scenarios involving 9-13 agents, whereas previous methods showed limited success. Moreover, we found that agents' ability to imitate each other's actions in unfamiliar states strongly correlates with their transfer empowerment, indicating that their behavior largely resembles that of their closest training counterparts. This finding highlights the usefulness of transfer empowerment as a tool for task selection within the online discovery framework.

Our ability to explore and navigate the physical world relies heavily on our ability to understand and identify materials, characters, and patterns. Human experts can accomplish this with ease, but the process is significant and often impossible for machines. Our goal is to enable computers with the same level of understanding and ability to perform one-shot learning, recognizing new concepts after seeing them only once. Previous attempts have successfully applied statistical techniques to one-shot learning in simplified environments, but we aim to an improve on this and make the approach more applicable and reliable in more complex situations by employing physical simulations and modeling uncertainty. By learning from a small number of real-world images, our system can accurately predict the appearance of materials under diverse conditions. Our one-shot learning framework combines image-based learning with physical simulations, recognizing that the same concept can have different appearances in various contexts. For example, we can recognize that a sample of metal will likely look the same even when deformed, by predicting its appearance under standard conditions. Our system can accurately predict the appearance of materials under diverse conditions. Our system can accurately recognize new concepts after seeing them only once.
