To effectively ground aggregates, we integrate them into the language by generating extended facts, then utilize graph theory to determine feasible combinations of non-ground structures for the modified program. This methodology results in two alternative algorithms for different use cases - one generating all ground expansions of the input program in any feasible configuration, and another generating the most constrained interpretation consistent with the aggregates. To ensure the correctness of our algorithm, we provide a detailed explanation based on the models satisfying the revised language, and also demonstrate its time complexity. Examples illustrate the algorithm's functionality in handling recursive aggregates and demonstrate how it handles hard and soft aggregates, as well as nested recursion.

A general framework for the second law of thermodynamics in the multi-resource setting has been established, leveraging a novel path-independent representation of Riemannian curvature. This new framework extends the first law of thermodynamics to any theoretical framework with multiple resources and attributes. It is expected that this approach will unlock innovative methods for verifying the second law and designing novel quantum machines. The theoretical framework will be demonstrated with examples from bipartite resources and attributes in different settings, including probabilistic processes and adaptive sequences.

We derive estimation methods for information measures such as mutual information, conditional mutual information, and total variation distance by analyzing the moments of variables and their reliability in estimating Gaussian mixture models. Based on these investigations, we propose the application of moment estimation to address the challenge of selecting the optimal number of components for a Gaussian mixture model, recommending an iterative process called moment-gmm. The effectiveness of moment-gmm is validated through both synthetic data and a real-world study on pancreatic cancer, which involves identifying subtypes based on genetic variants.

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the consistency of an estimator for the number of shared stochastic trends, previously developed, in contexts involving heteroscedasticity, conditional heteroscedasticity, and non-normal distributions. We demonstrate the suitability of this estimator across various sample sizes and moments, including heavy-tailed scenarios, and prove its consistency when examining asymptotic properties as sample size approaches infinity. We also demonstrate the finite sample correctness of this estimator and examine its distribution under non-normal conditions, where it is shown to follow a normal distribution, with specific estimates of its variance and the covariance between its values for multiple series. Furthermore, this work develops an alternative estimator based on an entirely within-sample analysis and shows its compatibility with the original estimator. We also provides evidence from Monte Carlo simulations of finite sample effectiveness as well as an application using real-world data to validate our findings.

Quantum codes constructed within the framework of the left-right Cayley complex of finite groups have been examined and analyzed. Previous research focused on central group elements. This paper extends that support to groups with non-central elements. We have developed novel quantum codes based on the underlying principles of the Cayley complex. Specifically, for groups with n-dimensional complex representations, corresponding quantum codes exhibiting high distillability and superior rate performance can be produced, often surpassing existing standards in the field. The underlying structure of the Cayley complex naturally enables the inclusion of predefined Pauli errors in the coding scheme, resulting in increased robustness and versatility. The proposed codes are poised to facilitate cutting-edge quantum computing and information systems.

We analyze the computational requirements for solving the distance-$r$ dominating set problem in a decentralized framework operating on graphs with bounded twin-free structure. We establish that this problem can be resolved within $O((2e/k)^k + \mathcal{O}(e)$ rounds when the graph in question has a diameter of $r$. Additionally, our research demonstrates the feasibility of a more precise approach, resolving the problem in a $O((2e/k)^{r+1}$ rounds. In each instance, nodes are able to communicate via an distributed message passing system involving simple, private messages. Our breakthrough allows us to provide a general general lower bound of $\Omega(e/k)$ rounds for the distance-$r$ dominating set problem in graphs with a diameter of $r$. We also show that the single-hop communication model limits the complexity of distributed algorithms for dominating set problems to $\Omega(e\log n / k)$ rounds.

In this study, we examine a one-dimensional higher-order topological insulator constructed from degenerate band ferroelectric materials, incorporating the influence of random disorder. Using two methods - numerical simulations and an analytical approach based on the Landau Hamiltonian - we investigate how disorder impacts the band structure, edge states, and transport characteristics of this system. Our findings show that, unlike what is observed in standard topological insulators, the mobility in the bulk does not directly mirror the edge gap in low bulk carrier concentrations, and that this relation breaks down even further at higher bulk carrier concentrations. Furthermore, we observe that the average scattering time near the termination edges does not directly proportional to the edge gap, and that this relation is violated. Our analysis also reveals that, contrary to the case for standard topological insulators, the average scattering time does not directly mirror the edge gap, and that this relation is violated. Our study provides valuable insights into understanding the fragile nature of higher-order topological insulators in the presence of disorder.

The 13 TeV proton-proton LHC data recorded over 41.5 fb$^{-1}$ by the CMS Collaboration is analyzed for a supersymmetry model featuring a pair of compressed, long-lived charginos decaying into muons and neutralinos, which then disintegrate into hadrons. A specific search is defined by the presence of hadronically decaying tau neutrinos and jets produced by the subsequent decay of these neutralinos into taus. As no excess has been detected above expected backgrounds, the search places limits on the production of charginos with masses of 100 GeV and 1 TeV for a lifetime between 10 ns and 100 ps. These results represent the most restrictive bounds on this specific supersymmetry model.

Our approach, DeepFLR, utilizes Deep Learning to efficiently reconstruct a 4D light field from sparse views, given only a point cloud to guide the process. This is achieved by generating high-quality 4D light fields even with just a few views. The key to our success lies in leveraging geometric constraints derived from the provided point cloud to establish a compact and meaningful reference frame, thus simplifying the estimation of scene geometry and image attributes. This is facilitated by a geometric neural network (GNN) that accurately represents the scene's geometry and maps it onto a 2D image domain. The refinement of 4D light fields and accurate texture reconstruction are then accomplished through a depth-aware volume rendering process combined with novel frequency-based and geometric losses. These tailored losses enable the precise reconstruction of intricate scenes. Our experiments and evaluations, encompassing both natural and synthetic datasets as well as real-world experiments using a handheld camera, demonstrate DeepFLR's exceptional performance and ability to accurately reconstruct complex light fields. Our results superior to state-of-the-art approaches both in terms of performance and geometric accuracy. Additional high-quality reconstruction artistry is available online.

Our research involved conducting speckle interferometric observations at the AO188 facility in 2020 during six run periods. We carried out a total of 435 measurements in 326 nights, obtaining high-quality data in 226 instances. Utilizing the software used by the speckle interferometry community, we performed a comprehensive catalogue update by combining our recent results with those from the Washington Speckle Interferometry Program (WSIP) database. Following the merge, our updated catalogue now features 4570 measured systems, boasting a total of 3071 unique pairs and exceeding 1400 binary subsystems. In 2020, we identified 26 new pairs or subsystems, as well as 16 further subsystems, among nearby dwarf stars. Moreover, our updated catalogue now includes data on 4570 measured systems, 3263 of which are binary pairs or subsystems. We located 3098 of these systems or subsystems within the solar neighbourhood and identified 277 variability sources. We have made our updated catalogue available in digital format.

We're studying the chiral structure of the operator-product expansion in four-dimensional self-dual (conformal) field theories where local primary operators combine associatively. Our investigation is specifically focused on theories with four-dimensional conformal symmetry. In these theories, both the operator-product expansion and a revised version with corrected associativity exhibit identical chiral structures. Our findings relate the associativity of the operator-product expansion to both the internal structure of self-dual field theories and scattering amplitudes of α-deformed versions of these theories through a specific formula. Additionally, we applied our results to the established Wess-Zumino model.

A newly identified stream in an FUV WIFS image, denoted as the FeII stream, travels at 107 km/s, potentially linked to a type II radio burst observed on the same day. The radio burst, detected at 15.25 MHz, emitted radio waves at ~35 km/s and was likely caused by a solar jet speeding at 212 km/s. The radio burst and FeII stream are thought to have originated from the same solar jet, possibly linked to a jet observed in He II7507 Å the previous day, though the structures observed in FeII stream and the potential loop seen in the jet are newly identified features of the jet. The mass loss rate and acceleration of the jet were estimated as high as ~$5.6\times10^{16}$ and ~$3.9\times10^4$ cm$^2$s$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, with potentially larger uncertainties, due to the jet being directed towards the Earth. The observed FeII stream, in addition to being linked to type II radio bursts, also bears similarities to other solar jet structures terminating in faint chromospheric features located relatively close to the limb.

Using various scalar potentials within the General Two Higgs Doublet Model, we analyze how different charge structures impact the model's predictions for upcoming collider events, focusing on the behaviors of Higgs, gauge bosons, and heavy particles. By comparing the computed results with the 2016 CMS and ATLAS data on Higgs boson production and for the first time on gauge boson and heavy particle production, we find the model satisfies the data. Additionally, we calculate future lepton collider observables, demonstrating that certain types of flavor violating processes remain unaltered. To constrain the model further, we examine its predictions for B meson decays and find them consistent with the current data. However, the model is expected to noticeably affect its predictions for these decays in the future.

The random vortex dynamics system is introduced, which offers a innovative approach to resolving three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations by gradually introducing vorticity through a stochastic process influenced by the signs of Laplacian values of the solution. This is simulated using the Lagrangian method, where vorticity is disseminated via a stochastic algorithm based on finite element discretization, resulting in an efficient solver for Navier-Stokes equations that facilitates high-performance computing and potential applications in fluid dynamics models.

Quantum information and non-local properties develop within an enchanted realm, governed by a non-commutative wave function, $Z$, originating from the vacuum's unique properties. This unique state has a specific energy eigenvalue, -1, when measured, no longer existing. As photons (light particles) are added to the system, its behavior becomes increasingly multi-faceted. This complex system is likened to a collection of spinning tops with varying moments of inertia, all interacting with each other. By linking these spinning tops in pairs, their collective angular momentum becomes the sum of their individual moments of inertia. Similarly, when photons are added to the vacuum state, their collective angular momentum reaches a maxima, thereby measuring the amount of entanglement present in the system. By studying these systems under different cuts, two distinct patterns of entanglement emerge, one resembling uniform chaos and the other, precise balance. As the number of photons approaches infinity, the entanglement's structure becomes increasingly uniform, no matter the size or number of interacting subsystems. This unique property, known as scaling symmetry, enables the accurate prediction of the system's behavior, even in complex scenarios, multiple photons. This enables the calculation of expected values, upper and lower bounds on key system properties, and the exact maxima and minima of these expectations. These results, derived from analytical methods and precision computing, differ from classical systems, thereby highlighting the system's unique properties under multiple particle counts.

Advanced computational methods, including deep learning and Relevance Learning, have revolutionized our understanding of time-series gene expression data. This advanced analysis not only identifies correlated genes but also categorizes them based on their functional roles. Building on previous work, a novel deep learning architecture was developed to identify predictive variables in time-dependent gene expression data, utilizing dynamic temporal correlations among genes and between genes and phenotypes. When evaluated using different expression correlation models, the proposed approach demonstrated superior performance across various practical scenarios and gene expression scales, surpassing existing methods. Importantly, this generalized method can be effectively applied to various modeling frameworks and gene expression scales. Additionally, the method's performance was successfully validated using both simulated and actual time-series gene expression data. This advanced tool is poised to facilitate the efficient identification of predictive variables from time-series gene expression data, thereby contributing to our understanding of complex biological systems and phenotypes.

In Temporal Difference Learning (TDL), a predictive model is not aware of its environment's uncertainty, forcing it to rely on approximations for optimal values in uncertain situations. In contrast, a similar learning approach, Belief Model Learning (BML), is proposed to account for this uncertainty by increasing the learning's focus on the various possibilities for the unknown state in uncertain situations. However, most existing works have demonstrated that both methods are capable of handling challenging control problems. In this paper, it is demonstrated that a specialized version of BML, incorporating key attributes from both the Belief Model Method (BMM) and TDL, is sufficient to derive the BMM. Notably, this is achieved without relying on direct optimization of the uncertainty-reducing entropy. Furthermore, this work provides evidence that both TDL and BML are fundamental components in achieving optimal optimal control in uncertain environments. Ultimately, this learning framework is shown to be capable of making decisions with the highest possible return in various complex environments, even when considering multiple possible environmental states.

This paper addresses the action detection task in videos by combining self-attention mechanisms with Graph Convolutional Networks. Existing pipelines for this task primarily rely on Mask R-C-3 D boxes and have focused on making predictions directly, often using hand-crafted features. We introduce an approach called CAM-Det that incorporates learned features and employs self-attention to capture the spatially invariant aspects of video data. We use these features in conjunction with a Graph Convolutional Network to derive relations between different boxes and then apply a Motion Mask R-C-3 D model to generate class-specific predictions. Our approach is taken further in a fully end-to-end framework, incorporating additional components, including a box estimator that refines the initial box estimates in tandem with the CAM. We achieve exceptional performance in the JaxoPet and ACT dataset benchmarks, setting multiple new records, and matching or matching frame rates with state-of-the-art models on other datasets.

This research introduces a novel approach, called DeepMD-CID, to the important task of image identification across dimensions. It combines two proven techniques: deep hashing for efficient similarity retrieval and context information detection for enhanced accuracy. DeepMD-CID contributes two main innovations: Firstly, it proposes a new deep hashing architecture that allows for simultaneous negative sampling during training, reducing computation complexity. Secondly, it develops a context learning method that introduces negative sample labeling, bringing the benefits of context information to this field. Evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepMD-CID, showcasing its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods using deep hashing. The source code of DeepMD-CID is publicly available on GitHub.

The analysis focuses on the initial-boundary value problems associated with a specific parabolic equation: $u_t=\Delta_{x,y,t}u+f(x,y,t)$. The problems are distinguished by their boundary conditions: Dirichlet $\partial_{p}u=0$ and $\partial_{q}u=0$ on a cylindrical domain $\Omega=[0,T]\times\Omega_0$ with specific partial derivatives $p$ and $q$. The analysis involves establishing the existence, uniqueness, and uniform boundedness in time for the solutions under non-smooth initial data and a particular class of functions $\Omega_0$. The results are effective for various types of equations including nonlinear diffusion, transport, and other boundary value problems with unique solutions. The approach draws on techniques from weighted Sobolev spaces, optimal continuous and discrete interpolation theories, and the Lax-Hopf principle. It is also notable for its use of $L_{\infty}(0,T)L^2(\Omega_0)$ estimates in place of the usual $L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega_0))$ bounds.

A novel study on nuclear matter at zero temperature has been conducted, 
using the Vishwakarma-Nishina (VN) model in the absence of a magnetic field.
Initially, researchers found that the energy and spin polarization display 
opposite behavior. Surprisingly, the VN model's results resemble the MIT Bag 
Model when the variable $a$ is set equal to the quark mass. Moreover, the VN 
model's equation for the spin density has been correctly determined. In the VN 
model, the eigenvalues of the Dirac operator with an even number of fermions 
are found to be a continuous and non-uniform set. By employing matrix-valued 
Green's function, the VN model's equations for the spin density, energy, and momentum 
can be correctly derived. Finally, a detailed analysis of the limit of vanishing 
Mellin amplitude has been performed.

Federated learning's compression technique, used for communication efficiency, has a distinct implication under data heterogeneity and the constraints of Differential Privacy (DP). Our research explores this relationship by proposing the first DP-validated compression technique for the federated linear regression task. Our results provide the first DP certification for the widely employed Vector Significance Figure (VSF) compression method, which is based on the principle of minimizing information loss. (The full version of this research can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.03137)

Our research utilizes a single pixel of the HST CANDLES project to map large areas in the far-ultraviolet by combining high-resolution data with cosmological simulations that employ a hierarchical technique to merge multiple pixels into larger regions. Through this method, we achieve a mapped area of approximately 300 square degrees in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex located at a distance of about 2 megaparsecs. By comparing our results against simulated data, we find that there is no evidence of missing far-UV radiation which suggests that the fluorescent emission from H2 contributes a significant amount to the total intensity of the region. Our data also reveals a strong correlation between 5000 Angstrom light and far-UV radiation which exists within giant molecular clouds but not in the surrounding interstellar medium. Furthermore, we generated synthetic maps using a simulated binary galaxy and found that the hierarchical method can extract the true far-UV intensity while removing the effect of nearby bright sources. Our work has now expanded to a new region, Cep OB1, located at a distance of about 780 megaparsecs.

Extracting tables from unstructured documents is a crucial initial step in various natural language processing tasks known as table detection or identification. To improve efficiency and reduce errors, a new Graph Neural Network-based model has been developed by incorporating boundary detection features. This approach first detects individual table cells using bounding boxes, and then employs a Graph Neural Network to model the visual connection between cells, thereby resolving ambiguities associated with table structure. Experimental results demonstrate that this novel model surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in accuracy on the ICDAR 2013 competition dataset.

In both human and artificial strategems, a misunderstanding of the opponent's knowledge base often prompts an exploration of the opponent's possible beliefs. This study examines a broad range of situations with varying levels of information unknown to both parties. Through an experiment involving three players, we found that lower-ranking players tend towards a conservative estimate of the opponent's knowledge, whereas higher-ranking players display more optimism. A theoretical model has been proposed which accurately predicts the results and is rooted in the idea that lower-ranking players anticipate the worst-case scenario in an effort to avoid exceeding the opponent's knowledge bounds, whereas higher-ranking players anticipate the worst-case scenario in an effort to avoid missing any unforeseen circumstances.

This paper proposes a novel method for estimating app population patterns by leveraging machine learning and pre-existing app store metadata. Trademark, category, and age data are utilized to characterize apps, and a clustering approach is employed to derive a ranking system of features for use in population prediction models. By testing this method across multiple platforms, including Google Play and Apple App Store apps with millions of downloads, we demonstrate its effectiveness in building accurate population prediction models compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, and showcase its practical application in identifying successful app characteristics.

A proposed method suggests using a dynamic approach to content filtering, incorporating user feedback into hash functions. This scheme can be viewed as an iterative system where each user's feedback triggers the modification of at least one hash function. The modification aims to minimize the number of false positives in the user's query result. Due to its iterative nature, this approach can effectively address the two primary challenges of static filters: the balance between minimizing false positives and reducing computation overhead, specifically in terms of memory and speed. Moreover, this scheme can be categorized as online learning. It utilizes partially labeled data and provides class labels or opinions for learning. The iterative process allows users to label objects in real-time during the filtering process. The algorithm iterates to achieve optimal solutions but also requires user feedback at each iteration, in effect charging for each solution. The method relies on SimHash and InverseQuantizationHash, two algorithms that are considered to be unsuitable for software implementation due to their computational complexity and thus more likely to be fixed in hardware. If this technique were implemented as a hardware component, our design would place the classificator within the network's edge, enabling faster operation while also reducing the amount of data being processed. The main drawback of this scheme is its reliance on components that are typically fixed in hardware and are not typically modifiable. Nevertheless, if this technique were to be implemented using Intel's MCP system, which allows for the modification of hash functions, then our design would be grounded in the circuit level, with

In this study, we adapt an rigid pendulum model to analyze a weakly interacting gas consisting of bosons featuring a narrow resonance and strong spin-flip scattering. Our modified model incorporates a non-relativistic Bohmian quantum system, where an ordinary particle and a spin-flip zero-range atom are combined, revealing that such a system exhibits an overall non-rigid movement. Utilizing this model, our findings indicate that it accurately describes the dynamic process of converting atoms to molecules and the emergence of instabilities within the quantum system. We further demonstrate that there exists an intersection point, located between these instabilities and a temperature-related fluctuation, beyond which the quantum system undergoes a transition from orderly to chaotic behavior in a finite time. Additionally, our analysis based on this pendulum model enables the description of quasi-classical trajectories in a effective classical system, where the complexity of quantum dynamics is simplified into two distinct motion types: as an interacting string or as an isolated loop. These findings are expected to provide insight into the experimental study of collapse and revival phenomena in ultracold atomic systems.

A versatile Multi-Phase SPh method has been developed and implemented within an SPH framework that seamlessly handles varying phases based on relative densities. The algorithm adapts easily to initiate multiple phases from a single SPh simulation by employing distinct phase indicators linked with thermodynamic properties. To ensure smooth phase transitions, a sharp interface is maintained through artificial mixing. The proposed model effectively addresses voids and extreme phase segregation resulting from high-density ratios. It also accommodates arbitrary initial conditions for complex scenarios. For accurate thermodynamic property predictions, relevant functions are preserved locally within individual particles. To maintain phase stability, an artificial diffusion mechanism is employed with adjustable parameters. The effectiveness of this new model was demonstrated through a series of tests, including single-phase scenarios, phase transitions driven by thermal methods, and simulations modeling solidification processes. Additionally, the model's ability to capture the intricacies of multiple phase flows was illustrated in scenarios involving rotating phase transitions.

A quantic version of the K-means clustering method has been developed for use with quantum data sets. This data type can be created by running quantum algorithms such as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm and IBM's adaptive Kurry-means protocol. Both classical and quantum data clusters are similar in nature - they consist of neighboring data points in a d-dimensional space. In this research, a quantum-friendly K-means clustering algorithm inspired by De Groote has been developed. Known classical methods for clustering have a time complexity of O(NK\lambda^K), where N is the number of data points, K is the number of clusters, and \lambda is the cluster radius. A quantum-based approach has been proposed, taking advantage of the benefits of quantum computing for clustering. With this method, a quantum-based clustering process has been devised that includes measuring, entangling, and post-selecting to achieve an asymptotic complexity of O(\sqrt{N} \cdot \lambda^{K/2}). This represents an improvement over classical methods for large values of N, exhibiting a quadratic reduction in computational complexity. Furthermore, this quantum-based approach for clustering holds promise in facilitating the resolution of complex clustering problems that are currently unsolvable with classical methods.

Generative neural models for speech can produce natural-sounding sentences with various pitch levels thanks to a straightforward modification of their training data. By including pitch-augmented speech datasets in the training corpus, the model learns to regulate pitch during speech production. This results in a highly controllable model that can easily produce speech with a range of pitches, while maintaining high-quality acoustic representation and language-based structure. Utilizing such a model in a text-to-speech system allows users to produce very expressive speech with a subtle and natural tone. We examined in-depth the effectiveness of this approach and compared it to a more complex method involving speaker adaptation. The results indicate that our simpler approach yields comparable quality to the more advanced technique and offer valuable insights for improving speech production with a controlled pitch. Moreover, we have made available a large, modified speech dataset and an efficient open-source toolkit for speech production with a controlled pitch.

Objects within a scene are interconnected through relationships in both space and time, yet current object-centric models that attempt to reason about these connections often overlook their temporal aspects. As objects within a scenario evolve over time, new objects appear while others disappear, and relationships between them change accordingly. In this study, a novel space-time object-centric approach is introduced, focusing on simultaneously identifying objects and their interconnections across time. A contrastive loss is employed to strengthen representations of objects and their interactions by comparing correct against incorrect pairings of objects and relationships. Additionally, a temporal regularization method is incorporated to minimize model predictions of objects' prolonged existence. Through evaluation on established spatiotemporal object-centric datasets, the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art object-centric models both in space and time. Comprehensive analysis reveals the critical role of contrastive loss in enhancing model capabilities for spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning.

The CC-FeynHex tool is used for the simulation tuning of charged-current Drell-Yan observables by incorporating information about the transverse-momentum distribution of lepton pairs. This distribution contains valuable details at low momenta that can be difficult to model accurately. In a first comparison with ATLAS data, various generator settings were evaluated and a strong correlation between the models and data was observed when using the inclusive transverse-momentum distribution for simulation tuning. This strategy proved effective across a range of W mass values, from 20 to 61 GeV, in a way that did not depend on the specific underlying models. This approach can now be applied to other Drell-Yan observables and studies, such as those involving different lepton pairs or angular distributions.

This study aims to identify users' mental impressions of the visual, navigation, and control aspects of telepresence robots, which are essential in improving the overall telepresence experience. To achieve this, we conducted an online survey among telepresence robot users to gauge their feedback. The results enabled us to create a mental mapping framework, illustrating the hierarchical structure of telepresence robot users' mental impressions. Our research provides practical insights that can guide the development of more user-friendly telepresence systems, taking into account users' perceived requirements.

An adaptive nitrogen strategy is demonstrated by fast-growing plants competing for space, employing a pre-existing root system to locate and exploit soil nitrogen sources. We hypothesize that resource finding is localized, and only the dominant shoot determines root system direction and elongation. This hypothesis is tested through the study of flax (Linum usitatissimum) seedlings and modeled using a hierarchical approach, specifically cellular automata combined with ordinary and partial differential equations. Our results show that root system elongation is governed by the dominant shoot's signal, and new primary branches emerge from the root system to locate nitrogen-rich areas. Moreover, our modeling highlights the root system's capacity to find and guide nutrient delivery to parts of the plant not reaching maximum size. This study contributes to the development of agent-based models capturing the complex plant behaviors associated with competitive and adaptive strategies.

Mafia is a multi-player online game that falls under the category of social deduction games. Its dynamics are heavily influenced by the intersection of probability, statistics, and game theory, which involves the killing of random players in the initial stages of the game. A thorough analysis of the game format with an arbitrary number of players and various roles has yielded a comprehensive set of findings. These insights encompass the distribution of killing outcomes, the survival rates of roles and their related role combinations, as well as the occurrence of specific role multiplicities. Notably, our investigations have revealed intriguing patterns of correlation, which challenge intuition but hold significance in understanding the game's mechanics. A crucial aspect of our work is the development of an analytical framework that accurately predicts the long-term distribution of outcomes and provides valuable predictive capabilities for future game scenarios.

Accumulating evidence from various studies indicates that many giant planets must have formed in close relation to their parent star disk. We introduce a theoretical model that simulates how multiple giant planets, each accreting from the same disk, cause the remaining planets in their orbit to converge towards a common mass range. We discover that this convergence occurs naturally due to two key interactions. Firstly, as planets accrete from their parent star disk, their orbital oscillations cause them to interact through gravitational forces, resulting in the merger of all planets within a specific orbit radius within approximately $10^5$ years. Secondly, as a result of this gravitational interaction, planets become locked in a synchronized orbit at specific distances from their parent star. We demonstrate that this phenomenon of planetary convergence occurs for a wide range of initial conditions for accreting planets within a specific orbit radius. We observe that planets tend to converge towards a mass range of approximately 10 times that of Jupiter, or larger, depending on various factors such as disk concentration and mass. We conclude that planetary convergence may explain the observed tendency for planets in multi-planet systems to have similar masses and adjacent orbital distances.

In this research, we examine the temperature-dependent electrical resistance of a $\text{Ca/MoO}_3$ thin film containing armchair single-wall carbon nanotubes. Initially, we explore the low-resistance region using single-channel transport models, and find that phonon coupling dominates this area. As resistance increases at higher temperatures, we notice a shift towards single-channel transport, and notice that only odd-mode and even-mode conductance are present, implying that the nanotubes are partially aligned in the film. This behavior closely mirrors that of carbon nanotube films, and we attribute this outcome to a combination of nanotube bundling, van der Waals forces between nanotubes, and the interaction between the nanotube walls and the thin film.

Several fuzzy k-means variations have been suggested to handle data sets with varying sizes and qualities. However, these methods often struggle to find meanwardard solutions due to the negative influence of entropy in their objective function. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a refined fuzzy k-means approach balanced with cluster density, aiming to enhance fusion accuracy and protect against over-fitting. To achieve this goal, we incorporate density-based entropy into the standard objective function before solving the non-differentiable problem using an optimization algorithm. Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our method against traditional fuzzy k-means variations are presented, utilizing seven diverse data sets. Moreover, the uniqueness of our approach is further substantiated by comparing its findings with existing literature.

The EXP3.Growth algorithm is known for efficiently estimating complex models, including Gaussian Processes, by converging to optimal parameter values at an accelerated rate. We introduce a novel variant of EXP3.Growth, applicable to Mixture-of-Experts models, to effectively estimate the parameters of this architecture. Our theoretical analysis proves the convergence of the estimator to the optimal parameter values, with some parameters converging to their optimal values at a potentially faster rate than previously reported. We also demonstrate that our algorithm can achieve the optimal growth in these models. Furthermore, empirical evaluations verify the accuracy and efficient growth of the proposed estimator.

This expository paper showcases connections between two fundamental areas of study, one emphasizing variety theory and the other focusing on moduli spaces, within the broader realm of algebraic geometry. The discussion begins by illustrating how Jacobians and Prym varieties arise from the perspective of variety theory. Subsequently, it is demonstrated that these varieties become moduli spaces for eigenspaces and isogeny factors. Key object constructions in number theory, the Jacobian and Prym varieties, are thereby recontextualized within the moduli space framework. The inverse approach – using moduli spaces to derive variety theory results – yields simpler proofs for renowned theorems, notably a Prym-Hugel theorem and its generalized form.

We derive a finite bound on the degree to which gravity breaks global symmetries in massless particles, which holds for graviton interactions with at least $n+1$ massless particles and involves a gravitational coupling constant $k^2$. This bound has significant implications for theories of quantum gravity, including several scenarios: 1) In certain gravity theories, constraints are generated that align with previously proposed non-Adiabatic Matchive Shifts (AMS) which help maintain AdS/CFT integrity. 2) We find the degree to which gravity breaks global symmetries in massive particles to be unbounded as gravity's coupling approaches infinity, indicating gravity may substantially break global symmetries in quantum gravity theories where these particles coexist with gravitons. 2) We found in gravity an upper limit on the degree to which it is broken by local (Lorentz) symmetries in spin-2 gravitons which holds for any number of graviton interactions; this specific bound on spin-2 breaking is mathematically expressed as $\frac{k^2}{M^2} \leq \frac{1}{8N} \left< T^{A}_{A}$> and its spatial counterpart. This specific bound on spin-2 breaking is mathematically expressed as $\frac{k^2}{M^2} \leq \frac{1}{8N} \left< T^{i}_{i}$> and its generic form holds for

Our investigation of NGC 5281's blue horizontal branch variants used enhanced photometry from its half-degree field of view. We utilized a versatile fitting method in Astronomical Observation Data Analysis Software to prepare the data, and then performed a detailed analysis within the Kepler field of view, successfully isolating sub-groups within the cluster. Three distinct sub-populations were discovered, one of which aligns with the main sequence and blue horizontal branch stars' characteristics. We identified the red horizontal branch and blue horizontal branch distinct sub-populations for the first time. The sub-populations exhibit differences in mean color and magnitude with notable gaps between them. The data also reveal a distinction in mean magnitudes between the r HB and b HB stars. The sub-populations' colors and shapes are consistent with an eccentric orbit model, suggesting the cluster's peculiar shape is due to an off-center configuration and possibly binary star mergers. This is supported by the cluster's position in the galaxy's halo and simulations indicating the cluster should have an eccentric orbital structure.

We explore an extension of the Madsen-Weiss theorem by incorporating the b-principle and building on the Madsen-Weiss moduli space, achieving a stability result for the spinal knots complement. To demonstrate the applicability of this approach, we derive a combination of the Arc-Resolution theorem and the spines theorem for the mapping class group of a punctured sphere, with further implications including Arc-Resolution as a consequence of the sinvariant version of the Madsen-Weiss theorem.

While much research has been conducted on the concept of transfer learning from pre-trained deep neural networks, most studies have focused on an assumption that the pre-trained model achieves optimal performance on the source task. However, this assumption is not necessarily accurate and has been found to be untrue in many cases. In this research, we examined the transferability of pre-trained CNN models, trained through stochastic gradient descent on the ImageNet dataset. We discovered that the early stages of these models, specifically the initial few layers, possess limited transferability in contrast to the subsequent layers, which learn basic image features. We attribute this phenomenon to the specialized characteristics acquired by the early layers in response to the large data set provided by the RGB-D input. We further demonstrated that the key to transfer learning success lies in the pre-trained representations' compact and semantic quality, which in turn is determined by the network's training objective, loss function, and the stability of the stochastic gradient descent. Based on our observations, we suggest evaluating transfer learning performance via a correlation metric, which we found to be more effective than classification accuracy in this context. Notably, we found that a pre-trained network's performance in identifying shape characteristics serves as a stronger predictor of its transferability in contrast to traditional measures. We recorded the largest known transferable representation (OTCR) threshold using our proposed framework and identified specific networks that set the current record. Leveraging our insights, we devised novel transfer learning objectives, based on the auto-encoder, denoising

Networks featuring spreadable information, such as rumors or computer viruses, are examined through numerical and analytical means in this study. We investigate the interaction between information spreading and network modularity, using a size-adjusted version of the z-score in our analysis. Our findings indicate that the optimal modularity for maximal information propagation is closely linked to the initial amount of seed information or the system's target propagation capacity. Additionally, we discovered that larger seed sizes or target propagation capacities tend to decrease the optimal modularity. Moreover, we found that communities within networks with low modularity still manage to resist information spreading via partial information retention during system evolution, leading to increased system robustness.

The properties of special Lagrangians are further examined using a geometric progression along their Lagrangian angles, with a particular focus on the behavior of Lagrangian angles near singular points as they converge. It's proven that special Lagrangians defined on Lagrangian cones with a Cauchy-Riemann operator equal to the Laplacian are analytic and form a unique set, up to translation. This is also applied to the study of Lagrangian cones under the flow of their characteristic directions, with an demonstration that nearby special Lagrangians have smooth, varying volumes for small time periods.

In space communication, unguided radio waves are used for channel measurement, with results from previous studies indicating that discrete-time channel models based on unamplified links are inaccurate. This discrepancy is attributed to a mistake in the model representation, which is corrected in this study. A new discrete-time channel model is proposed using the reflection and refraction coefficients derived from multimedium wave optics. This model is valid in the case of weak links, with findings showing that the traditional model is flawed and leads to inaccurate estimation of channel parameters. Utilizing terrestrial microwave links with diverse characteristics, we collect channel measurement data and employ maximum likelihood estimation to determine the model's reflection and refraction coefficients. By comparing the performance of the proposed and traditional models, we conduct an exhaustive analysis of various link configurations. With a comprehensive evaluation of multiple scenarios, we demonstrate that the proposed model is more accurate and capable of achieving greater parameter estimation precision. This breakthrough leads to improved estimation of channel parameters with low estimation errors. This research is a significant step towards developing reliable discrete-time channel models using real-world measurement data.

A novel taxonomy for categorizing problem-space evasion attacks is introduced, which differentiates between attacks classified as Standard, Novel, Unconventional, and Unpredictable types based on the analysis of 97 evasion attacks observed over two decades. The proposed categorization is made possible by the application of Framing, Sizing, Positioning, Dimensioning, Attacking, Retargeting, Adaptation, Rebound, Backflow, Reappearance, Reactivation, Re-assemblage, Re-entry, Re-infection, Re-visitation, Re-collision, Long evolution, Long-term, Long lasting, Long lived, Long lasting lifecycle based attack characteristics. This hierarchical categorization is unique in contrast to the existing approaches that solely rely on evasion techniques. The findings indicate that each category possesses distinct features, and the corresponding attack detection, prevention, mitigation strategies will significantly vary. The presented taxonomy will facilitate the enhancement of in-depth analysis, detection, prevention, and mitigation of problem-space phishing attacks by accurately mapping their types.

A novel container called Ozy is introduced, designed to automate the deployment, monitoring, expansion, optimization, and management of cloud applications based on functional units. Orchestration in Ozy takes the form of code integration, enabling user-defined strategies for containerized services through easily embedded customization points. Ozy's efficacy is demonstrated by comparing it to traditional service orchestration methods in scenarios involving serverless and microservice settings, showcasing improved performance and more advanced tooling for cloud application management. Furthermore, Ozy is presented as a template for future integration with other containerization tools, potentially leading to the creation of specialized containers tailored to various orchestration engines, enabling more refined control over cloud resource utilization.

The reentrant anomalous $
u= rac{1}{2}$ phase differs from the known Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases by incorporating a unique combination of these instabilities, thereby excluding their conventional  $\mathcal{S}=2$ ground states, with the knowledge that no pair of gapped Moore-Read phases can be combined at the same time. At $
u= rac{1}{2}$, any two non-interacting Moore-Read phases are coupled with a quantized vorticity $L=\pm1$, demonstrating a failure to form an $\mathcal{S}=2$ Laughlin mantle, and displaying an incompatibility with the Haldane pseudopotential, the long-range one-rho interaction, and non-abelian quantum point contacts. An important property of this "in-between" phase is its tendency for the anomalous quantized phase to reenter at finite density with the implementation of an inhomogeneous  $\mathcal{S}=2$ interaction. This unique failure to completely eliminate the anomalous phase at finite density distinguishes the newly-proposed quantum reentrant effect from the known reentrant effects at filling $
u=1, rac{3}{2}, rac{4}{3}$ and could potentially be experimentally validated via microscopical population analysis.

Researchers initially assumed that the Thakurta metric behaved identically in all directions at the origin, which led them to rely on specific constraints on primordial black hole formation. However, this assumption can be repealed. New research indicates that if primordial black holes exist, their expected abundance is not necessarily compromised even if they form within regions of high curvature. This is because such areas would likely be surrounded by additional singularities, creating topological complexities that could potentially trap black holes. Trap regions correspond to areas where energy conditions are violated, which can be mapped using the Thakurut metric. This model outperforms previous models by offering improved constraints on black hole abundance, even if formed in highly complex topological environments. Crucially, these constraints remain valid regardless of previous assumptions.

The process of core growth within a protoplanetary disc is significantly influenced by the confinement of pressure waves in pressure-dominated discs. Recent research has discovered that pressure wave confinement is linked to sub-millimeter wave patterns in the discs of young stars. These patterns cause ring-like patterns of stochastic density and potentially destabilize the disc, increasing the likelihood of the Migrating Instability occurring. Notably, the Migrating Instability can lead to the formation of dense, resonant modes within the disc, and subsequent interactions may result in the coalescence of modes and a disc's eventual instability. Our research aims to examine how local and non-local disc mechanisms impact the evolution of protoplanetary discs through 2D simulations of core growth in pressure-confined discs. These simulations tested whether local and non-local disc mechanisms could prevent the development of the Migrating Instability by strengthening pressure wave damping and found that in most cases, the Migrating Instability occurs. However, in scenarios where the Migrating Instability occurs, it leads to rapid core merging and the creation of long-sweeping density patterns at less than one-tenth the speed of tidal waves. Notably, the formation of these density patterns makes it possible for further instabilities to occur and faster-than-expected core growth may become more likely due to a process of secondary mode interactions.

Deep neural networks' training methods can be categorized into robust and non-robust categories. Robust training, which utilizes adversarial training to enhance model resilience, necessitates more model parameters than non-robust training. However, the key factor contributing to model robustness is not the number of parameters, but rather the quality of those parameters. This article delves into the quality of robust training parameters, demonstrating that these parameters create functional sub-spaces enabling predictive generalization. It also introduces a new theory for adversarial training, synthesizes prior research, and provides an in-depth analysis of the underlying mechanisms driving adversarial training. The findings presented can serve as a foundation for future research and investigation.

For each $n$, denote the upper Banach density of the set $\left\{\sum_{k=0}^{m} x_{n k}\right\}$ by $\mathbf{u} (\eta_{n}^q)$ where $Q$ is an integer and $0 \leq m \leq Q$. A common challenge in online optimization is minimizing costs associated with route adjustments. To address this, a novel approach called Information Utilization via Real-time Community Knowledge (IRCK) is introduced. This method leverages real-time information about the community's itineraries to pinpoint likely origin-destination pairs and thereby predict fixed travel paths. In a simulated environment on a 2500 x 3200 grid, it is demonstrated that IRCK can efficiently gather information by selecting key sensors. Furthermore, a proposed suboptimal algorithm utilizing IRCK's predicted fixed paths enables significant cost savings compared to traditional methods, with results comparable to a more complex optimal algorithm based on global information.

Recent years have seen a surge in deep learning research focused on multi-modal
learning from various sources of knowledge. Despite the promising outcomes,
the field poses significant challenges, primarily related to limited data availability
and the expense of processing extensive input modalities. To tackle these issues,
we introduce Knowledge Modality Augmentation, a novel approach that utilizes
derived knowledge to enhance both learning robustness and efficiency. By
leveraging the potential of multiple knowledge sources, KMA creates new, comprehensive
datasets that improve the quality of input data, thereby benefiting both model
accuracy and training efficiency. Experimental results on digital medical images
demonstrate the efficacy of our method in comparison to established baselines.

Recently, deep learning methods have been used to analyze multimodal data from
clinical trials and estimate Alzheimer's disease progression stages. These
approaches can be either supervised, relying on labeled data, or unsupervised,
utilizing only the labels from a small group of patients. To compare the efficacy
of supervised and unsupervised methods with varying levels of available patient
information, we conducted a series of experiments. We employed unsupervised
reconstruction tasks instead of the traditional supervised classification, as
this approach allows for the evaluation of feature importance in an unsupervised
manner. We also adjusted the amount of patient data available for training and
assessed model performance on an independent group of patients. Our results,
obtained across 10 trial datasets and multiple models, indicate that unsupervised
methods often match the performance of supervised convolutional neural networks in
predicting disease progression stages. Additionally, unsupervised methods prove
effective even when trained on patient groups that are not similar to the test
group, without the need for data augmentation. Moreover, these methods provide an
unbiased set of features that can be used in future studies without fears of
overfitting to a specific patient subset. In contrast, supervised methods require
access to a broad range of patient data for reliable results. Our experiments
also demonstrate the significance of selecting appropriate comparison baselines in
