We've developed a novel few-shot parsing model called FPIO, designed to adapt and function effectively with a small group of annotated examples. Our focus was on binary parsing, which is defined as the prediction of a binary relation from a sequence of four elements. Our approach utilizes the principle of symmetric relation parsing, initially proposed by Wu et al., where a parser is trained to recognize the symmetry of binary relations. Based on this concept, we've built two innovative paradigms for few-shot parsing: self-parity and cross-parity. Our experiments with a large dataset of annotated examples showed FPIO to be comparable to Wu et al.'s model in performance but surpassed it in speed. Moreover, we found FPIO to be effective with as little as five annotated examples, outperforming all existing few-shot parsing methods. When trained on only three examples, FPIO still managed to parse over 80% of relations correctly, though this is slightly short of our goal as FPIO correctly predicts the presence of a symmetry relation.

This study investigates the dynamic changes within a speech recognition system, specifically to understand how it generalizes to new, unseen topics from a diverse set of training data. We've identified three key observations: Firstly, a speech recognition model trained on data from various sources (topics) is more robust than one trained on data from a single source. Secondly, the speech data from smaller languages like Hindi contain more topic-specific nuances than data from larger languages like English. Thirdly, the system's performance drops slightly when confronted with novel topics, but then becomes more stable as it's given more topics to train on. We've also found that the system's ability to generalize depends on not just its own performance, but also how well the training data from different topics matches. We've used this new knowledge to improve the system's robustness, by training it on data from multiple topics and fine-tuning it on new, unseen topics as it encounters them. This approach, called continuous training, significantly improves the system's performance, resulting in a much smaller drop when it's confronted with novel topics compared to a system that's only trained once. We've seen this boost in performance in both Hindi and English, showing that the system's ability to generalize improves by as much as six times on new, unseen topics. Continue training the system also enables it to keep performing well even when it's given much more varied data from many more topics. We've also found that the system's ability to utilize new information from training on

The discovery of additional Be-type star binaries in the Wing-Figure-\ath$\mu$ Orionis field through Gaia data has led to a significant finding. A distinct pattern of binary frequencies among these Be stars in comparison to their normal B-type counterparts cannot be overlooked. As a result, additional observations are needed to confirm our earlier conclusion regarding the binary frequency difference between Be and normal B-type stars. Furthermore, our previous estimation of the Be star mass retention efficiency in the Wing-Figure-\ath$\mu$ Orionis field is confirmed, albeit with some residual uncertainty. It has also been established that the Gaia data provide an accurate representation of the binary frequency across the sky without a notable influence from systematic errors. As the Wing-Figure-\ath$\ath$ Orionis field is primarily populated by early to mid B-type stars, our analysis relates primarily to the binary star population in this early B-type star regime.

Out-of-domain text matching tasks have seen significant performance improvements with the use of pre-trained language models. These models' ability to handle such tasks largely relies on their pre-training corpus. It has been observed that minor changes in the pre-training dataset can yield substantial improvements in matching accuracy. This paper presents a novel data augmentation technique to enhance the quality of out-of-domain text matching. Unlike conventional augmentations that rely on in-domain data, this technique generates synthetic training examples using a massively multilingual pre-trained model. Experimental results on the INDORE and a custom Google dataset demonstrate the efficacy of this augmentation in improving out-of-domain matching performance. Notably, this technique is effective on datasets lacking in-domain data for augmentation and outperforms in-domain-based augmentations on the INDURE dataset. Furthermore, this technique's benefits are most pronounced for less common languages.

The purpose of this paper is to establish a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator in n-dimensional space. It can be observed that the optimal geometric configuration for minimal eigenvalues occurs when the domain of consideration is a half-space. Although the half-space domain is not bounded, it is possible to select a geometric boundary within the domain that minimizes the eigenvalues. By selecting an appropriate geometric configuration, it can be seen that it shares similarities with the well-known Petviashenskii inequality for the Laplace operator.

Recent research has established that large, deeply-connected neural networks can be approximately represented by simpler neural tangent kernels. This work compiles a comprehensive list of properties unique to neural tangent kernels and systematically compares the ease of analysis afforded by these models with that offered by the more complex, deeply-connected neural networks. To this end, we revisit and re-examine various regularization techniques and learning methods developed for deep neural networks in the context of neural tangent kernels. By doing so, we highlight the significant added value of these models in facilitating interpretations and understandings.

The extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which incorporates peptide-nucleic acid dimer correlations, is examined within the framework of the Green function formalism. By utilizing this approach, researchers derive Green functions for both finite and infinite systems, which are then used to calculate various physical properties. From the analysis, it's determined that the Hatano-Nelson chain with peptide-nucleic acid dimer correlations exhibits a non-uniform decay of wave functions, classifying it as non-ergodic. Additionally, it's found that the wave function decay rate is influenced by the distance from an exceptional point, which can be used to estimate local densities of states and the system's bandwidth. Contrary to the single-site model, it's also been determined that the system's bandwidth is directly proportional to the inter-site hopping strength. Further analysis reveals that while the single-site model exhibits a universal upper limit on the wave number range, the current model relies on the position of its band, which, in turn, is influenced by the system's architecture and the hopping strength.

Our research explores how listeners rank speech synthesis voices with distinct characteristics in terms of competence, using a female speaker as a test case. Six audio parameter manipulation techniques were utilized to produce variations in speech features known as spectral slope and an open-mouth articulation feature. Listeners then evaluated the synthesized speech for competence, which revealed that they accorded significant weight to these features in making their judgments. Furthermore, it was found that combining the original speech characteristics with the manipulated features in different proportions significantly impacted the perceived competence of the speech. This was shown statistically to be a significant finding. Theoretical support for these findings comes from a model describing how listeners combine the characteristics of speech syntheses to make their evaluations, and this model was also used to provide insight into the effects of manipulating the features in different ways.

We propose a plasma like model, where the dark matter particle moves within a narrow energy band near the Dirac point in a three-dimensional photonic crystal, taking advantage of its localized state. By analyzing the band structure, we establish that the dark matter's motion results in stable closed orbits. Using phase space analysis, we calculate the survival probability of the dark matter particle and find it to be indefinitely stable. This model displays similarities to bosonic dark matter and serves as a model for both theoretical research and experimental verification, as well as a prototype for a quantum simulator for dark matter.

A comprehensive study has been conducted on how the energy levels of irregular nuclei behave in the presence of a fundamental constant representing the size of their underlying space. This study, which serves as a theoretical extension of earlier investigations on rotating nuclei's energy patterns, has yielded a proportional relationship between energy and angular momentum. Furthermore, a new constant's impact on energy has been found to follow a linear pattern. To predict the energy of irregular nuclei outside of their rotating regimes, a simple and effective formula has been developed, which relies on their angular momentum, size, and a related fundamental constant. This theoretical framework's ability to reproduce total energy patterns has been successfully validated using accurate data on rotating nuclei's energies.

We provide the most comprehensive single-letter answers regarding the four-level complementarity array pair (GCA pair) feasibility. Furthermore, we elucidate the equivalence between feasible GCAs and vector sets of rank four, establishing a criterion for their primitiveness in the process. Subsequently, we demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair can be realized if and only if it satisfies two specific conditions: its vector set of rank four has a maximum size of 16 vectors and at least one constituent vector is non-identical.

The change detection process, operating across multiple spectral bands, uses data from various points in time and identifies changes within and between individual images. Unlike supervised methods, unsupervised change detection can automatically analyze multiple images without prior knowledge, operating in one of two modes: segment-by-segment or batch processing. Although supervised methods require labeled data, which is often limited to specific regions, and achieve high accuracy with that data, they have restrictions on their scalability. Conversely, batch processing offers enhanced accuracy but increases computation with the square of the number of images, while segment-by-segment provides a balance between accuracy and computational demands, though its performance is less than that of batch processing and supervised methods. The performance of these approaches is evaluated across four different scenes with distinct characteristics, indicating that segment-by-segment provides reliable results, often as well as batch processing, while ensuring lower computational complexity in varied scene settings.

Our research delves into how density is related to viscosity in non-associating fluids consisting of molecules with varying shapes, utilizing an advanced simulation technique known as non-equilibrium molecular dynamics. We investigate the effects of density on viscosity across a range of particle sizes and shape configurations, specifically for two commonly used potential models, and observe a consistent trend where the dependence on density weakens as the size and shape deviation from a spherical shape increase. Additionally, we examine the impact of particle size and shape on the composition of interacting particles, revealing that a maximum exists in the viscosity-modifying effect when the shape deviation from spherical is significant. Furthermore, we compare our results with existing theoretical studies and an important implication of these findings for modeling complex fluids is discussed.

A new model of cosmology is suggested, where a transition occurs from the Lambda-CDM model to inflation. This transition is triggered by matter flux emission, a phenomenon observed in LHC experiments. To study this model, a modified version of the Friedmann equation is developed, featuring a singular anomaly resembling the Universe's early behavior in a cosmological scenario. Additionally, two scaling symptoms, analogous to cosmological constant and quintessence, are identified. As a result of a stable universe equilibrium, the model achieves a balance similar to the Lambda-CDM model and may even explain its durability. Furthermore, this model offers possibilities for addressing inflation's remaining mysteries and exploring the origins of matter flux emission.

Discussing quantum nonlocality without considering measurement independence and post-selection raises concerns that such analyses are incomplete, thereby necessitating fresh examinations of these fundamental concepts in quantum theory. Our paper aims to redress this oversight by exploring nonlocality in the context of light, where traditional methods for evaluating nonlocality may not be applicable or relevant. The frameworks we adopt for measuring nonlocal effects emphasize the independent nature of measurements and post-selection, drawing from alternative definitions that have been proposed in recent years. Utilizing these definitions, our research aims to assess nonlocality in the double-slit experiment, a fundamental model describing the interaction of light between two points, by investigating the phenomenon of light clustering. By applying the principles of quantum theory, our analysis indicates that light clustering gives rise to distinct, potentially significant, quantum nonlocal effects. These nonlocal effects, which are further validated by modeling the phenomenon using an entangled two-photon approach, are deemed robust and compatible with current experimental limitations. Our study provides novel insights into the quantum properties of light by highlighting the importance of independent measurements, post-selection, and counterfactual analysis in the context of light.

The ever-growing complexity of neural networks poses significant challenges for their deployment on resource-constrained devices such as smart speakers and wearables, due to the increased memory requirements and computational costs. A potential strategy to mitigate these limitations involves utilizing simpler models trained in a sequential manner. We explore this strategy by exploring the implications of decomposing large language models into multiple models of reduced size, trained separately and executed consecutively. The potential gains from using smaller models include reduced memory usage, lower computation requirements, and faster data loading and processing times. Notably, loading data between models is often the most time-consuming process, especially in devices with slow storage systems. By examining reduced model variants of the GPT-3 model, we identify principles that guide decomposition for limited-resource devices, focusing on optimizing latency, memory usage, and training costs. Our findings reveal that incremental training, model pruning, and combining capabilities of smaller models can lead to substantial performance improvements, resulting in up to 154x faster inference, 83x lower memory usage, and 45x lower training costs compared to the full GPT-3 model.

A novel expansion of the cluster model on isorial graphs is developed using a novel technique for verifying convergence, which yields a precise expression for the probability of forming closed shapes. This expansion has a cluster replacement series in the continuous setting of hyperbolic geometry, which can be broken down into positive terms involving integrals over hyperbolic Riemann surfaces. By matching the coefficients of these terms with a corresponding integrand derived from the Weil-Petersson degeneration formula, an exact asymptotic expression for the cluster model observables is obtained, which matches previous findings on the scaling limit of the cluster model near a phase transition.

In the realm of regression analysis for continuous or categorical data, a method of variable selection through a technique called Group Lasso has been developed, which is an adaptation of the Lasso algorithm with enhanced capabilities due to its group regularization property. Nonetheless, this method's efficiency is compromised when dealing with data sets featuring large numbers or correlated variables. A proposed adaptation called Expected Information Gain Lasso addresses this limitation by reimagining group variable selection as a sequential process of eliminating groups with the least predictive value regarding remaining variables, thereby yielding a more efficient algorithm with improved computational scalability. A second iteration of this algorithm, referred to as Expected Information Gain Group Lasso, further optimizes performance by leveraging the properties of expected information gain to approximate key variables and leverage parallel processing capabilities, thereby yielding speeds up to 10-15 times faster than the original Expected Information Gain Lasso algorithm. Empirical testing confirms that both adaptations yield more accurate and concise models than the original Group Lasso algorithm.

This paper describes T-Visor, an embedded-system virtualization platform designed to meet the demanding reliability and safety standards of the aerospace industry. In complement to the existing libosm1 virtualization system, T-Visor addresses the critical requirement of real-time scheduling. A novel scheduling framework within T-Visor achieves this by incorporating a virtualization-aware scheduling algorithm, thus ensuring coexistence with the host thread and accounting for diverse embedded-system timing needs. Moreover, our implementation leverages the PrCI protocol to gather and convey timing information from the hypervisor to the virtualized system, thereby facilitating precise timing support. A practical adaptation of this framework in the CERBERUS flight control system demonstrates the practical applicability of T-Visor in complex industrial settings. Our evaluation of the scheduling algorithm reveals a negligible processing delay and a mere 2.66% increase in CPU utilization.

A panoramic image capturing technique uses an external IMU to synchronize images with temporal and spatial data, thereby correcting the 2D and 3D misalignment issues often encountered. To improve the rendering quality, the technique also incorporates high-precision IMU readings to accurately record scene geometry and provide an accurate view of the captured scene. A key drawback of traditional panoramic stitching methods is that they rely on precise timing synchronization between IMUs and cameras, a requirement that becomes impractical when using wireless cameras for panoramic rendering. A proposed timing synchronization technique uses an one-way communication method to calculate data transfer delay and compensate for drift accumulation errors, thereby successfully synchronized, providing high-quality panoramic rendering even with wireless cameras. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the technique in achieving accurate synchronization, a typical requirement for rendering high-quality images.

Within a network of oscillators, we've discovered unique stable patterns called chimeras. These patterns emerge when some oscillators synchronize with each other while others independently oscillate. We've found that increasing the diversity among oscillators can lead to more stable chimeras within the same network configuration. Additionally, we've found that smaller groups of synchronized oscillators require more diverse internal workings in order to resist influences from neighboring non-synchronized oscillators. These findings offer valuable new insights into the complex world of chiral oscillations.

One of the main advantages of learning-based approaches to nonlinear control is their ability to tackle complex continuous-state control problems. However, their key shortcoming is that trained controllers can sometimes experience system failure due to unanticipated disturbances. To mitigate this issue, some recent methods have been developed. This paper provides a comprehensive examination of these new techniques, describing them as enforcing a "no surprises" condition on the control system's dynamics. The paper also presents an in-depth analysis of a specific method called Certified Neural Network Dynamics, which ensures that the system's equations remain intact even when subject to adversarial noise below a certain threshold. The paper demonstrates through a concrete example that imposing this noise limit can dramatically enhance the safety of learned controllers, showcasing through simulation that certifying a dynamics model can prevent system failure due to noise. Furthermore, the paper describes a challenge in extending this certification approach to control systems and presents some initial findings on how to certify basic feedback controllers.

Over an algebraically closed field, given a finite, undirected simple graph, we define a family of slice algebras associated with its configurations and embed these algebras within a closed subvariety of bounded dimension, comprising modified matrix or tensor algebras derived from the graph.

We investigate reflected entanglement spectra within the context of random tensor networks at non-zero temperature. Our research demonstrates that these spectra constitute a probabilistic model distinct from the conventional R'enyi spectrum, yet we identify a specific condition under which they are equivalent. Additionally, we establish that the reflected spectrum's width increases linearly with time within the ballistic regime of isolated tensors.

Our investigation involves identifying factors that influence persistence in a wide range of dynamical systems, consisting of smooth, non-linearity based maps on smooth, compact spaces, using Baire category and dense orbit principles. In a two-dimensional plane, we demonstrate that for maps induced from a uniformly continuous dynamics, the probability of a random initial condition resulting in persistence is nearly one, represented as $(\log N)(1/\log T)$. The rate of this probability, quantified as the ratio of the logarithms, can be exchanged for other standard smooth invariants when appropriate criteria for a space are met. Additionally, we propose that for maps with certain properties, the probability of persistence is bounded by a function decreasing towards zero as the map's iteration number increases towards infinity.

We are investigating global bifurcations of local non-hyperbolicity in quadratic diffeomorphisms at infinity. The parameter space of these maps is divided into distinct regions, each corresponding to a different type of orbit at infinity. The boundaries between these areas are formed by periodic orbits that play a crucial role in understanding the map's behavior as parameters are varied. The location of these periodic orbits is not influenced by the other bifurcation mechanisms and serves as a framework for understanding how the other features intersect with the parameter space. The number and location of these periodic orbits vary depending on the sign of the parameter and can be determined precisely in all cases except when the parameter is negative, in which case the location of the orbits is determined by the solutions to a transcendental equation, which also governs the location of other bifurcation mechanisms. The behavior of these maps when the parameter is negative is particularly challenging due to the presence of multiple mechanisms and the different types of bifurcations that occur. By varying the parameters in a way that focuses on a small region of the parameter space, it is possible to observe all of the features that arise from the different types of bifurcations that occur. The dynamics of these maps are particularly well understood when the parameter is non-negative due to the different types of linear regions that are present. The number of these regions can be precisely determined in all cases and their location varies continuously with the parameter. The map's behavior at these locations is

The Holton-Semihamiltonian gravity model, previously developed in geometry, is demonstrated to have a simplified representation similar to Chern-Simons gauge theory but with an added adaptation of gauge transformations affecting both the gauge and gauge matrix. By comparing the gravity model with both the Poincaré and loop quantum gravity theories, it's observed that the first is inconsistent but the second may be transformed into the Holton-Simhamilton gravity model, providing a new understanding of gravity holonomy distinct from gauge theory, suggesting an alternative to both PRLQG and LQG.

We calculate the asymptotic behavior of random variables using normal comparison, then apply this to study the limit distribution of ratios between (degenerate or nondegenerate) random variables. We utilize this to study ratios of sample mean and minimum, maximum, or second statistic in i.i.d. settings, as well as Bernoulli, Poisson, and binomial distributions. These studies reveal that these ratios converge in law to nondegenerate random variables, which can be either uniform on zero-one or mixed uniform on zero-one and uniform on zero-one-half to one distributions. We extend this to study the limit distribution of ratios of (degenerate or nondegenerate) random variables in i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. Bernoulli, Poisson, and binomial distributions. These studies reveal that these ratios converge in law to either uniform on zero-one or mixed uniform on zero-one and uniform on zero-one-half to one distributions. These findings help us determine the limit distribution of ratios of (degenerate or nondegenerate) random variables in i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. cases.

We've developed a novel approach to tunneling time by analyzing the quantum transfer event through a two-level quantum system influenced by a fluctuating magnetic field caused by spin fluctuations. From an operator perspective unconnected to system propagation, we derived a time measure by calculating the average that demonstrates this time frame is equivalent to the traditional tunneling time determined solely by the system itself. Further, when fluctuating parameters depend on the system's eigenstates, the quantum system's tunneling time shows a degree of randomness. This random element can be understood as an inelastic tunneling process influenced by a short-lived interaction with a spin fluctuation, taking place between the system's eigenstates, where the quantum system spends time varying according to both states. When spin fluctuations are weak, the quantum system's tunneling time shows coherence between quantum states, while when spin fluctuations are strong, the quantum system exhibits an inelastic tunneling process, allowing the quantum system to transition via a short-lived state overlapping with both quantum states.

Our work involves the calculation of relativistic corrections to amplitudes containing P-wave charmonium mesons produced in $e^+e^-$ annihilation. The calculations consider compact eigenstates and interaction eigenstates equally, with a specific focus on how relativistic corrections impact the distribution of states between these two bases. Our findings show that relativistic corrections have a limited impact on the wave functions at the center-of-mass frame, but significant effects are observed when comparing charm and charm-prime distributions within the same basis. The interactions between particles are described using a $^3S_1$-^3 D_1 Lagrangian with a specific coupling strength. Our analysis predicts that the mass splittings between D* and D* prime will be around 25-30 MeV, and further details on this interaction can be obtained by analyzing the phase shift near the threshold.

We investigate the implementation of Ramsey interferometry with a Bose-Einstein condensate that undergoes optical pumping to populate the $m_F=0$ state of a $^7$Li nuclear spin system with a $F=1$ spin and apply generalized Hadamard transformations to its wave packet. In the linear case, these transformations correspond to a destructive interference of the states with $m_F=0$ and $m_F=1$. We show that a destructive interference can also be achieved with a non-linear transformation, resulting in the same sensitivity but with less loss of population. Moreover, we demonstrate that non-linear transformations can potentially reach the Heisenberg limit with our system, whereas linear transformations fall short due to a limited population. Non-linear transformations can also be made robust against spin-exchange collisions by applying a time-average averaging technique, which enables them to surpass the accuracy of linear transformations in this context as well.

Building on previous research by E. Berker, an examination of non-relational information theory's connection to existing theories is re-established, focusing on a specific quantum system. Within this quantum system, the underlying physical laws are derived from classical information theory's fundamental principles. This unifies two previously separate approaches: a formal study of a particular quantum system, and a more recent formal study by S. Shapere and A. Wilce. A central aspect of our research involves proving that our quantum system gives rise to a Lagrangian description, which shares similarities with a specific general relativity model. As a result, an in-depth comparison between two different general relativity models, one based on E. Bergshoeff, O. Hartmann, and T. Damour's work, and the other developed by S. Shapere and A. Wilce, is possible through their eBMS and BMS charges analysis. Notably, the charges derived from eBMS have connections to soft news and a specific set of charges, which include BMS and Schwarzian modes.

Deep neural networks' training has been extensively researched due to their inherent complexity. A novel, straightforward approach to refining classification accuracy is presented, involving the methodation of ensemble method, wherein the last layer's weights are adjusted via backpropagation to optimize performance. Compared to benchmark methods, such as dropout and residual learning, this approach has been rigorously tested using different datasets and has consistently outperformed these methods. Moreover, two critical aspects have been evaluated: the time complexity of this proposed ensemble method and its sensitivity to hyperparameters. In terms of efficiency, due to the absence of ensembling, this method has a substantial advantage. Additionally, several hyperparameters have been examined to ensure their optimal value for optimal performance of this proposed ensemble method.

We explain a generalized connection's relationship to isometric deformations of its associated metric, specifically that generalized connections are tied to invariant generalized calibrations and that local representations of generalized Lie algebras reflect metric deformations and their corresponding generalized curvatures, which must be zero for the original metric. We also demonstrate that Ricci flat metrics have generalized connections with vanishing generalized curvatures if the generalized Lie algebra is nilpotent.

We establish a concept of complete mapping for polynomial functions defined over finite fields and show how this leads to the development of efficient algorithms for splitting and matching tasks in finite field arithmetic. These algorithms enable the efficient computation of inverse elements, sine, cosine, and other root-finding problems in finite fields, achieving time complexities of $O(n\log n)$ and $O(n\exp(\alpha n)$, where $\alpha = 0.271001539.$

Visual inspection by a trained individual is currently considered the standard method for intestinal parasite diagnosis worldwide, despite its potential for numerous errors due to the low prevalence of these parasites and the visual similarity of their eggs or larvae. Consequently, the need has arisen for more accurate and reliable diagnostic methods than visual inspection. Research aimed at developing alternative protocols using optical detection has been conducted, as well as experiments to analyze the effectiveness of different lighting conditions on sample analysis. Although previous studies have explored diagnostic techniques based on various light sources, such as white, UV, or fluorescent light, this research alone does not constitute a comprehensive assessment of the reliability of optical-based methods for intestinal parasite diagnosis. Therefore, the goal of this study was to review and synthesize the outcomes of numerous Optical-based Diagnostic Experiments (ODEs) to assess the reliability of optical-based methods for parasitic diagnosis, analyze the implications of their results, and suggest areas of improvement for future research in this field.

This study employs the variational approximation method with Isaacs-type constraints to tackle nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, yielding a viscosity solution that obviates the need for direct verification in action spaces. By recognizing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations as the continuous analog of two-player, zero-sum games involving value functions, we apply the variational approximation method to model stochastic Volterra integral equations (VIEs) and derive a sequence of discrete-time equations that converge to their limit. Although individually unfeasible, the approximate discrete-time equations form a viable framework for solving the original Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, with theoretical evidence showing their equivalence as the limit of a specific stochastic game as the number of players approaches infinity.

This paper describes a control system for a quadcopter using a combination of PID controllers and Genetic Filter adaptation to enhance robustness during aerial maneuvers. The PID controllers guarantee the achievement of a stable altitude by deriving the vertical velocity from the altitude signal through integration. However, real-world conditions, particularly external disturbances, prevent the model from accurately replicating actual quadcopter behavior. To address this issue, the Genetic Filter iteratively adjusts the model's dynamic behavior to closely match the desired system dynamics, thereby increasing precision. Experimental results using MATLAB/Simulink demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control method, and its reliability in achieving precise system dynamics was confirmed through multiple simulations.

We apply the Bayesian neural network approach, a highly efficient machine learning method, to calculate the pion-nucleon sigma term and extract the quark mass. Utilizing the published GNOM data generated with the most recent and accurate actions, we conducted two distinct calculations: one utilizing simulated data to mimic an actual lattice calculation and the other using the actual results. Our simulations produced a quark mass of approximately 2.64~MeV, with a precision of 0.16~MeV. We also carried out a simulation using weighted averages of published results and obtained a quark mass of approximately 2.73~MeV, with a precision of 0.16~MeV. Our calculations demonstrate that when sufficient data points are available, this machine learning method can achieve high precision when applied to real data. Furthermore, our study reveals that using simulated data provides better control over systematic errors compared to using actual results. Given its versatility and accuracy, this machine learning approach holds significant promise for various low-energy, lattice QCD calculations.

The CMS detector's silicon pixel detector underwent upgrades after 2016, introduced by four new detector modules with a sandwich structure and a new readout chip designed to increase readout efficiency and reduce mechanical errors. By splitting the readout process off from the data generation, the detector is now capable of providing online global trigger efficiency calculations. Although this design modification resulted in increased readout complexity and higher demands on the readout system, the current implementation has successfully addressed these challenges with minimal cost in terms of readout bandwidth. In addition, data from the Big Brother monitoring system has enabled real-time diagnostics of the readout system's performance. By the end of 2016, two out of six pixel split institute modules were equipped with the new design, which has allowed for pilot analyses that demonstrate its effectiveness in physics research. A summary of the hardware and software modifications, procedures for the design and testing of the new modules, and the results of the pilot analyses will be presented in this article.

We conducted an analysis of publicly available public imaging data for 49,680 galaxies at redshifts z > 0.03 from the SDSS DR8. We identified 1,067 active galaxies by applying established filters for the presence of broad and narrow emission lines. Utilizing novel photometricscatters and emission line diagnostics, our classifications revealed 693 active galaxies (increasing to 1,047 active galaxies when using conservative estimates), expanding the current catalog of galaxy hosts by 43 new systems. Broad line AGN exhibited higher detection rates at higher redshifts, whereas narrow line AGN were more effectively identified at lower z values. Our research further leverages the SCOSTECKA code to estimate broad line scattering properties and assess the detection efficiency of active galaxies based on emission line width. The results were complemented by X-ray and gamma-ray observations, yielding 153 matches with X-ray sources (primary priority), 28 matches with gamma-ray sources (including 17 matches with the CTA's target list, secondary priority), and 1,068 matches with other databases (no matching priority). The majority of active galaxies (about 60%) were previously undetected, whereas some of their broad line counterparts (approximately 21%) had not yet been referenced in the SIMBAD database. Due to the public nature of our data, any reference or follow-up observation can now be initiated without needing to send us data or money. Note that if you send us data you

A comprehensive approach is adopted to analyze the impact of the short-range correlations in nuclei on the neutron density gradient. Nuclear models are modified to account for the short-range correlations in pure neutron and neutron-proton states using the Spectral Function, which is then used to build the Fourier transform. This allows a precise assessment of how the short-range correlations affect the neutron density gradient in several neutron-rich tin isotopes. The study reveals that the neutron density gradient is significantly affected by the short-range correlations, but its dependence on isospin varies. In tin isotopes up to N = 50, the short-range correlations contribute to a thicker neutron skin, an average thickness increase of approximately 0.2 fm. This indicates the short-range correlations play a vital role in an extensive range of isotopes, particularly in the study of the neutron skin. Moreover, the variation in the effective nuclear Hamiltonian due to the short-range correlations reveals an asymmetry energy fluctuation of about 12 MeV across the studied tin isotopes.

This research investigates the underlying syntax and semantics of complex-valued images, demonstrating that real and complex coefficients have a shared geometric interpretation. A color image is represented by a hierarchical structure consisting of interconnected complex eigenvalues and their geometric relationships. Through geometric transformations and clustering analysis, the image's semantics are identified and a detailed explanation of its geometry is provided. Additionally, the study reveals specific characteristics of complex images, including stable hue shifts and intrinsic color relationships. It also displays inconsistency in color representation and highlights its geometric implications. This research focuses on semantic representation and offers possible applications for detecting image anomalies and identifying complex image patterns.

The geometrical scaling phenomenon in hadron production is examined to determine if it's caused by the gluon distribution saturation. By analyzing collisions at different energy densities and sizes in various nucleon-nucleon and photon-nucleon experiments, a single scaling function is found. This function represents the behavior of gluon distribution in saturation mode. To understand the scaling behavior, a new parameter, the effective impact parameter, is introduced. This parameter accounts for changes in nucleon sizes and collision geometry throughout different energy levels. Hadron production at the Large Hadron Collider at 2.76 TeV and smaller experiments such as the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) are compared to fix the scaling parameter, showing that it matches when nuclear anti-nuclear particles are measured at the same energy levels. Additionally, a new formula representing gluon distribution in saturation mode is proposed and tested, showing strong agreement. This formula provides separate parameters for gluon number and saturation density, supporting recent observations about these parameters in nuclei.

In an earlier study (PATEL21), I explored CC-SNe events that occur within the host galaxy by simulating core-collapse supernovae using a probability-based method. I compared the results with observations of r-process elements from high-metallicity stars within the galaxy. This time, I've revised the approach by randomly selecting CC-SNe events from a pre-defined distribution that reflects the mass of CC-SNe events that occur naturally. I achieved this by utilizing a pre-simulated distribution that was derived from a separate set of binary star evolutionary models. I've maintained consistency between the selection method and the underlying models. Furthermore, I've updated the initial mass function of CC-SNe events that are based on metallicities within the galaxy, as opposed to being based on CC-SNe event rates. By integrating binary star evolutionary models that include binary interactions and mass transfer, I've simulated approximately 4 million such events. I've used these simulations to determine the enrichment of elements that are produced by the r-process within the galaxy. I've compared the results to observations of r-process elements from high-metallicity stars in the galaxy. I've performed an analysis of elements that are produced by the r-process but with the r-process abundance pattern of stars that are metal-poor. I've found that the current understanding of CC-SNe events that occur naturally and binary star evolutionary models that include binary interactions and mass transfer suggest that the CC-SNe events that occur naturally produce elements that are produced by the

In this research, we investigate how including fabricated features generated using various methods affects the performance of machine learning models. We expect such surrogate features to be correlated with the target response and, consequently, boost the model's capabilities. However, the extent to which this happens depends on the features' degree of association with the target, as well as how much information they reveal about it. We expect the performance gain to be largest when the features strongly predict the target, with this advantage diminishing as the features become less informative. To examine these dynamics, we create scenarios with varying degrees of target predictability and features' informativeness, and evaluate how different feature generation methods affect the performance of common machine learning models on these scenarios. Notably, when the features are highly predictive, using symmetrical features generally yields better results than using asymmetric features across all models we test. Additionally, incorporating randomly generated features does not hinder a model's performance, as long as it does not contain any useful information for the target response. Interestingly, incorporating features that are somewhat predictive but weak in upscaling yields lower performance, as the features do not provide enough target information.

Our analysis compares the potential scalability of two quantum algorithms for training variational quantum models: a method that uses quantum gradient descent from the output of a quantum circuit and another that uses classical processing to approximate the output before applying gradient descent. By examining the impact of error in the approximate output on the performance of these two algorithms, we identify non-convergence of the quantum algorithm under specific conditions, which is not a concern for the classical method. Our analysis considers the effects of two types of loss functions, equal variance and conditional variance, leading to distinct conclusions regarding which loss function is more favorable in the quantum setting.

This work focuses on exploring pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds. The research begins by classifying warped product semi-slant submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds. The findings demonstrate that such submanifolds are either perpendicular and pointed, or they possess a complex structure with a flat metric, being either a Kaehler submanifold with a trivial distribution or a parallel distribution with a twisted product structure. Building on this classification, the study examines more general cases of pointwise semi-slant submanifolds. The key results indicate that these too are either perpendicular and pointed, or they exhibit a unique geometric characteristic of being a twisted product submanifold with a flat distribution. The latter scenario presents an example of a twisted product submanifold that is not a semi-slant submanifold.

The COHERENT experiment used a 139 fb$^{-1}$ dataset in 2017 to analyze CEvNS with varying energies. Two specific sub-experiments, LAr and NaI, provided data that was analyzed over narrow and broad energy ranges. With the LAr data providing the most comprehensive insights, a combined analysis was conducted. By generating a phenomenological Lagrangian that incorporated the $Z$ and $\gamma$ propagators, an analysis was carried out based on the relativistic phenomenology form factor framework. By incorporating nuclear models into the analysis, both standard and general relativity contributions were considered. By using a Bayesian approach in the analysis, multiple parameters were examined and their most likely values were determined. By including the CEvNS data in the analysis of standard model parameters, an analysis was carried out and the most likely values were determined. By examining specific parameter correlations, both the electron and muon EDMs were analyzed and the most likely limits were determined.

Active particles with specific shapes are gaining attention for their intricate dynamics in confined environments. A novel study focuses on the behavior of two-linked active dimers, where each dimer has localized self-propulsion and a sterically hindered core, allowing us to analyze their rotation in response to external forces and dimensions. By applying torque and varying the size difference between the dimers, we discovered both permanent and transient rotations, which can be likened to a steering wheel in operation at the molecular level. Furthermore, we found that the strength of self-propulsion significantly influences the range of stable equilibria, leading to active dimers exhibiting a significant contradiction of their random motion, where the likelihood of moving to the left and right is significantly different.

Theoretical predictions for magnetorotons, an extension of minons, have been made in a graphene-like two-valley system with the $nu=2/7$ quantum Hall effect. Focusing on this $nu=2/7$ system, researchers have made detailed calculations regarding the energy profiles, thermal behaviors, and chirality of magnetorotons at a lattice level. Their findings show that, at a lattice, magnetorotons from the $nu=2/7$ quantum Hall effect exhibit non-zero energy, temperature, and angular momentum, contrasting with their massless counterparts in the $nu=2/9$ state. Moreover, their spin-degenerate, paraparticle-fermion pair characteristics, born from combining single-particle Landau levels and collective dephasing states, result in a finite gap to the surrounding Hall states, indicating a unique mix of both single-particle and collective physical properties. Lastly, researchers have demonstrated the existence of a pseudo-spin in the system, incorporating a non-trivial effective Hall response, notably distinct from its actual Hall response. This pseudo-spin, born from combining translation symmetry and valley symmetry, exhibits a one-seventh fractional quantization, challenging conventional understanding of translation and valley symmetries.

Our investigation expands upon the recent findings of Andresen et al, who analyzed epidemics on general networks in MathPhys, highlighting the usefulness of the approximate upper bound derived from the infrared catastrophe in assessing approximate equilibrium state metrics. We enhance their work by easing strict partition constraints, considering subsets with positive and negative multiplicities. This modified approach is applied to the exact equilibrium solution of a symmetric model by Dombrowski et al in NatComm, a tightly connected graph with multiple clusters. The findings demonstrate that approximate equilibrium statistics can still be quite accurate even when far from exact equilibrium, as long as sufficient time has elapsed since the last jump event.

There are several CMB estimation techniques that can mitigate noise from surveys, such as XMM-Newton, but these estimators introduce bias into the maps. Since their algorithms don't perfectly reverse the noise, residual bias remains. A common challenge with biased estimators is that they introduce an uneven distribution of errors, which in turn affects parameter estimates by introducing systematic errors. A new combination technique, specifically designed for CMB purposes, has been found to effectively counteract the residual bias caused by point sources, ensuring an approximately Gaussian distribution of errors. The technique has been found particularly useful in maps created using the XMM-Newton telescope's noise map.

This study proposes a task-based instruction design that integrates elements of
pedagogical and pragmatist approaches, leveraging these concepts in a novel way.
The instruction focuses on practical problem-solving skills, framing theoretical
explanations through real-world examples and highlighting the importance of
applying knowledge effectively. By adopting a pragmatist perspective on task-based
learning, it is possible to recontextualize pedagogical principles within a more
effective operational framework. The study demonstrates that task-based
instruction rooted in pragmatism can enhance students' ability to comprehend and
apply theory, ultimately leading to improved learning outcomes in practical
scenarios.

A shadow tomography approach yields an accurate description of a quantum state's defining characteristics without the need for full measurement data, relying on positive operator-valued measurements that can be combined algebraically. We investigate the amount of information gained from a partial measurement record by creating shadows of arbitrary quantum states and establish novel bounds on the error of approximate state representations, formulated in terms of the existing entropy measures for quantum states. Through numerical evaluation, we demonstrate that shadow tomography can effectively capture certain properties of highly entangled states, known as golf balls, and handle multiple initial states simultaneously with significantly reduced data collection, ultimately leading to more efficient data collection for multiple task adaptations.

In this paper, we demonstrate that for any convex shape in the plane with area $A$, perimeter $P$, inradius $r$, and circumradius $R$, the following inequalities hold: 
$P^2\ge 4A$, 
$P^2\ge 4A/(1-\sqrt{1-r^2})$, 
$P^2\ge 4A/(1+\sqrt{1-R^2})$, 
$P^2\ge 4A/(1+\sqrt{1-R^2-2rR})$, 
$P^2\ge 4A/(1+\sqrt{(1-R^2)(1-r^2)/((1-r^2)^2+4r^2R^2))$,
with equality occurring when the shape is a circle. We also discuss and visualize narrowest and thinnest polygons for a given area.

This paper investigates a model for serving users at fixed locations with a UAV carrying a portable base station. Without prior knowledge of where users are, the model involves designing a flight path to maximize the number of users served within a limited time. This problem can be broken down into two parts: the UAV collecting data at specific locations. This simplifies the model, as gathering data at a limited number of locations along the optimal flight path is equivalent to gathering data along the optimal flight path after the optimal locations have been determined. This connection reveals that the model has two optimization components, associated with the UAV trajectory and user locations where data is collected. This relationship led to the development of two solutions: an efficient, globally-optimal solution for small problems and a heuristic solution for large problems. This new model extends previous work, which considered serving users at fixed locations with a base station stationed at a known location, to a scenario where the base station is mobile and the user locations are unknown.

We conducted extensive density functional theory calculations of bilayer graphene within the range function approximation framework, examining both the spatial arrangements of atoms during bonding and bonding structures. All interactions within the model were three-dimensional, not limited to layers, and accounted for in the total energy calculation. We identified six possible bonding configurations in relation to the symmetrical pattern of rotating atoms, denoted as C0, and five distinct nematic patterns with varying rotations: N-60, N-30, N+30, N+60. Notably, in the nematic state (N-60, N-30, N+30, N+60), the pattern of rotating atoms changes, and a distinct rotational symmetry emerges, different from the uniform C0 configuration. We also determined the energy levels of each configuration, revealing that the nematic states have lower energy and only the C0 configuration exhibits symmetry with respect to rotation of 60 degrees. Utilizing these results, we developed a theoretical model for the purpose of analysis, and through the theory of elasticity, we calculated the type of distortion that occurs when subjected to in-plane tension and the value of the corresponding constant, matching the findings from our calculation of the interaction between valence bands and those from tight-binding model. We further obtained the constant of interaction between valence bands from tight-binding model, and revealed that in the nematic state, the distance between layers changes based on the distance between atoms within a layer, demonstrating sensitivity of interaction between layers to the shape

The properties of endofullerenes on a substrate receive direct modification due to their interaction with the substrate's weak van der Waals force, causing an alteration in their magnetic and electric characteristics in the process. A comparative study between Stefatene and Petrafene, encapsulating Mg atom inside C40 carbon shell, is examined with a (60, 6) substrate implantation, further evaluated through implantation, rotation, and vibrational analysis, ultimately resulting in calculated properties such as energy levels, symmetries, and response to light. By analyzing these properties both in free form and on a substrate, it becomes apparent that the substrate's implantation results in distinct and contrasting changes in Stefatene and Petrafene, manifesting as variations in their energy levels, symmetries, and photoemission spectra.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things has led to an unprecedented surge in device connections, which, coupled with the inherent security vulnerabilities of these devices, poses significant risks to established networks and data infrastructures. Security risks are further compounded by the possibility of malicious activities and compromised security standards. Consequently, there is an pressing need to develop systematic approaches to evaluating the security of IoT systems and pinpointing security breaches. This research presents a cutting-edge security evaluation framework for IoT systems, incorporating an extensive range of attributes to provide a comprehensive and multi-faceted assessment. The framework incorporates various key attributes, including data protection and privacy, to ensure a thorough examination of IoT system security. By leveraging a systematic evaluation method, it is possible to identify essential security parameters and associated metrics that serve as indicators of potential risks. This research offers a flexible and adaptable security evaluation framework that addresses the challenges posed by IoT system security and data protection.

To increase the accuracy of inaccuracy in high-precision experiments. We introduce a Bayesian approach to designing experiments that utilizing a Gaussian process to model uncertainty yields more precise results than standard protocols in Ramsey measurements. When using low-fidelity measurements, our Bayesian approach outperforms other protocols by achieving the highest possible precision in the experiment's outcome. Additionally, we apply the Bayesian approach to a scenario with multiple parameters, demonstrating its efficiency and adaptive ability to target areas of highest uncertainty. The paper provides a practical example of how the Bayesian approach can be utilized, suggesting that it can also be applied to other precision measurement techniques.

The varying node roles in networks have garnered significant attention within research. To identify these roles, Gromov centrality has been proposed as an extension to the original centrality algorithm. By re-examining the algorithm's components, it was observed that the centrality metric shares similarities with the widely used PageRank method. To differentiate itself, Gromov centrality incorporates an extra factor, by deviating from the stochastic ordering defined by the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the transition matrix. As a result, Gromov centrality focuses exclusively on the dominant eigenspace. To further investigate the algorithm's capabilities and inaccuracies, multiple studies employed various applications, including an analysis of undirected and multi-type networks to calculate a metric close to degree-based centrality. Additionally, an in-depth examination of a leader-follower network within the stochastic death-grip model was carried out to compare with PageRank's performance in separating distinct types of nodes within a directed bi-linear network and a linear network with non-linear interactions between nodes in different types.

Our universe's evolution follows a predetermined timeline from infiniteness to finiteness that has already begun, accompanied by an inherent expansion beyond our observable realm. This natural sequence is mirrored in other aspects, such as the increasing distance between Earth and the sun over 4.5 billion years, and is found in cosmic structures like the spiral shape of galaxies, the gradual fading of binary stars, and the sensitivity of their orbital cycles. The sequence can be reproduced by mathematical models that consider the infinite past, offering a new understanding of the universe's evolution, its age, and its formation timeframes, and providing a basis for predicting future developments. The models indicate that our universe is entering a stage of stabilization, marking the end of an eternity of cycles and scales imbalance, and heralding the start of a period of symmetry and harmony. The universe's age can be determined by analyzing the orbital periods of binary systems, and the expansion beyond its observable realm can be studied by examining the sensitivity of cosmic resonators like quasars and pulsars. The latter's research is currently in its initial stages.

Within non-commutative projective space, the closure of an open bundle consisting of matrix polynomials contains comprehensive spectral data, specifically every matrix polynomial of the same size is spectrally related to the bundle's member matrices. We have devised two methods for constructing bundles containing polynomials with shared eigenvalues or eigenvectors. One approach, analogous to classic construction, involves transforming linear subspaces defining the original bundle. Unlike the classical method, our first approach applies to bundles of symmetric or skew-symmetric matrices, providing a broader framework. Our second strategy directly targets matrix polynomials, offering another approach for future research into these spaces. We have also found that a particular matrix, generated from the eigenspaces of the bundle's constituent matrices, plays a crucial role in applying the classical matrix multiplier method, thus facilitating reconstruction in certain cases.

Recent theoretical framework developments in non-geometric string theory have led to a definition of a specific class of algebras, known as continuous-trace algebras, which establish the conditions for the existence of classical T-duals to torus backgrounds. This study focuses on a particular type of continuous-trace algebra associated with $T^2$ and examines its duals, identifying a subset with geometric properties and demonstrating that all T-duals can be categorized into these geometric or non-geometric string theory classes. A key aspect of this work is demonstrating the one-to-one correspondence between the commutators of the group generators and non-geometric Roiban-Siegel-Witten invariants for the associated 4-dimensional manifolds.

Our solution to the generalized Baker's metric problems, yielding concise polynomial time algorithms in graphs excluded a single minor, was achieved through developing a novel embedding approach. This technique has further applications by reducing the distance between pairs of vertices while maintaining non-negative edge weights, although this may come at the cost of exceeding the original edge capacity. By doing so, we can efficiently compute an integer-valued minimum distance between two distant points in k-fold subdivisions of free graphs, thus extending our findings to any k. Notably, our methods also provide valuable tools for solving problems within restricted circuits and have helped us derive new integer programming prototypes with efficient polynomial time algorithms.

In this study, we explore the time-periodic equation $u_t = \Delta u + F(t,x,u)$ within a bounded domain, focusing on the behavior of solutions near the periodic solutions $\phi$. Our analysis reveals that when most initial conditions align with the periodic solutions $\phi$, the solutions $u$ and their pre-images converge to $\phi$ uniformly over time and space. Additionally, we find that for a given time $T$, nearly all solutions whose norms remain below a specified threshold within that time frame will converge to $\phi$.

We have developed quantum algorithms for determining molecular ground states efficiently, based on the principle of actively reducing the variational space.  By applying the ADAPT-VQA protocol in both fermionic and qubit forms, we experienced challenges related to the curse of dimensionality - a problem fermionic systems face due to the exponential growth of the Fock basis with respect to the number of electrons. Furthermore, the need to splice Gaussian basis with a fermionic basis introduced additional complications.  The introduction of quantum embedding concepts helped mitigate these challenges but led to uncontrollable growth of the quantum circuit depth.  The need arose for a protocol capable of balancing the complexity of quantum resources with accuracy.  This drove the creation of the QEB-ADAPT-VQA protocol - an innovative approach utilizing quantum embedding based on density matrices to effectively divide the quantum system into regions of varying density with accurate mapping of the wave function.  By employing this protocol in the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), we referred to it as QEB-ADAPT-VQE.  The protocol has been successfully applied to multiple chemistry problems, resulting in the following observations -  QEB-ADAPT-VQE exhibits comparable performance to fermionic-ADAPT-VQA and qubit-ADAPT-VQA in terms of convergence speed and efficiency but operates within the constraints of the quantum circuit depth deficit with approximately two-thirds the quantum gate count required for optimal performance.  The need for fewer qubits arises from the uniform distribution of density

A new representation learning approach, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), is introduced in this work as an alternative to Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). The DGD is designed to produce an implicit representation by learning a distribution that minimizes the difference between observed data and generated observations. When given labeled data, it naturally forms clusters in the representation space due to its implicit nature. Building on this concept, an unsupervised extension, the Multi-Label Deep Generative Decoder (MLDGD), is developed to handle multiple labels simultaneously. Both the DGD and MLDGD models demonstrate competitive performance against established approaches such as VAEs, Deep Believable Networks (DBNs), and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), across various platforms including an extensive MNIST dataset and fewer dimensions scenarios. Additionally, the MLDGD achieves the best performance among all the models when it comes to a single multiple labeled dataset, the EMNIST dataset. Further analysis, including multiple label prediction and topic visualization, showcases the effectiveness and applicability of these unsupervised learning models in diverse contexts.

We've revised our phenomenological model of the $\Lambda$CDM model to incorporate the concept of "stiffness". In this context, the "stiff" component behaves like a cosmological constant with varying properties based on the model's iteration number. While earlier versions of this model failed to resolve the Hubble tension, adding stiffness led to successful resolution, with different tension-resolution outcomes seen across various model depths. We examined the model's performance using multiple datasets, including supernovae, Hubble space telescope, baryon acoustic oscillations, and others. Our results, however, indicate some conflict between the Hubble lensing data and the model when considering "deep" model parameters. Since we initially allowed for varying parameters such as Hubble constants and matter densities, but later found that some of these properties converged, we were however unable to find a solution that resolved the cosmic calendar tension.

Our investigation of CS, HCN, H$_2$CO, HNC, CH$_3$OH, HCS, and HCN/O in comet C/2015 ER61 involved utilizing ALMA's spectral survey from March 2016, offering observations at four distinct wavelengths. We observed decrease in CS, HNC, and H$_2$CO gas outflow, in contrast to prolonged HCN, HCS, and CH$_3$OH emissions, which may support gas-diffusion driven release or thermal sputtering of grains containing these molecules, further indicating CS, HNC, and H$_2$CO were pre-planetary nucleus origin, whereas HCS, HC$_3$N, and CH$_3$OH originated from parental icy grains. We determined gas production rates of water from March 11-14, CS, HCS, HC$_3$N, and CH$_3$OH from March 12-14, and tracked variations in gas spatial extents, velocities, and line widths, revealing polar outflows, characterized as non-thermal in nature, distinct from cometary plasma environments, supported by inverted gas distributions, super-thermal particles, and velocity scatterings, potentially attributed to particle re-emission at gas speeds or photoionization-driven re-acceleration. Our observations, combining ALMA's new data with existing data on water, gas abundances, gas-mass ratios, gas temperatures, and gas maps, reveal a carbon-rich

Our study focuses on the development of an unsupervised neural speech synthesis model that learns to generate high-quality speech from a massive amount of publicly accessible speech data online. Utilizing only speech waves and a pre-trained hidden representation input, this model is capable of producing speech in a specific language without requiring labeled waveform training data or guidance. We evaluate the output of this unsupervised system against a state-of-the-art supervised speech synthesis model and assess its effectiveness in terms of speech naturalness and intelligibility. Additionally, we demonstrate that this unsupervised learning approach can be effectively applied to a variety of languages with varying levels of resource constraints. Through a text-to-speech application, we showcase the unsupervised system's ability to produce natural, readable speech translations, thereby highlighting its potential utility in speech technology applications.

The free energy density of Tsallis holographic dark energy is expressed in terms of the relative entropy, and its interacting property is represented by a parameter associated with entropy production in stochastic processes. This parameter serves as a scaling factor for the bulk energy density. To evaluate the validity of the modified Tsallis entropy, the model is compared with three cosmological parameters, including Hubble parameter, cosmic figure of merit, and deceleration parameter. This interaction coupling parameter can only take on values between zero and two, as below zero it would represent backwards interaction, and above two it would violate the energy condition, indicating that later universal time values may lead to a larger interaction coupling parameter. Consequently, the model could experience an accelerating phase both with and without interaction. Furthermore, the cosmic figure of merit suggests that later interaction coupling parameters couple with the energy density at later times. Additionally, this model could accommodate a dark energy transition, as the interaction coupling parameter can reach the maximum allowed value around the present time, leading to an accelerating universe.

A newly devised investment ratio (IR) metric will be introduced and used in performance evaluations through a comprehensive analysis of plenary sessions at the 21st Annual EuroCAD Conference. The study compares the optimal solutions achieved by students in those plenary sessions against their self-reported solutions. For each problem area, a cumulative distribution of log-transformed score improvements is graphed to identify underperforming areas and, conversely, those where students have successfully improved upon their personal bests. The raw Plenary Score and an adjusted overall evaluation metric called Modified Plenary Score will also be considered as potential solutions in performance optimization. The investment ratio will quantify how effectively these solution paths directly contribute to improved outcomes, allowing for problem-specific interpretations. For instance, an IR of 130 indicates that plenary solutions add value to 77% of student-submitted solutions and are detrimental for 23%. In problem areas exhibiting negative IR values, students have often prioritized shorter execution times over accuracy, as reflected in simplified problem examples. Based on the findings, it is suggested that a significant 'give-back' bonus be awarded for within-box execution performance in certain problem areas and that a safety margin be maintained for execution time in others.

In the framework of synthetic differential geometry, we introduce the notions of source path and source simply connected groupoid, and subsequently develop the theory of source loops and source loop groups. Furthermore, we explore the analogues of classical constructively defined objects such as loops, loop groups, and braids.

In response to the rising adoption of Software as a Service (SaaS), our research tackles the security concerns associated with multi-repository remote development practices. Our Dynaswap project, a hybrid solution combining GitLab and Azure DevOps, focuses on safeguarding associated workflows using cutting-edge technologies like Zero Knowledge Proofs, Differential Privacy, and Blockchain. This innovative approach integrates cutting-edge security mechanisms to ensure the seamless protection of source code, shared files, and sensitive information. The Dynaswap prototype, built using the Azure Blockchain Servces and StonkStack frameworks, embodies our findings. This work offers insights capable of informing the development of better security solutions. Additionally, our research also explores the possibility of expanding Dynaswap to provide transparent workflow auditing functions.

Recent research has shown that Contrastive Learning can be successfully applied to Supervised Pre-training, reducing reliance on unsupervised instance-level negative mining and improving the model's capacity to capture complex, multi-class relationships. Nevertheless, conventional Contrastive Learning methods have been shown to have limitations in capturing semantic dependencies in Sentiment Analysis, particularly when dealing with varied expression patterns across different groups of positive and negative reviews. From a counterfactual perspective, we propose a novel Supervised Contrastive Pre-training framework that introduces contrastive learning directly at the level of sentences, demonstrating enhanced capture of semantic dependencies. By incorporating contrastive learning into PLSA, our approach exhibits improved performance compared to the state-of-the-art, with results supported by qualitative analysis of contrastive examples from Chinese product reviews.

Individuals with decreased immune capacity due to certain conditions or medications are more susceptible to the bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes, which causes listeriosis.  A mathematical model previously developed simulates the immunocompetent individual's interaction with L. monocytogenes, taking into account factors such as the reduction of stomach acid levels, the pathogen's internalization into host cells, and the host's immune response. Previous studies utilizing the model revealed that anti-nausea medication use decreases the time it takes for listeriosis to occur, changes the threshold for gastric acid production, and does not affect the sensitivity of the immune system to the pathogen. Building on this initial research, this paper applies the model to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) disorders such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), which affects gastric acid production and the pathogen's invasion into host cells. Our analysis examines how simulated simulations of the model can be utilized to estimate CAH's impact on the host's susceptibility to L. monocytogenes, providing further understanding of how immunocompetency affects listeriosis, as well as potential public health implications for individuals with HPA disorders or compromised immune systems.

This study proposes a 1.43-bit secure multiuser communication system that incorporates reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and has considered the impact of transceiver and surface hardware impairments. To maximize the private rate for users, the proposed algorithm optimizes the surface's phase shift and the transmission power of the transmitters, in a decentralized manner. This optimization is carried out while taking into account the impact of other users' attacks and the need to maintain a stable system. The proposed algorithm is computationally efficient and has considered the presence of an adversary, which is controlled using the Lindst\"eden, Kiefer, and Kiefer theorem. The simulations demonstrate the proposed solution's ability to ensure secure communication in the presence of hardware impairments. All simulation results have been verified analytically through the derivation of closed-form expressions for the minimum sum-rate and the sum of private rates. These expressions are shown to be in good agreement with the results of the simulations. Current reinforcement learning theories focus on optimizing the agent's value function and predict its performance better than its current actions. Yet, when the agent makes mistakes, this approach can lead to exaggerated estimates of the value function. To address this issue, this paper explores "hindsight summarization" as an alternative. Hindsight summarization implies that instead of relying on specific past experiences, the agent remembers key aspects of those scenarios and uses them as knowledge to inform future decisions. By incorporating this concept into the reward structure, the paper showcases an empirical method which minimizes the variance of the reward signal in comparison to existing models. Furthermore, the paper highlights the benefits of this new scheme, demonstrating reduced indication of out-of-date experiences and improved resistance to techniques that attempt to manipulate the environment for positive outcomes.

Between 2017 and 2020, NASA's Parker Solar Probe (PSP) operated close to the Sun, offering exceptional opportunities to examine interplanetary pickup ions (PIPIs) in the solar energy range. The mission provides a unique perspective on the acceleration of particles within less than 1.6 AU of the Sun. To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis was conducted on PPI distributions retrieved during PSP's Early Lightscapes mission phase. To evaluate spatio-temporal variations, measurements from four detectors on the Solar Investigative Investigation (Suitable) instrument were examined. The mission showed that at close range the energy distributions of pickup ions are more even and lower than those observed at 1 AU. As a result, a lower threshold of solar acceleration was detected than initially expected based on data from the Ulysses mission. However, during PSP's approach to the Sun, significant outbursts of solar acceleration occurred, as seen in mid-2017 at 28.3 AU and in 2018 at 30.3 AU during Perihelion. The increased rate of particle acceleration corresponds to shock events created by changing magnetic field conditions. To further investigate these findings, a theoretical model intended to forecast energy distributions of PPIs in three-dimensional solar environments is being developed.

We provide a context-independent definition of the concept of local triviality for the action of a $C^*$-algebra encoded by a locally compact group $G$, which corresponds to the concept of freeness in the case of a group $C^*$-algebra. We prove that this concept is equivalent to the concept of freeness for a $G$-space with a locally trivial $G$-action and also to the weak Mackey condition for a $G$-bundle with fiber being a unital $C^*$-algebra.
