We've developed a hybrid random network model with adjustable preferential attachment and edge rewiring capabilities. This type of model can capture diverse real-world networks by balancing the effects of degree distributions and clustering. Our analysis focuses on smaller-sized networks, revealing details such as in- and out-degree distributions, as well as the relationship between a node's in- and out-degrees. Notably, our findings indicate that for our model, the in- and out-degree distributions converge as the system evolves, whereas for earlier models with preferential attachment and edge rewiring, these distributions remained distinct. Unlike a typical preferential attachment network, our hybrid model exhibits degree distributions that manifest more rapidly in the initial stages and then settle at a power law in the long run. Furthermore, the model features pair-wise degree correlations that diminish over time, as well as a mixing rate that grows linearly with the number of nodes and a clustering coefficient that approaches a power law as the system evolves. Our investigation also reveals that at the initial stages, nodes with higher degrees accumulate more rapidly, as well as the approach to the power law observed in the in- and out-degree distributions. Notably, the mixing rate of our hybrid model is similar to that of a pure preferential attachment network, as well as other rewiring models. Our research demonstrates that the evolved hybrid network shares key statistical characteristics with a pure preferential attachment network, as well as other real-world and theoretical models, making it a versatile tool for modeling complex networks

In the context of Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G technologies, IoT devices operate simultaneously using diverse radio access technologies to facilitate simultaneous communication. However, this coexistence leads to signal interference, especially in crowded environments with numerous devices. Our study, however, focuses on a single device employing multiple radio technologies to send diverse signals, which are subsequently indistinguishable in an environment containing rich multipath. Our research involves three categories of data: radar signals, weak wireless communication packets, and moderate-strong physical layer communication signals. We build upon the existing binary classification methods, enhancing them with novel deep learning approaches to improve signal classification accuracy, especially in scenarios featuring cross-tech interference. We observe improved classification results when employing our novel approach, especially when dealing with cross-tech scenarios, where accuracy increases from 60.98% to 93.11% compared to a same-tech scenario, which already boasted a 99.68% accuracy rate.

This passage explores the link between the Dirac equation and the Klein-Gordon (KG) equation in curved spacetime environments. By establishing relationships between the Green's functions for the Dirac equation and those for the KG equation, we investigate various KG-particle properties in curved spacetime. In particular, our analysis focuses on particles with spin-zero and half-spin in a 2D de Sitter spacetime, where we examine the role of gravitational effects on these particles. Our examination leads to the discovery of particle-antiparticle differences, examination of the mass spectra for both spin cases, and a look at the precession frequencies for spin-half particles. Our findings reveal that the mass spectra for spin-zero particles are positive across all dS$_2$ values, whereas the mass spectra for spin-half particles are positive for dS$_2$ values less than one-half. Our study also demonstrates that the precession frequencies for spin-half particles are zero when certain conditions are met. Additionally, our results include the creation/annihilation operator relationships for KG-particles, which corresponds to the conventional probability amplitudes for spin-half particles as derived from the Dirac equation.

Under the assumption that $\sigma$-finite measure algebras can be parameterized by a real number, it is demonstrated that this parameter must have a minimum value of $\aleph_0$, and the problem of determining whether this parameterization is possible is a long-standing issue in mathematics. Our proof establishes that the $\sigma$-finite measure algebras can be parameterized by a set that has a cardinality of $\aleph_1$, and the parameter is unique in the standard model. Furthermore, it is also a long-standing issue in mathematics to determine whether these parameterizations are feasible.

The process of twist-2, zero-transverse-momentum helium-3 production offers significant opportunities for studying parton distribution functions at an even lower $x$ threshold than current experiments, particularly when performed in deep-inelastic scattering or fixed target collisions where the measurement of a key PDF, the function $E$, is difficult due to current technological constraints. By comparing cross sections from complementary viewpoints, namely from calculations at the partonic and hadronic levels, the measurement of this PDF becomes feasible. Initially theoretical models have suggested a potential for this method, and the next step involves analyzing data from recent and planned COMPASS experiments at an even lower $x$ threshold than earlier studies to further understand and validate the measurement of this PDF.

We've developed a method to link the capacity for learning high-dimensional classifiers in P and NP with the ability to fix mistakes in these classifiers, utilizing an existing technique that leverages computational complexity and using concepts like VC dimension and P polynomial degree to measure a data set's diversity. This diversity measure gauges a data set's capability to effortlessly recognize and differentiate various patterns on the data set itself rather than an unknown pattern. Unlike most high-dimensional data sets, those with excellent diversity can accurately learn and correct complex classifiers. Traditional complexity theory fails to capture the potential of these diverse data sets as they become harder to optimize but more capable of correcting mistakes. Conversely, advanced complexity theory reveals a stronger connection between correcting errors and learning, highlighting a disparity between fixing errors on large data sets and learning on smaller data sets. Furthermore, we've developed an improved model to assess the error correction capacity of large data sets, featuring a novel technique called bet-hedging, which has potential for broad applications in advanced complexity theory.

In systems with strong spin-orbit interaction, different types of superfluids can occur, encompassing not just single-orbital but also multi-component superfluids. By applying an external magnetic field, these unique superfluids can be divided into separate phases. Notably, research has often focused on the inter-species interaction being stronger than the intra-species interaction, but our investigation explores the opposite scenario with intra-species being larger than inter-species interaction. Our study examines how spin-orbit coupling affects single-site symmetry breaking in an N-component Bose-Hubbard model and identifies an additional repulsively bound five-body state that influences this effect. As a result, in the two-component system with intra-species being larger than inter-species interaction, a single-site superfluid and a two-site superfluid are distinguished, while in the strong spin-orbit coupling regime, a different type of superfluid known as the symmetric mixed superfluid (SMSF) emerges, characterized by having two distinct sites but being symmetric.

Achieving a supernatural (p-1)p-r)-weight system is equivalent to establishing a saturated chain of Young diagrams of length r, where each diagram contains only odd-numbered rows. We derive a finite abelian p-r group from this chain by subtracting the degree of each row from the total number of group elements. We use this method to find a set of 5-group weights that correspond to 20 distinct irreducible characters, demonstrating that these characters have distinct characterizations.

Through the AdS/CFT correspondence, black branes offer a distinct representation of surface and line defects in the bulk, and their holographic counterparts, consisting of a bulk spacetime and a localized surface or line, emerge naturally. In an effort to comprehensively examine the representation of these defects and spacetime properties, we'll provide an in-depth overview of both the bulk and holographic interpretations of surface and line defects.

As Asymmetric Tree Kernel Functions' applicability in real-world data analysis expands due to their fast computation and robust predictive capabilities, their intrinsic nature remains understudied. Contrasting traditional kernel functions, which either rely on empirical distribution estimates or uninformative prior distributions, Tree Kernel Functions are grounded in a probabilistic model of data properties. By representing samples as leaf nodes in a tree framework and defining probabilities based on common ancestors, Tree Kernel Functions naturally capture the structure of data within finite metric spaces. This initial analysis reveals that common metrics for information and influence in such systems can be used to establish connections between statistical properties and computational complexities. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that sample geodesic entropy determines the computational performance of tree kernel computations, while sample influence determines the statistical accuracy and robustness of predictions. An open-source R package, called caret2tree, has been developed to facilitate the application and parametric optimization of Tree Kernel Functions in machine learning tasks under different information criteria.

A key consideration for a muon collider is minimizing delays for its participants, in large part because delayed muons from their colliders pose significant difficulties for detectors to overcome. Given that much of the delay occurs during the transportation process from the production target to the focusing stage at an interval of several meters, one effective strategy to mitigate this problem involves shortening the focusing time. Although naturally an essential design criterion for a muon collider, this paper examines an alternative method that makes use of a novel focusing technique called the double-bend active focusing system to achieve this end, thereby allowing for an overall reduction in the focusing time or, alternatively, an increased intensity of the muon beam. A proposed detector concept for this geometry incorporates a fully covered air-tight chamber equipped with a silicon vertex detector and a calorimeter designed to withstand the high rates of particle collisions and muon decay. Furthermore, the study includes detailed physical analyses of various physics benchmarks that employ Monte-Carlo simulations based on two distinct detector designs, one featuring a silicon vertex detector and EMCal equipped with scintillating electromagnetic calorimeter, along with physics reconstruction tools that demonstrate the study's findings along with relevant recommendations for future detector development.

A novel approach for efficiently training sparse neural networks is introduced, called Spartan. This method employs a specialized regularization technique and tailored optimization procedures for the non-pruning areas of the networks. In comparison to the standard technique, Spartan enables earlier pruning, achieving up to 25.15% fewer FLOPs while maintaining similar accuracy on the CIFAR10/100 and ImageNet datasets. Furthermore, Spartan's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art methods, outperforming them significantly in terms of FLOPs reduction. Spartan's source code is freely available for download at https://github.com/yding91/SparseNetworks.

We are examining a three-dimensional system consisting of polaritons within a Bose gas, where Pauli blocking is taken into account due to interactions within the system. This is achieved through the application of a complex non-local self-energy that incorporates the long-range correlation associated with Pauli blocking. Utilizing a Gaussian expansion technique for the thermal density operator, we derive the thermodynamic properties and macroscopic behavior of this system, focusing on its thermodynamic behavior across a wide range of temperatures and densities. This is based on a thermodynamic approach for determining the Pauli blocking effect self-consistently. Our findings show good agreement with experimental data in the parameter regimes corresponding to a Planckian regime at high temperatures and a Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) regime at lower temperatures. Additionally, we observe that the application of Pauli blocking has a substantial impact only when the system is in a mixed regime at intermediate temperatures and densities.

Our study delves into how software developers assess the severity of test smells within their codebase, and the potential consequences they anticipate these problems may incur on maintainability. By means of a controlled experiment, we evaluated the responses from two groups of developers. One group received pre-collected data on test smells from an open-source system, accompanied by a brief explanatory note. In contrast, the second group retrieved the same data but without any additional context. Each participant then answered a multiple-choice questionnaire designed to gauge their perspective on the severity of test smells and the impact on maintainability. Interestingly, nearly all developers overestimated the severity of these smells and also overestimated the consequences for maintainability. Our results suggest that providing access to data on test smells, along with an explanation of their implications, may actually lead developers to consider them less critical than they actually are. Our study sheds light on the underlying causes of this overestimation, offering practical advice for how to effectively highlight the significance of test smells to developers.

This study introduces a type of differential process that incorporates smoothing and unilateral constraints and is defined by a Cauchy problem: $\dot{u}(t)=\int_{M}f(t,\omega,z(d\omega)\delta_{u(t)}(dw)$ with initial condition $u_0$ where $T$ is a non-decreasing continuous function that maps $\mathbb{R}^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^d$. It is proven that the solution to this problem is continuous with respect to its initial value and that it satisfies a variational equation of viscosity. Moreover, it is shown that the solution to this problem can be obtained through the limiting process of a sequence of differential inclusions as the smoothing parameter approaches zero.

The event generator KKMCee, developed for $e^+e^-$ interactions, is derived from PYTHMC, which is based on matrix elements, and Fortran 90 code. Our KKMCee updates the original Fortran 77 code for enhanced usability and efficiency. The generator now includes a more advanced Monte Carlo integration algorithm, enhanced predictability, and improved handling of polarized initial states and finite mass effects in lepton and quark pair production. The incorporation of charged particle decays for particles like $W$, $Z$, $\tau$ introduces reduced uncertainty compared to the previous approach using Breit-Wigner functions. According to internal comparisons using the old code, refinements yield reductions of approximately 1 DO, 0.1 DO, and $10^{-3}$ in precision for the dominant, less probable, and finest cases respectively. This updated event generator for $e^+e^-$ interactions is now available online in C++ and is also suitable for other processes.

Deep learning techniques have enhanced the production of high-quality synthetic images. To a similar degree, deep learning can be applied effectively to extracting vital signs from noisy sensor data. This study utilizes deep learning methods to improve the extraction of inter-beat intervals from electrocardiograms recorded in challenging environments. Beat period extraction is a crucial step in computing the RR interval, a vital indicator of autonomic nervous system function or disease. We integrated multiple deep learning models to determine the optimal approach for extracting inter-beat intervals from ECGs of infants in noisy conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the integrated model surpasses existing methods, both human-intervention-based and automatic. This study showcases the benefits of using deep learning methods for extracting biosignals from noisy data. We also present approaches for addressing data imbalance, improving model robustness against noisy data, and reducing errors in patient measurements. These strategies can be adapted for extracting other biosignals, such as blood pressure, to support clinical research in hypotension and hypertension. Ultimately, our research can help reduce the number of false alarms in medical diagnoses, a critical concern due to the high false positive rate of patients diagnosed with hypotension.

In this research, we describe a new randomized algorithm for computing the singular value decomposition (sVD) of a tensor. Our method performs fewer passes over the data tensor compared to the current state-of-the-art randomized algorithms for this computation. We demonstrate that our approach is both efficient and precise. By applying subsampling techniques to the data tensor, we can reduce the computational complexity of certain tensor-based methods for low-rank matrix recovery. Our findings are validated through the analysis of a specific medical imaging problem involving the reconstruction of unknown sources from measurements contaminated by a source-related tensor process. We utilize the singular value decomposition of this tensor process to represent the unknown sources. Our source reconstruction results using the singular value decomposition show significant improvement in terms of numerical accuracy when compared to other techniques, such as wavelet and sparse bases.

Although significant progress has been made in neural network modeling for static graphs, a significant gap persists in modeling dynamic graphs. This disparity is due to two key challenges that exist in modeling dynamic graphs but not static graphs: capturing underlying structure and handling label temporal coherence. Unlike static graphs, dynamic graphs possess inherent structure such as node and edge embeddings that evolve over time, thereby requiring embeddings to be tracked across successive time points. Furthermore, temporal sequences of labels often exhibit inherent temporal coherence which needs to be captured by the model. We propose a novel neural network model designed specifically for dynamic graphs that models edge embeddings and captures temporal label coherence. The proposed model, called DELAC, dynamically adjusts its edge embedding capture policy according to the inherent structure of the graph, thereby making generalizations applicable to various types of graphs. Experimental results across five datasets reveal that DELAC consistently outperforms existing baseline models in modeling edge evolution and temporal sequence coherence. Notably, DELAC outperforms existing models on seven datasets, including ones with single-shot and multi-shot labeling policies.

Our studies of $^7$H resonance have been conducted using a two-nucleon cluster model where one alpha particle and three nucleons coexist. By applying a standard variational method, we calculated the energy spectrum of the 7H system as it depends on the relative motion of the alpha particle to the three nucleons. We found that at energies below 2 MeV, the 7H system exhibits a single resonance with a narrow width, however our results show this resonance doesn't have enough energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier when both the alpha particle and the three nucleons are charged. Additionally, our calculations show the 7H system doesn't produce a bound state when either one of the three nucleons or the alpha particle is neutral. We observed that an unbound 7H resonance exists at an energy of approximately 1.3 MeV if the 7H system contains an electron. By comparing our calculations with the experimental data from the Tokyo University group, we observed a discrepancy between the two. We found that the absence of a narrow 7H resonance at energies below 0.55 MeV isn't consistent with the experimental results from the Tokyo University group.

Our work builds upon an extension of a previously established finding related to
a Nirenberg-type problem on a half-sphere by Ghimenti and Pistoia. We demonstrate
that as the parameter with a value greater than 4 approaches zero, the set of solutions
satisfying a specific equation converges uniformly towards a subset of the set of solutions
satisfying a comparable equation on a full sphere. Notably, these solutions have distinct blow
up patterns; whereas half-sphere solutions generally experience a multiplicity one blow up,
sphere solutions exhibit a uniform blow up of multiplicity two in the principal variable, which
occurs at a different location, specifically at a point with a specific negative curvature value.

While class-balanced sampling has become a standard practice in large-scale discriminative tasks, its effectiveness solely relies on the quality of pre-allocated class labels. If these labels are inaccurate, the learning of relevant features becomes compromised. This issue is particularly prevalent in multi-label scenarios where multiple labels are assigned to each sample, making balanced sampling even more challenging. In this study, a novel approach called Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL) is proposed to enhance the learning of relevant features. DCDL monitors the ratio of samples labeled with each class within an embedding space and penalizes discrepancies from the ideal balanced state. Since manually allocating class labels can be inaccurate, the study proposes an unsupervised clustering method to determine class labels based on the Euclidean distance between samples and their respective cluster centers. The proposed data-driven unsupervised clustering method estimates the optimal number of classes and learns an embedding that accurately represents the true class labels. The study evaluates the proposed DCDL in two scenarios: (1) a synthetic experiment with multiple labels, and (2) a real-world dataset for codebook creation. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DCDL is capable of learning a relevant feature space even in the presence of inaccurate or multiple class labels. Additionally, the study showcases the effectiveness of the proposed unsupervised clustering method in achieving high accuracy, especially in local aggregation scenarios.

A year ago, England implemented a massive tracing program as part of the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic. The program's success relied heavily on local partnerships with test and trace, which were established to identify and contain virus outbreaks. Despite the program's rollout being guided by clear guidelines and a uniform structure, significant variations and complexities emerged in how the different local partnerships designed and executed their tracing efforts. This study examines the evolution of these variations and partnerships' performance. It analyzes the different strategies and approaches adopted by the various partnerships and assesses their impact on contact tracing efficiency. A model predicting the outcome based on specific partnership characteristics is also developed. However, the analysis finds mixed results. While some partnerships experienced improved outcomes over time, others showed no significant progress. Moreover, partnerships that excelled initially did not necessarily maintain this performance, and those with the lowest initial performance showed mixed improvements. Despite this, the research finds a link between higher-tracing quality and increased survival rates of local test and trace partnerships. It concludes that while there are temporary fluctuations, the long-term performance of these partnerships is determined by the initial quality of their tracing efforts.

Our goal is to determine whether young open clusters exhibit lower surface gravity due to the presence of weak spectral features. To achieve this, we carefully analyzed the spectral characteristics of the relatively young Milotte 72 open star cluster, which is approximately 200 million years old. Employing state-of-the-art computer models that take into account photospheric features and various atmospheric compositions, we created synthetic spectra for cluster members across a range of masses. Analyzing medium-resolution 0.8--1.4 $\mu$m spectra of 15 members allowed us to identify a prominent discrepancy between observed and modeled surface gravity. By modeling the effect of hydrodynamic shock waves in the upper atmospheres of hot stars, we attributed this disparity to normal star behavior. Our accurate determination of the radial velocity, radial extent, and age of the cluster indicates that it is exceptional due to its relatively extended formation span lasting around 15 million years. During this time, it is one of the oldest known clusters to continuously produce new stars at a rate equivalent to those found in the Cam Super Association in the Small Magellanic Cloud. The models we created serve as a reference point for future observations aiming to detect low-level chemical variations among young stars in the Galaxy. Additionally, the models provide critical information about the atmospheric structure of hot stars in the context of radiative transfer solutions. The calibrations we developed for the IRAC fluxes of stars in the 0.8--1.4 $\mu$m domain will be useful for

We investigate the level distributions, $L^{(v)}$, of excursion levels at height $v$ in discrete and continuous percolation models on a 2D lattice, where site values are randomly assigned. From the joint probability density of neighboring site excursion levels, $P_{ij}$, we develop a partial differential equation (PDE) that relates $L^{(v)}$ among nearby sites. By solving this PDE, we derive an explicit formula for $L^{(v)}$ and use it to study the phase transition from Gaussian to power-law behavior, which is caused by a self-referential relationship between $L^{(v)}$ and the probability of nearby sites sharing a common neighbor excising their connection. This PDE also enables the computation of joint probability densities, $P_{ij}$, which increases from a Gaussian form as the connection probability increases. Our work leads to the development of an approximation method, which allows the calculation of critical percolation thresholds with high accuracy across various 2D lattice geometries by considering the excursion levels of site valuations.

Camera calibration is a complex process that involves calculating the camera's intrinsic and rotational values based on 2D image coordinates and corresponding 3D point information. Traditional methods typically employ least squares optimization using projection equations to achieve this goal. Recent research by Xu et al. in 2020 presented a direct regression approach, claiming it can simplify the calibration process. Our work contradicts their claims by revealing that their technique is essentially a derivative-based optimization method disguised as regression. We further demonstrate that their approach performs similarly to traditional methods, using calculated gradients, often with little to no advantage. To validate our findings, we created multiple synthetic datasets with varying levels of noise and found no support for the direct regression method. Consequently, we recommend against using it for camera calibration.

We introduce a framework for incorporating constraints in the context of reinforcement learning through the use of a learned constraint that utilises constraints imposed by other, constraint-adhering agents. Initially, our approach assumes a common purpose among agents but allows for diverse behaviour to coexist, generating a safety-enabling environment for reinforcement learning. As an example, our experiments involve multiple autonomous cars governed by reinforcement learning, striving to avoid one another safely across a crossroads. Our findings demonstrate that the learning of constraints leads to stable behaviour in the presence of other, constraint-adhering agents. Furthermore, the paper explores various levels of knowledge acquisition within the learning constraint, encompassing complete, partial, and unknown understanding of the underlying system dynamics. Ultimately, the paper discusses the potential for reinforcement learning to enable diverse cooperative behaviour among agents sharing a common goal.

GAIA's mission to chart the galaxy's contents across its six degree field of view marks a significant milestone in the history of space astronomy. The mission's extensive dataset holds immense value in studying the galaxy's structure and composition. In GAIA's internal datasets, we've identified a pattern that indicates a shortage of brown dwarfs within GAIA's early data release. This imbalance is most pronounced at near-solar mass ranges and may be attributed to a methodological issue related to how GAIA treats parallax data. Our findings also reveal further research opportunities using GAIA's datasets to study the galaxy by conducting colour-separation analytics based on various astrophysical sources. The findings create a strong foundation for the galaxy and brown dwarf communities to further explore and understand the galaxy's structure and composition with further analysis of GAIA's datasets.

Trees are effectively utilized to decompose and analyze graphs, facilitating the efficient solution of fundamental problems like Vertex Cover and MaxCut. This abstract presents an overview of an unsupervised learning approach for automating tree-based algorithm design. The underlying methodology employs inductive program derivation to generate algorithms for vertex classification, leveraging search strategies including guided evolution and tree-based reinforcement. The primary focus of this abstract lies in describing the incorporation of trees into the inductive search process and outlining experimental results that compare the efficacy of manually crafted algorithms with automatically generated ones.

The widespread use of graph theory in descriptions of linked systems within natural sciences and industry has led to the development of various indexing and clustering algorithms, which are based on the local connectivity of vertices in graphs. Specifically, the focus of this paper lies within the realm of graph theory. It examines two distinct cases for the clustering of vertices based on the local structure of their immediate neighbors: the continuous clustering coefficient of community detection methods and a specific instance known as the Zhang--Horvath clustering. Our investigation involves an evaluation of these functions against a common benchmark in artificial networks and a set of real-world networks, with a special emphasis on their sensitivity to different parameters such as the size of the network and its degree of connectivity. Notably, the results of our analysis indicate that the Zhang--Horvath clustering exhibits a degree of order that matches the order of the community detection method for the majority of our tests, but there are instances where the two perform differently.

Predictions generated by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) lack certainty, 
as the lack of overfitting prevents confidence in their results. To address this, 
an a posteriori error estimation method based on explicit time integration techniques 
for differential equations is presented, which also improves the training process of 
PINNs. By incorporating a posteriori error estimation into the learning process, 
the method aligns training with a posteriori error estimation methods, thereby 
allowing for the inclusion of approximations into the loss function. As a result, 
the method offers refined predictions by leveraging approximate solutions and 
therefore achieves higher precision than pure regression. Furthermore, this approach 
ensures the prediction of upper and lower bounds makes it possible to certify the 
accuracy of predictions. The effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through 
experiments on multiple test cases.

Outdoor air quality models are being increasingly replaced by more sophisticated versions that take into account the spatial relationships between monitoring stations, along with the characteristics of the surrounding environment. This paper represents an important initial step in a comprehensive study aimed at developing and evaluating spatial models for analyzing and predicting ground-level ozone levels. First, the key characteristics and potential advantages of spatial models are outlined, compared to traditional methods. Next, the paper focuses on a specific type of spatial model, examining issues related to model identification, estimation, and validation. A thorough diagnosis of the assumed underlying conditions is conducted, employing various criteria. A real-world dataset from a US national monitoring network is employed in this study to evaluate the performance of different models. Several diagnostic tools are also used to assess the models, including a priori information and post-processing diagnostics. Based on these analyses, the most suitable models are selected and compared in terms of their predictive capabilities, both within the training sample and on newly collected data. The study's findings are instrumental in developing an efficient method for selecting models, along with suggestions for future areas of research and model improvement.

Recent studies on topological superconducting nanowires reveal a zero-energy peak in conductance that is accompanied by non-Majorana-related zero-energy states. Utilizing a times-of-flight technique, our experiment demonstrates the existence of these non-Majorana states at room temperature, differentiating it from standard Majorana modes which are sensitive to in-plane magnetic fields due to being bound to the nanowire's edge. As explained through a mean-field Dirac-superconducting model, the observed behavior is the result of pairing between zero-energy Majorana modes and edge states, a process that is robust against in-plane magnetic fields and temperature variations. The minimal impact of in-plane magnetic fields on the subgap states, in conjunction with their significant influence on the nanowire's edge when subjected to out-of-plane magnetic fields, further validates the findings, thus differentiating them from previously studied topological insulator surface states.

This paper examines spectral limitations in linear bandits, considering both model selection and clustering. We investigate the spectral characteristics of action sets and design methods to tackle both tasks. We establish restrictions on achieving better loss rates than certain cluster-centered regret metrics. We also introduce a sharpness metric that dictates whether better loss rates are attainable. We leverage this notion to generate new regret bounds for model selection and clustering. These results generalize prior analyses, encompassing both settings. Experimentation confirms our theoretical findings, highlighting the necessity of incorporating additional information for precise clustering.

The Valley Hall effect in 2D materials with low symmetry has gained significant attention, but its interpretation is hindered by ambiguity. To clarify this, the researchers propose the Orbital Hall effect, which offers a more unambiguous measurement of conductivity. By defining this new effect and distinguishing it from the Valley Hall effect, the team highlights its utility in analyzing confidence intervals of Edelmann's equation. This equation, which links the Orbital Hall effect and the Quantum Anomalous Hall effect through an intrinsic property called Berry's curvature, facilitates precise experiments to measure Berry's curvature in 2D materials.

Recent studies employing adversarial machine learning methods like adversarial training and generative adversarial networks have explored the development of adversarial defenses through reinforcement learning or direct gradient optimization. Despite focusing on analogous problems, these approaches demonstrate distinct differences in perspective, techniques, and applications. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of research in adversarial machine learning via reinforcement learning, classifying approaches into Markov Decision Process and Deep Reinforcement Learning groups. It also compares and contrasts various representations, objectives, reward design, environmental settings, evaluation methodologies, and assesses their effectiveness in terms of robustness, generalization, model accuracy, and training stability.

In homework 3, we matched sources from one catalog to another utilizing positional information. This time, we expanded our technique to incorporate additional photometric data to refine the source matching process. We discovered that making use of this extra information leads to a significant enhancement in the source matching accuracy. To make the most of the positional and photometric information, we applied both binary and cross-correlation techniques. The cross-corology method turned out to be more effective than binary queries and cross-match, particularly when dealing with smaller datasets. Furthermore, we found that our cross-corology method outperforms established methods like SExtractor and TopCat.

We show that for any set of cardinals, $\mathcal{S}$, such that no element of $\mathcal{S}$ is stationary in a given ordinal $\kappa$, it follows that $\mathcal{S}$ is 'nowhere stationary' in $\kappa$. Under the same condition, it is further proven that $\mathcal{S}$ is not 'weakly doubled' in $\kappa$. Our results apply even when $\mathcal{S}$ contains only infinite cardinals. On the other hand, it is demonstrated that the property of being 'weakly doubled' can be obtained unconditionally for a set of only two cardinals, though it is shown that the general case is undecidable.

Ontology visualizations have gained significant attention in recent years due to the widespread use of ontologies in various fields, including knowledge engineering, medicine, and biology. Despite this, users often find visualizations difficult to understand, as the available tools are not user-friendly and do not accommodate non-technical individuals. We present OntoPlot, a simple and intuitive visualizing tool designed to make ontologies easily comprehensible for end-users. OntoPlot's user-centered design focuses on presenting central information first and guides users through the visualization of peripheral data. In contrast to other visualizing tools, OntoPlot's interface is clear and uncluttered, featuring a minimal number of buttons and a simple hierarchy of concepts. We have applied OntoPlot's on two biomedical ontologies and gathered users' feedback through user testing to validate the tool's efficiency. Our research reveals that OntoPlot enables non-technical individuals to understand and operate on ontologies without requiring professional expertise.

Our proposed method integrates CycleGAN's domain adaptation capabilities into 
the self-supervised pretraining of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). 
Previous studies on CNN self-supervised pretraining were based on either 
contrastive learning or normalisation techniques, but lacked control over input 
features. In this research, we utilize CycleGAN to enforce cycle consistency 
between input features from different domains, while introducing contrastive 
learning to maintain key characteristics. The application of SelfSupCycleGAN 
on ImageNet and Mini-ImageNet datasets demonstrates superior performance on 
transfer learning even after removing 90% of input data. Additionally, 
SelfSupCycleGAN's domain-specific transfer learning results surpass state-of-
the-art performance. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/
uapanel/SelfSupCycleGAN.

Generative models have the potential to utilise deep learning techniques and create realistic data through competition and imitation of observed sensory data. Advanced generative models can generate high-quality data replicating key characteristics of the training set. Utilizing novel generative models and employing established ones effectively can lead to substantial improvements in data simulation. Furthermore, these models can be viewed as functional compressors that accurately represent complex data through compact representations and allow accurate data reconstruction. We have successfully applied various generative models and feature extractors to fundamental signals and events, and our findings demonstrate the potential for significant data reduction in specific cases. This study may inspire the development of novel generative models and highlight their applicability in realistic data simulation for cosmic events.

A critical aspect of molecular flexibility has been identified in a theoretical study involving a binary mixture of molecules with flexible and rigid shapes, which was analyzed through simulations and by calculating thermal diffusion factors based on these configurations. It was observed that when temperature gradients are applied, flexibility typically contributes to a more substantial separation of components than would occur without flexibility. Notably, the study found that directional hydrogen bonding can influence this separation either by enhancing or diminishes it, contingent upon the degree of flexibility. The study's simulations revealed that an increase in flexibility leads to a greater difference in thermal diffusion factors between the two components. Furthermore, the simulations showed that when hydrogen bonding is present, the greater difference is associated with a lower thermal diffusion ratio, while the opposite is true when hydrogen bonding is absent. The study's simulations also demonstrated that hydrogen bonding diminishes thermal diffusion in flexible molecules but amplifies it in rigid molecules. The study's simulations aligned with theoretical predictions which indicated that hydrogen bonding would have a greater impact on thermal diffusion in flexible molecules but a smaller one in rigid molecules. The study's simulations showed that hydrogen molecules interact flexibly with carbon tetrachloride when temperature gradients are applied, resulting in a greater difference in thermal diffusion in flexible and rigid mixtures of these substances.

This research investigates the effectiveness of minimalisten, a minimalist transformer-based model, in performing an specific task. Minimalisten was designed to enhance the capabilities of a baseline model, M-BERT, and achieve a more efficient architecture for complex tasks. We evaluated Minimalisten's ability to score essays in a specific competition and found it to be comparable to larger, more complex transformer-based models in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, Minimalisten's reduced parameters resulted in a 52% decrease in its computation cost, making it a more feasible option for integration into an automated writing coach system, which places higher demands on computation resources. Our experiments also highlighted Minimalisten's ability to achieve strong performance with a reduced computation cost, offering a promising solution for applications involving multiple tasks with limited computational resources.

Our primary goal in this research is to overcome the challenge of unsupervised false positive suppression in information retrieval. Incorporating a variety of weak signals is key to addressing this issue, and employing a box re-ranking model is an innovative way to utilize these cues. Notably, our proposed model leverages a unique arrangement of inputs, comprising a passage's top k ranked terms, along with k chosen negative terms, under the guidance of a weak signal-generated box. To further enhance our approach, we introduce a weighted box re-ranking model, where the weight simulates a ranking score that is derived from the weak signals. The outcome of our experiment indicates that our method not only achieves significant accuracy in suppressing false positives but also achieves better performance with less post-ranking data. Moreover, our study shows that our solution excels despite being trained under an unsupervised setting.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant improvements in the restoration of degraded audio, particularly in challenging conditions. In contrast, there has been significantly less research focused on the enhancement of high-quality music recordings, with even less attention devoted to the specific task of music mixup – combining multiple separate music recordings into a single audible mix. This paper presents a novel deep learning approach for the music mixup task, leveraging a novel objective function optimized by a fully convolutional autoregressive model that generates spectral patterns from a common latent representation. We examine the efficacy of this technique using two distinct datasets: a custom generated dataset and the MUSDB18 dataset. When tested on the MUSDB18 dataset, our method achieved an objective evaluation score surpassing the existing state-of-the-art. Furthermore, we propose a novel subjective evaluation metric that considers not only the overall music signal but also individual instrumental components. Using this metric, we demonstrate that our approach produces superior subjective quality results, notably on the MUSDB18 dataset.

This research develops a novel method to create throwing animations through character simulations, focused on the specific task of simulating throwing motions along a straight line. A novel parameterization technique is presented to represent throwing poses, enabling efficient extraction of throwing parameters from articulated character animations. These parameters are then learned from existing datasets to create realistic throwing simulations. Unlike existing optimization-based methods that rely on hand-coded physics constraints and rigid body trajectories, this approach leverages a variety of existing character animations to fit articulatory model deformations, enabling more natural physics-based animations. Perceived realism of the generated throwing motions is influenced by the quality of existing animations and the accuracy of the learning algorithm. Real-time character throwing demonstrations are presented to facilitate learning from a variety of existing animations. Multiple throwing animations are created in real-time utilizing our method, as demonstrated during video playback.

This paper focuses on enhancing the CoNMTTools toolkit by integrating structural constraints into NMT systems via its RNN-SMT reordering framework. We develop a novel attention model based on the RNN-SMT distortion matrix, showing that this syntax-aware approach significantly improves translation fluency and logical order, with notable support from human evaluation metrics. Notably, this syntax-inspired attention model also enhances the translation's grammatical accuracy and preserves a more natural sentence order.

We carried out a comprehensive study of the snow lines in forty-two protoplanetary discs surrounding A-type to M-type stars. Using our established method, we calculated the locations of snow lines within the discs and explored how different water ice line formation processes, binding energies, and other factors influence snow surface calculations. Our results show that water ice lines emerge at distinct radial distances depending on these factors, with the simplest scenario using a temperature-based water ice line yielding snow surfaces between 30-75 AU for stars of different masses. When considering various water ice line models, snow surfaces become more concentric with incrementing water ice line binding energy, ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 kT. Notably, incorporating different gas models produces relatively insignificant effects on snow surface calculations, with the notable exception of snow surfaces shifting 0.2-0.5 AU inward for stars like the Sun due to adopting the CONDES model instead of conventional diffusion coefficient models. Snow surfaces remain largely unaffected by disc mass, with the exception of discs of higher mass hosting a third type of snow surface. Snow surfaces in hot and warm stars are predicted to extend to larger radii with increasing stellar temperature. Our analysis using U-band and visible light magnitudes suggests that the majority of snow surfaces in OB stars lie outside detection capabilities, with snow surfaces in M dwarfs predicted to lie 40-50 AU beyond M-dwarf detection limits. Our snow surface study provides crucial insights into the pivotal role of snow

To align the output of a statistical model with the observed distribution, we can fine-tune its parameters by analyzing the shift between theoretical and empirical distributions, a process which can be expressed as a linear combination. This adjustment process depends solely on the model's properties, which can be computed through a single calculation based on the theoretical distribution, and a subsequent fit to the empirical data. This method has applications in the field of acoustic wave scattering where it can be used to analyze the experimental Stern-Ruderman representation. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness in multiple scenarios, including the application to the Rayleigh-Brillet formula, which relates to gravitational waves emitted by binary systems, as well as other models such as the Gaussian beam, the Swerling 1 model, and vectors of random variables. This technique is versatile and can be used with a variety of statistical models by providing equations to transform theoretical distributions into the Stern-Ruderman domain, facilitating a straightforward adjustment process.

We explore the limitations of learning a quantum state when accessing it is expensive, using multiple copies and only measuring expectations of relevant observables since individual measurements can't accurately distinguish between the quantum state and the zero state. Since expecting to see a non-zero outcome doesn't reliably locate the quantum state, we must quantify how much information can be gained from a fixed number of trials for any given observable. Furthermore, we examine how to select from an infinite set of possible observables to extract the most valuable information and apply our methods to real-world problems, such as estimating a mixing angle in the qutrit case and simulating experiments with photons to evaluate SU(3) symmetry.

As computational speed increases, the need for more accurate solutions arises, which can be addressed by enhancing geometrical optics asymptotics. This study improves and implements refined asymptotics for the Helmholtz equation, first developed by Robineau and DeLuca, for a wide range of parameters and practical scenarios. With practical applications in mind, we provide numerical results for scattering and absorption analysis under various conditions, including multiple waves and oscillating boundaries. By generalizing the approach, we also obtain exact formulas for a class of oscillating targets, which confirms the third-order term in the asymptotic expansion and allows us to state a general absorption estimate. Furthermore, we illustrate the significant improvement achieved with a range of test cases involving a square obstacle.

We've introduced a new type of mutation, known as transmutation, that changes the category of a sample in an unsupervised model. In contrast to mixture mutations, which combine elements from different categories, transmutations isolate a subset of the original class and move it towards another subset of a different class. To better understand this new type of mutation, we have established an approach to set upper limits on the formation probability of specific stellar remnants, as well as a method to track the development of remnant masses through the PRISM code. Our study in this area focuses on binary systems containing two white dwarfs and discovers both transmutations and mixture mutations lead to identical changes in the system's mixture composition and final remnant configurations. However, the manner in which transmutations arise differs from previously thought mixture mutations and is now understood to involve initial star interactions and merging of electron clouds in a collapsing star. Furthermore, our analysis of the LAMOST dataset reveals the presence of a transmutation valley, spanning from log(g) of 0 to -2, within the white dwarf star categorization. Our findings indicate that only star interactions can produce the entirety of white dwarf star categories, including extremely low-gravity and dark carbon stars. Moreover, we found the rate at which transmutations in stellar systems is significantly lower than previously estimated for the entire galaxy and only accounts for 0.5% of new star formations. Our analysis also suggests that transmutations can produce distinct clustering patterns in the relationship between stellar gravity

Multi-task linear regression, where we predict multiple related outcomes from the same input, is typically simplified by sample-efficient algorithms that require only linear input processing, regardless of the number of predictions made. However, this common assumption doesn't hold for tasks that involve predicting the presence of multiple medical conditions from the medical history of a patient. We've found that, under a specific probability model for these conditions and their relationship, the minimum number of examples needed to learn these tasks grows quadratically with the number of predictions made. Consequently, the tasks can't be learned efficiently in parallel. We support our findings with detailed analysis and a formal proof of the lower bound on the number of required examples, as well as by training a typical machine learning model on data derived from the established probability model and observing that it fails to efficiently handle multiple tasks when the number of predictions becomes very large.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest in building task-specific language models, fueled by their potential to solve real-world tasks efficiently. This trend has sparked the creation of multiple in-task and down-stream task data sets intended to improve the performance of these models. This study seeks to assess the impact of various data augmentation and compression techniques on a multilingual model configured to process 54 languages, employing 9 external data sets to enhance its performance. The research indicates that Data Augmentation and Knowledge Distillation consistently outperform other methods such as random data augmentation and post-training quantization in improving the model's performance capabilities. Notably, the consistency of performance variations across all external data sets was highest for post-training quantization and lowest for early fine-tuning. This study suggests that building efficient multilingual models for specific tasks may be more effective when trained on task-specific data rather than incorporating task-specific data through data augmentation. Additionally, the research finds that task-specific data augmentations positive effects vary across languages, with some increasing performance and others reducing it. This study further indicates that these effects are typically much smaller than the differences in performance caused by using general data augmentations or quantization.

Recent studies on r-Uniform Turan free graphs, initially investigated by Jensen in depth, have yielded significant results, including a precise determination of Turan density by Baber and Talbot. In a different area of study, Petridis uncovered precise large subgraph density limits for r-Uniform Turan free graphs. However, at r = 3, these subgraph density limits remain theoretically unknown. In an effort to shed light on this gap, this study identifies the precise densities of all r-Uniform K_r-free subgraphs. As a consequence of this, the paper provides an upper bound on the K_r-2 subgraph density in r-Uniform graphs with minimum degree greater than (r-2)^2. Furthermore, the paper describes a method to calculate exact densities for r-Uniform K_r-2 subgraphs given specific constraints on their minimum degree.

In the midst of the COVID-19 crisis, the global community is striving to address the immense challenge posed by the disease. As part of the efforts to combat its spread, the United Nations and World Health Organization have designated imaging as a key element in diagnosing and tracking COVID-19 infections. By leveraging advances in self-supervised imaging benchmarks, researchers are now able to effectively address data labeling complexities and reduce the need for extensive annotated data sets, thereby increasing efficiency. By implementing state-of-the-art techniques for unsupervised boundary detection and selecting a diverse range of image augmentations, we evaluated the impact of varying amounts of annotated data on Pneumonia detection. Our results, obtained on distinct data sets, highlight the significance of the type of image augmentations used, and demonstrate that the annotation requirement can be reduced by a factor of 80 while maintaining performance by using a carefully selected method.

Our P-LinET model, integrated with the image captioning framework, offers the
benefits of prompt learning, including increased generalization and interpretability.
Unlike traditional prompt learning that relies on fixed texts, our embedded prompt
is dynamically generated from an attention vector obtained through visual input, thus
improving performance both with small and large language models. By incorporating a
prompt learning component, our image captioning system achieves enhanced coherence
and human-like language characteristics, such as telling stories through image sequences. 
We evaluated our model's performance on COCO, Visual Genome, and VCGEN, achieving
substantial gains in performance compared to prior models, notably a 12.8 gPT3
performance boost of 15.0 BLEU scores on COCO. Our work sets the foundation for
integrated language modeling, one that combines computer vision and text generation.

Contrastive causation emphasizes the contrast between an actual and hypothetical scenario to define harm. This perspective refines how harm is related to an actual outcome and utility. It offers a distinct concept of enablement, implying that a factor enabling a harm brings about the same outcome through another mechanism. The notion of superenablement goes a step further by introducing a scenario in which enabling a harm results in the opposite outcome. According to contrastive causation, superenablement leads to irrationality and, by definition, entails transitivity. A transitive scenario is characterized by an intermediate factor enabling the target harm. The contrastive approach to disablement suggests that disability hinges on an excluded alternative cause, thereby precluding disabled factors with causal alternatives. It also offers a notion of disablement scope, expanding the concept to factors not only precluding the target cause but also those precluding potential causative factors. The scope allows for distinctive logical and moral dilemmas that the original concept cannot accommodate.

The widespread adoption of camera traps in wildlife conservation has led to the accumulation of vast image datasets, which are now in need of efficient human analysis to ensure effective monitoring of wildlife. Advances in deep learning have made significant improvements in handling complex image analysis tasks. This report outlines the applications of deep learning in wildlife monitoring through the classification and localization of animal images. It also introduces two deep learning techniques: Inception-ResNet A for animal identification and VGG19 with support vector machine (SVM) for animal detection. Our study utilizes a dataset of 25,000 images from the ImageNet dataset, annotated with species information, to demonstrate the capability of training a classifier capable of identifying frugivorous mammals. Additionally, a detection system is developed for recognizing images of primates, with remarkable results achieved on the primate dataset obtained from the ImageNet. Moreover, animal detection accuracy is achieved on the ImageNet dataset with a VGG19 model coupled with SVM. These methodologies have the potential to significantly reduce the substantial burden of manual analysis on wildlife conservation efforts.

In the area of spoken language translation, most previous research has been
devoted to translating complete sentences, whereas a newly emerging trend,
spoken language understanding, separates the process into two distinct stages -
first breaking down the audio input into meaningful units and then translating
those units into a different language. Although this approach offers greater
flexibility, it poses significant challenges in terms of model design. As
result, existing solutions often demand extensive training data and struggle
with reduced data scenarios. In order to overcome these limitations, we
suggest and evaluate an innovative design where speech recognition, text
translation, and text generation share a single, multi-task model trained on
annotated data. We evaluate our approach's effectiveness using zero-shot and
few-shot translation performance on EN-DE language pairs,, also introducing
new evaluation metrics that isolate individual stages of the SLU pipeline.
Our experimental findings showcase that multi-task training yields improved
speech-to-text, text-to-speech translation results, and increased robustness in
each individual stage.

Traditional Fourier's heat conduction law relates heat flux to temperature through the equation $j = -k\partial_{x}u$. The method of generalized Fourier's laws allows various heat conduction models by replacing $k$ with a thermodynamic tensor that may depend on temperature, enabling the study of non-Gaussian heat conduction systems. The book explores two such models where the thermodynamic tensor's dependence on temperature leads to heat conduction equations that incorporate memory factors, ultimately resulting in the extension of the heat equation with integral components. The book delves into the fundamental aspects of these models, including their mathematical implications for stability and the existence of solutions to the Cauchy problem, as well as the property of unique weak solvability.

Utilizing advanced deep learning models, including LSTM, VRNN, and PKNN, we've conducted an experiment using 12 consecutive days' data from 28/07 to 39/07 to forecast the day-ahead energy demand. Combining historical forecasts with peak hour forecasts has yielded superior outcomes when compared to individual applications of these models. The newly proposed PKNN model, optimized with Poisson, has demonstrated performance parity with the more sophisticated VRNN model, while a simple statistical method like KNN can achieve results comparable to the more advanced LSTM model with limited training data required. Integration of peak hour forecasts with the PKNN model enhances energy demand prediction during peak hours, with an improvement of 2.2% for peak hours and 1.4% for off-peak hours. Interestingly, incorporating peak hour forecasts along with the statistical models results in decreased accuracy, suggesting a negative impact on model performance due to increased noise during peak hours. This finding indicates that a portion of the signal in peak hours data is actually noise and needs to be removed for successful integration with statistical models. With the PKNN model alone failing to surpass the performance of the more sophisticated methods like LSTM and VRNN, this research aims to improve the PKNN model or identify modifications for enhanced energy demand forecasting.

Machine learning algorithms may achieve improved performance and increased efficiency through the incorporation of knowledge. Several methods have been developed to utilize existing knowledge and facilitate the training of neural networks. We are investigating the incorporation of knowledge via a attention-based semantic decoding approach, which involves decoding an image using semantic primitives and comparing the decoded primitives with known classes. The comparison is a critical component of our method, as it enables the incorporation of network features and by-products not initially considered. We tested our approach on the COCO-stuff and SUN52K datasets and observed superior semantic decomposition performance relative to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, modifications to the decoding objective allow our method to achieve competitive segmentation accuracy. The source code that supports our approach is publicly available at https://github.com/gregorysk/semi-primal-decoding.

We introduce an image-driven method with category-level labels that enhances lesion localization without needing detailed annotation. Utilizing only general annotations, our approach leverages image-level labels to develop a long-range image understanding. To improve localization precision, we use adjacent expert annotations as detailed guidance. As an added benefit, our method also generates high-quality expert annotations. Experimental results on a medical imaging dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing lesion localization with accurate visualization results and generated expert annotations. Our code is available for public use.

Our approach to vertebra identification involves first using a deep neural network
to generate a 14-dimensional vector of features for each frame in a video,
and then utilizing these features in a CRF-MPRNN model to identify and track
vertebrae. By comparing our method with alternative models, we demonstrate
improved identification rates with 98.53%, 97.15% and 97.11% better than the
models based on long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural networks and
recurrent neural networks, respectively.

We investigated the emergence of electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations within
the context of microcavity polariton physics. In a cavity-based system containing
GaAs quantum dots as light-emitting sources, these polariton states are generated.
A comprehensive study revealed that the significant energy gaps present in the
system's quantum dots lead to the rapid depletion of polariton pairs through the
process of polariton-pair stimulated emission, resulting in the polaritons'
instability within the system. Furthermore, within a particular parameter range,
the application of an external polarized laser field can induce a dynamically
stable polariton state that solely emits single photons. This phenomenon is
attributed to the highly suppressed rate at which polariton fluctuations arise,
accompanied by a balanced rate at which these fluctuations are absorbed and an
overwhelming rate at which they are emitted. The flip-principle is applied to
determine the parameters that influence the appearance of this stable state,
thereby allowing for a deeper understanding of the underlying physics involved.

In the field of robotics, particularly for active legged locomotion, spring-based actuators demonstrate significant advantages, including efficient energy storage and release, enhanced force capabilities, improved compactness, and reduced weight. Utilizing universal universal springs to create robotic actuators poses technical limitations, however, due to the universal spring's defined displacement and rotation capabilities, which may not effectively match the requirements of the robot. In this paper, a novel approach is presented to design a universal spring that can be easily adapted to various robots, enabling user-defined positions and rotations while enabling online adjustment of the spring to accommodate changing robot configurations. We provide the mathematical framework for this method and illustrate the concept using a robotic foot example. Additionally, we outline the process for manufacturing the universal spring. In a practical application, we design and produce a spring for a robotic dog named M6, a 15 kg robot featuring 8 degrees of freedom and four spring-actuated legs. We also showcase the designed spring's performance in comparison to a traditional spring used in the same robot.

This research uses the full separability problem of quantum states to illustrate how noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices can be utilized in solving complex mathematical issues. By carrying out experiments on the described devices, we investigate the effectiveness of different methods in solving separability problems. Our analysis involves examining the ability of NISQ devices running the quantum algorithm to correctly identify fully separable states, as well as how device noise affects the results. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of this quantum algorithm in taking advantage of the devices' inherent properties to achieve precise solutions.

In a magnetized, electron-ionatized plasma with a guided magnetic field, the controlled growth of micro-instabilities is studied. Specifically, the focus is on a unique tearing parity instability characterized by a Hall effect that differentiates it from its general Sweet-Parker equivalent. This distinct tearing parity instability has properties such that its magnetic energy density and electron entropy increase exponentially over time, despite remaining relatively undetectable in terms of electron temperature via ion velocity measurements. Interestingly, the instability shows a pronounced response to specific, fine-scale variations in its magnetic field, while its growth is sensitive to the physical constraints of the system. This study provides an analytical description of the controlled growth of the tearing parity instability, providing insight into a previously underappreciated aspect of the general Sweet-Parker instability and its behavior in restricted geometries.

A fundamental task in the realm of fashion technology, fashion instance-level image retrieval (FIR) is crucial for enabling users to find similar items like outfits and styles. The existing few approaches to FIR are either plagued by low query response time or compromised as trade-offs in terms of accuracy. This limitation in current methods is attributed to their reliance on the precise localization of items in images, the reliance on hand-tuned parameters for constructing the indexing codebook, and the reliance on computational heavy methods like convolutional neural networks for extracting visual features. Our novel contribution, Fashion-CAPs, is a real-time capable model that accurately captures the complex visual patterns in clothing items, which are utilized to develop a new approach to indexing that requires minimal adjustments. The evaluation of our model reveals its superiority over state-of-the-art models, including a 24.8% improvement in query accuracy over the best alternative. Furthermore, our approach is capable of processing images within 0.5 ms on a typical GPU, making it highly practical for real-time applications. A live demonstration of our model's performance can be accessed at the link https://research.styletechlabs.com/research/fashion-cap/.

We investigate the application of the signorini method, an optimization technique, to address ill-posed gradient flow equations. This involves regularizing problems that don't have a well-defined solution, let alone a way to track a solution over time. Our signorini method integrates discrete in time versions of the problem that incorporate a stopping time, which significantly impacts the accuracy of the approximation. By varying the stopping time and choosing an approximate solution at that point, one can yield a tight theoretical bound on the error. However, choosing the stopping time is a critical task. Our work focuses on two approaches to selecting this time, both of which involve proving convergence, albeit with differing rates. Ultimately, these methods are tested computationally to provide further insight into their performance.

We introduce a fully automatic method to convert a raw video into 3D point clouds, enabling reliable object detection and motion analysis even with partial visibility. Existing depth estimation techniques typically require annotated reference points or rely on pre-existing 3D models, which are not suitable for video-based applications. To overcome these limitations, our approach uses geometric constraints and eliminates the need for complex annotations or models by incorporating a minimal amount of hand-designed shape primitives. We define a cost constructor that adapts to changing objects in real-time, combining implicit object geometry and occlusion for unbiased depth calculation. This approach enables seamless object switching and validates our method's robustness. We evaluate our method's performance using Video Dataset I and II, demonstrating superior results compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The implementation details can be accessed on our GitHub repository.

The Fokas-Lenells equation, a nonlocal integrable generalization of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I equation, is equivalently expressed in terms of boundary values on a horn shape geometry. Using boundary element methods, we formulate the direct map for exact solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation by combining recently developed boundary elements with a linear IE of the sine-Lenells equation, thereby circumventing the need for the $Q$ function. This approach is specifically applied to the case of zero mass in the Fokas-Lenells equation and reveals connections to the massive Thirring model at various levels of nonlocality.

An alternative framework for describing various gravity theories is proposed by embedding them in double field theory. DFT provides a framework for a broad range of gravity theories by effectively encoding them as solutions to specific equations of motion. This paper presents a unified formulation for certain non-Riemannian gravity theories, including Regge calculus and spin gravity. By embedding these theories in DFT, we are able to derive equivalent forms of the equations of motion and identify novel insights into their properties. Additionally, we explore Regge calculus in the context of deformed analogs of gauge theory. Our analysis in DFT offers a fresh perspective on the non-Riemannian geometry underlying these theories, highlighting both the strengths and limitations of the framework.

This research introduces a channel load-aware association mechanism for home WiFi networks to enhance overall performance and quality of service. To achieve this, we propose a non-intrusive and low-cost method using IoT devices with functional firmware to collect and share real-time data on channel load, allowing a central controller to make informed decisions on association. These IoT devices can be introduced as typical home devices with no additional cost, without requiring modification to existing equipment. We also suggest a strategy for effectively collecting and sharing data on channel load. We evaluate the performance of this approach through simulations, comparing it against a base scenario where devices associate based on signal strength. These simulations show that the proposed mechanism leads to improved network performance and quality of service, outperforming association based on signal strength metrics.
